1.0 Course roadmap — what L1 previews (L1)

🎯
Your practice set for L1 (your file w10): 50 questions · 12 easy · 28 medium · 10 hard. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 1.

Added after checking your practice set for L1 (file w10). About a third of that set asks about this roadmap, so it is worth one read.

  • Course objective: give an overall picture of what cloud computing is, its major components and the recent trends. The first lectures introduce the NIST model, properties and characteristics. Then come architecture, service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS — “anything as a service”, XaaS) and deployment models, with the stack “moving towards SOA”.
  • SLA = agreement between service provider and consumer.
    • The consumer wants a guarantee of minimal services.
    • The provider must work out the back-end resources needed to honour it.
    • Example: during an exam, availability must be ≈ 100 % (redundant services); during a practice session the requirement may come down. The provider sizes resources, and charges, according to the availability promised. Higher availability → more resources → higher price.
  • Cloudonomics (economics of cloud) asks: is the cloud always beneficial, i.e. buy or hire resources?
    • Analogy: if you commute a long way every day, buying a car pays off. If you drive 50–100 km once a month, hiring is cheaper.
    • So for occasional or spiky demand, hire (cloud).
  • Resource management is mainly a provider-side problem. Resources: CPU, RAM, disk, network connectivity.
    • Over-provisioning → idle resources → extra cost.
    • Under-provisioning → starvation.
    • Analogy: a stationery shop must neither run out of stock nor overflow. Getting this right is a “serious challenge”.
  • Data management: is the conventional DBMS approach still good for cloud? Storage as a service, e.g. Dropbox: what has to be managed in the background.
  • Security — the data and the computation sit in someone else’s domain.
    • “You can reinstall an application or OS, but you cannot reinstall your data.”
    • Issues: infrastructure security, data/storage security, identity and access management (IAM), access control (e.g. role-based access control).
    • Trust, reputation and risk are the “three nodes of a triangle”: they are interlinked.
  • Case studies/demos: open-source and commercial clouds, possibly a cloud simulator.
  • Recent trends (fog computing etc.) and research opportunities: pointers for UG/PG projects and research.
  • VANET (example of an ad-hoc distributed system): vehicles form a short-lived network for safety-related and infotainment services.

1.1 What “computing” means and how cloud evolved (L1–L2)

Core concept

  • Computing (ACM Computing Curricula, 2005): any goal-oriented activity requiring, benefiting from, or creating computers — hardware/software systems for a wide range of purposes, making computing systems intelligent, using communications, finding and gathering information.
  • Cloud computing is not a brand-new invention; it evolved from earlier paradigms that each solved a need:

Centralized (mainframe) → Distributed computing → Grid computing / Cluster computing → Utility computing (concept) → Cloud computing (practical realization of utility computing)

The lecture stresses these did not appear strictly one after another; they are different aspects that together made cloud feasible. Distributed computing is called the “mother” of them all.

Distributed computing

  • Definition: a field of computer science that studies distributed systems; use of distributed systems to solve computational problems.
  • A distributed system = several autonomous computational entities, each with its own local memory, that communicate by message passing over a communication network.
  • OS view: processors communicate over communication lines (high-speed buses, telephone lines); each processor has its own local memory.
  • Examples: the Internet, ATM/bank networks, intranets/workgroups, ad-hoc networks such as VANETs (vehicular ad-hoc networks), ubiquitous network-connected devices.
  • Typical nodes: workstations (end-user computing), server systems (provide resources/services), personal assistance devices (handheld devices on wireless networks).

Common properties / benefits of distributed systems

Property Meaning
Fault tolerance Works (maybe at lower performance) even if some nodes fail — unlike a centralized system where one failure stops everything
Each node plays a partial role Work is divided across nodes
Resource sharing Nodes share resources
Load sharing / load balancing Work can be distributed among nodes
Easy to expand Add more systems to the network as needed
Performance Parallel computing is considered a subset of distributed computing

Why distributed systems are needed: (1) nature of the application demands it, (2) performance — compute-intensive or data-intensive workloads, (3) robustness — no single point of failure; tasks of a failed node can be executed by other nodes.

Distributed applications: a set of processes distributed across a network that work together as an ensemble to solve a common problem (needs orchestration). Forms: client–server (resource management centralized at the server; a server can itself be a client of another server) and peer-to-peer (a move toward truly distributed applications built from peer processes).

Grid computing

Three definitions given in the lecture (all examinable):

  1. A form of networking that, unlike conventional networks focused on communication among devices, harnesses unused processing cycles of all computers in a network to solve problems too intensive for a standalone machine.
  2. Grid computing enables virtualization of distributed computing and data resources (processing, network bandwidth, storage) to create a single system image, giving users and applications seamless access to vast IT capabilities. (This is a key stepping stone to cloud.)
  3. A computing infrastructure that provides dependable, consistent, pervasive and inexpensive access to computational capabilities.
  • Analogy: the electrical power grid — users tap computing resources (processors, storage, data, applications) as needed, with little or no knowledge of where they are located.
  • Characteristics: efficient use of (often under-utilized) resources across organizations — e.g., UG/PG lab PCs pooled after lab hours for research via a middleware layer; joining local communities (biology, genetics etc.); interaction with underlying layers must be transparent and seamless to the user; get resources without having to purchase, install and maintain them.
  • Who uses it: mainly the scientific community — physics, weather, material science, reactor applications; data analysis/visualization, simulation and modelling, collaboration across continents; exploiting under-utilized resources.

Types of grids

Grid type Focus
Computational grid Computing power (processing cycles)
Data grid Data storage/access
Collaborative grid Collaboration among users/groups
Network grid Fault-tolerant, high-performance communication services
Utility grid Not only data and cycles but software or just about any resource is shared

Grid players: the grid itself, users, groups, heterogeneous sites (resource locations), and policies (what can be shared, where things run).

Cluster computing

  • Definition: a type of parallel or distributed system consisting of a collection of interconnected stand-alone computers working together as a single integrated computing resource.
  • Key components: stand-alone computers (PCs, workstations, SMPs), operating systems, high-performance interconnects, middleware, parallel programming environments, applications.
  • Deployed to improve speed and/or reliability over a single computer.
  • Typical properties: network is faster/closer than a typical LAN; low-latency communication protocols; more loosely coupled than SMPs.
Cluster type Purpose
High-availability (failover) cluster If a node fails, others take over
Load-balancing cluster Distributes load across nodes
Parallel/distributed processing cluster Runs parallel and distributed jobs

Operational benefits: system availability, fault tolerance, scalability, OS and application reliability, high performance.

Utility computing

  • Utility = get something as and when you need it, without caring how it is produced (railway/flight ticket via an agent, plumbing via an office).
  • Definition: a service provisioning model in which a service provider makes computing resources and infrastructure management available to the customer as needed, and charges for specific usage rather than a flat rate.
  • Named by analogy with electricity (metered; you don’t care how power is generated) and telecom/mobile services.
  • Pricing: pay-per-use / pay-as-you-go, metered.
  • Utility computing is “purely a concept which cloud computing practically implements.”
  • Viewed as a form of virtualization: storage/computing available appears much larger than any single system (“open the tap when needed, close it when not”).
  • Data-center virtualization and provisioning: carve customized virtual instances (e.g., a VM with 16 GB RAM) from a large pool; solves the resource-utilization problem, enables outsourcing and service-level delivery, and allows automation (workflows).
  • Shift noted in the lecture: from a data-driven architecture to a service-driven architecture.
  • Example — on-demand cyber infrastructure: temporary infrastructure for an online exam, a conference/event, or disaster management (real time) — provision when needed, release after.

Provider–consumer issues that tie them together: pricing, SLA (availability, downtime), security (incl. DoS protection), access mechanisms, application sizing (size the application to my need).

Payment models: flat rate, tiered, subscription, and customized pricing per customer based on scale, commitment, payment frequency. “The pricing model is simply an expression of the provider’s costs.”

Risks of utility computing (all five are list-type MCQ material):

  1. Data backup — what if the provider crashes or goes out of business?
  2. Data security — is someone else reading my data?
  3. Competence — is the provider competent?
  4. Defining SLA — each side wants it in their favour; no standard approach.
  5. Getting value from charge-back.

These evolved into the full cloud computing model.

MCQ traps (1.1)

  • Grid = harnessing unused cycles / single system image across organizations; Cluster = interconnected stand-alone computers acting as one integrated resource, usually tightly managed, low latency. Don’t swap the definitions.
  • “Clusters are more loosely coupled than SMPs” — true (an SMP is tightly coupled shared memory).
  • Utility computing is a concept/business model; cloud computing is its practical realization.
  • Parallel computing is a subset of distributed computing (lecture’s view), not the other way round.
  • Distributed-system nodes have their own local memory and communicate by message passing (not shared memory).

Quick revision (1.1)

  • Evolution: distributed → grid & cluster → utility → cloud.
  • Grid analogy = electric grid; cluster types = HA/failover, load balancing, parallel processing.
  • Utility computing = metered, pay-as-you-go, charges for usage not flat rate.
  • Five risks of utility computing: backup, security, competence, SLA definition, charge-back value.

1.2 NIST definition and characteristics of cloud (L2–L3)

NIST definition (memorize the structure)

Cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.

Key phrases tested: shared pool, configurable, rapidly provisioned and released, minimal management effort or service-provider interaction → this is what makes pay-as-you-go possible (provision when needed, de-provision when not).

Five essential characteristics (NIST)

Characteristic What it means (lecture wording)
On-demand self-service Consumer provisions resources as needed, by itself
Broad network access Resources are geographically distributed and pooled, so good network access is essential; accessed through standard clients
Resource pooling Resources pooled to serve many consumers — a multi-tenant model, physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned (e.g., one user gets a Windows VM, another an Ubuntu VM from the same provider)
Rapid elasticity Scale up and down quickly (e.g., grow a VM from 4 GB to 8 GB RAM while a simulation needs it, then shrink)
Measured service Usage is metered — “I pay for what I use”

NIST model also has 3 service models (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS) and 4 deployment models (private, public, hybrid, community). (Standard NIST structure; the lecture presents all of these.)

Common characteristics (beyond NIST) listed in L3

Massive scale · resilient computing · homogeneity (user sees homogeneous resources even if back end is heterogeneous) · geographic distribution · virtualization · service orientation · low-cost software (multi-tenancy lowers cost per consumer) · advanced security (access control, attack blocking, no data loss).

Advantages of cloud (L3 list)

Lower computing cost · improved performance · reduced software costs · instant software updates · improved document-format compatibility · (theoretically) unlimited storage · increased data reliability (distributed with redundancy) · universal information access · latest versions available · easier group collaboration · device independence.

Disadvantages of cloud (L3 list)

Requires a constant Internet connection · does not work well with low-speed connections · features may be limited · can be slow (provisioning takes time) · stored data might not be secure · stored data can be lost (crash, provider exit) · cloud is not truly a high-performance computing (HPC) system · general concerns (APIs, database connectivity).

Why cloud-sourcing is becoming important

High-scale/low-cost providers · anytime-anyplace access via web browser · rapid scalability, incremental cost and load sharing · (but you still need to focus on local IT).

Concerns with cloud-sourcing: performance, reliability and SLAs · control of data and service parameters (how is “95 % availability” audited?) · application features and choices (fixed, not customized) · interaction between cloud providers · no standard API (SOAP vs REST mix) · security, privacy, compliance, trust, competence.

Cloud storage: data stored remotely and temporarily cached on desktops, phones and other Internet-linked devices (sync); examples cited: Amazon EC2/S3, Dropbox.

MCQ traps (1.2)

  • There are five NIST essential characteristics. “Virtualization”, “multi-tenancy” and “service orientation” are not among the five (multi-tenancy is how resource pooling is achieved; virtualization is a common characteristic/enabler).
  • Elasticity ≠ scalability alone: elasticity includes scaling down/release as well as up.
  • “Cloud is a high-performance computing system” → False per lecture.
  • “Cloud works well with low-speed connections” → False.

Quick revision (1.2)

  • NIST: 5 characteristics + 3 service models + 4 deployment models.
  • Mnemonic for the 5 characteristics: “O-B-R-R-M” → On-demand self-service, Broad network access, Resource pooling, Rapid elasticity, Measured service.

1.3 Service-Oriented Architecture view (L3–L5)

  • Cloud’s major aim is to realize a service-oriented architecture (SOA).
  • SOA triangle: service provider publishes to a registry/catalogue → service consumer looks up (finds) the service in the registry → consumer binds/invokes the provider. Registry is distributed but logically centralized. Analogy: telephone directory / yellow pages.
  • Client–server (legacy) vs SOA: client–server is tightly bound (every service needs its matching client and server program); SOA lets heterogeneous services talk to each other with more flexibility. (Detailed SOA/Web services: Week 2, L10.)

Client–server model details (L5)

  • Server process listens on a well-known port (e.g., httpd on port 80; also ftpd, telnetd); client connects to that port. Client and server can be the same or different machines.
  • Concurrent server (serves many clients at once) vs iterative server (one after another).
  • Request–response messaging; clients often thin; server may be a load-balanced cluster or standalone.
  • Realizes a three-tier architecture: presentation (top) → logic → data (bottom).

Client–server vs cloud (L5 comparison — classic MCQ)

Aspect Client–server Cloud
Service model Simple: server serves client requests Variety of complex models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS…)
Load balancing May or may not be load balanced Load balanced
Scalability Scalable to some extent (in a cluster) Theoretically infinitely scalable
Virtualization No concept of virtualization Virtualization is the core concept

1.4 Service models — IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, XaaS (L3–L5)

Core concept

Model What the consumer gets Typical components in the lecture’s stack
IaaS Raw infrastructure — servers, storage, network, OS — on demand, usually as VMs Virtual machines, servers, storage, load balancers, network
PaaS A virtualized development and runtime platform to build, test, deploy, host apps Execution runtime, database, web server, development tools, sandbox
SaaS Ready-to-use application over the Internet, pay-as-you-go/subscription CRM, email, virtual desktop, games, word processing, spreadsheets
BPaaS Horizontal or vertical business processes on a subscription basis Orchestrated processes/workflows (e.g., BPEL)
  • Transportation analogy (L5): roads = infrastructure; cars and trucks = platform; goods and people = software/information.
  • Client access: web browser (universal), mobile apps, thin clients, terminal emulators.

SaaS — characteristics, where useful, where not (L5)

Characteristics: web access to commercial software · software managed from a (logically) central location · delivered in a one-to-many model · users not required to handle upgrades/patches · APIs allow integration between pieces of software.

Useful when: significant interplay between the organization and the outside world (e.g., email, newsletter campaign software) · need for web and mobile access · software needed only for short-term use (e.g., a one-off online recruitment test) · demand spikes significantly (e.g., tax, billing at year end). Example: Salesforce CRM.

Not the best option when: extremely fast processing / real-time data is required (e.g., disaster management) · legislation or regulation does not permit data to be hosted externally · an existing on-premise solution already fulfils all needs.

PaaS — characteristics, where useful, where not (L5)

Characteristics: services to develop, test, deploy, host and maintain applications in the same integrated development environment · web-based UI tools to create/modify/test/deploy · multi-tenant architecture (many concurrent users use the same development application) · built-in scalability · integration with web services and databases · support for development-team collaboration · tools for billing and subscription management.

Useful when: multiple developers work on a project (possibly across countries) · external parties need to interact with the development process · developers want to automate testing and deployment · agile (iterative, incremental) development. Examples cited: Microsoft Azure, Google App Engine.

Not ideal when: the application must be highly portable in terms of where it is hosted · proprietary languages/approaches would impact development · a proprietary language would hinder later moves to another provider → vendor lock-in · application performance needs customization of underlying hardware and software.

IaaS — characteristics, where useful, where not (L5)

Characteristics: resources distributed as a service · dynamic scaling · variable cost (utility pricing) · multiple users on a single piece of hardware.

Useful when: demand is very volatile (spikes) · new organizations without capital to invest · pressure to limit capital expenditure · specific line-of-business, trial or temporary infrastructure needs (e.g., proof of concept).

Not the best option when: regulatory compliance makes outsourcing of storage/processing difficult · highest levels of performance are required and on-premise/dedicated infrastructure can meet them (virtualization layers consume some resources).

Provider comparison tables shown in L5 (recognition level)

  • SaaS providers differ in pricing model — some pay-as-you-go, some free, some subscription (e.g., pay per year).
  • PaaS providers differ in target use (e.g., .NET platform, web development, enterprise applications) and database offered (e.g., BigTable-based).
  • IaaS providers differ in hardware capacity, operating systems supported and billing mechanism.

Who manages what (responsibility split, L5)

Layer (bottom → top) IaaS PaaS SaaS
Networking, storage, servers Provider Provider Provider
Virtualization Provider Provider Provider
OS Consumer (provider may supply guest OS or let you choose) Provider Provider
Middleware, runtime Consumer Provider Provider
Data, applications Consumer Consumer Provider
  • SaaS: provider responsible up to the application.
  • PaaS: provider responsible up to the runtime; data and applications are the user’s.
  • IaaS: provider responsible up to virtualization/providing VMs.

Networking responsibility on the OSI stack (L5)

Model Provider responsible up to…
IaaS Data link layer (rest is consumer’s)
PaaS Presentation (sometimes session) layer
SaaS Whole stack

XaaS — “anything as a service”

  • XaaS = generalization of cloud services delivered over the Internet rather than locally; XaaS is the essence of cloud computing.
  • XaaS = Service-Oriented Infrastructure (SOI) + cloud computing.
  • Instances named in L4: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, BPaaS, storage-aaS, security-aaS, database-aaS, monitoring/management-aaS, communication/content/computing-aaS, identity-aaS, backup-aaS, desktop-aaS; also data-aaS and “science as a service” (L3).
  • XaaS fulfils the four demands of a service provider: broad network access, resource pooling, business-driven infrastructure on demand, service orientation.
  • BPaaS: a business process = orchestration/integration of sub-processes with timing relationships, forming a process execution graph/tree (e.g., P1, P2 → P3; P3, P4 → final output). Sub-processes may come from different heterogeneous providers. Language mentioned: BPEL (Business Process Execution Language).

MCQ traps (1.4)

  • Lecture examples: Amazon (EC2) → IaaS; Microsoft Azure → PaaS; Google Docs/spreadsheets → SaaS; Google App Engine → PaaS; Salesforce → SaaS (CRM). Use these classifications.

    ⚠️ Lecture vs today: Azure today also offers IaaS (VMs) and SaaS; for the exam follow the lecture’s classification (Azure = PaaS example).

  • “Users must handle upgrades in SaaS” → False (provider handles them).
  • Vendor lock-in is a PaaS concern listed in the lecture.
  • “IaaS is best when highest performance is needed” → False (dedicated/on-premise is better then).
  • Real-time/extremely fast processing → SaaS not suitable.
  • In PaaS, the consumer manages data and applications.

Quick revision (1.4)

  • Stack bottom→top: IaaS → PaaS → SaaS (→ BPaaS).
  • SaaS = one-to-many, no upgrades for user; PaaS = develop/test/deploy in one IDE, multi-tenant, team collaboration; IaaS = dynamic scaling, variable cost, multiple users on one hardware.
  • Each model has a “not suitable when” list — know them.

1.5 Deployment models (L3; detailed again in Week 2, L6)

Model Description Lecture example
Private Built and used by one organization Meghamala — IIT Kharagpur’s private cloud on open-source software, mainly IaaS for researchers; accessible only inside the IIT KGP network; no charge (institute funded)
Public Open to the public Amazon (IaaS), Microsoft Azure (PaaS), Google Docs (SaaS)
Community Shared by several organizations with common goals (“semi-public/semi-private”) Banking cloud (RBI as nodal agency), government-funded institutional cloud, geospatial cloud
Hybrid Mix — private + public, or with community —

1.6 Virtualization basics (L3; detailed in Week 2, L7)

  • Virtualization stack: bare-metal hardware → VMM (Virtual Machine Monitor) / hypervisor → multiple VMs, each with a guest OS and applications.
  • The VMM emulates the hardware; one physical machine (or several machines pooled together) can host multiple VMs of different specifications. (Pooled capacity cannot be split arbitrarily — virtualization has its own overhead/requirements.)
  • Virtual workspace: an abstraction of an execution environment that can be made dynamically available to authorized clients using well-defined protocols (e.g., a 14-day project environment).
  • Meghamala provisions three categories of VMs based on availability.
  • Popular VMMs/hypervisors cited: Xen, VMware.
  • Advantages of VMs: run an OS where physical hardware is unavailable · easier to create new machines and backups · software testing with clean installs · emulate more machines than are physically available · test/debug on many OSs.
  • Cloud and virtualization “come hand in hand”; performance of para-virtualization can be close to raw physical performance (Week 2).

1.7 Cloud computing architecture (L4–L5)

Three-level architectural view

Business goals → Quality attributes → Architectural tactics

Level Items (lecture lists)
Business goals (CSP’s view) TCO (total cost of ownership/to the organization), stakeholder satisfaction, compliance with standards, market share, flexibility
Quality attributes Availability, elasticity, interoperability, security, adaptability, performance, usability, maintainability
Architectural tactics Stateless design, loose coupling, heterogeneity handled via interconnection/homogeneity, caching, claims-based authentication

Major building blocks

  • Technical architecture: structuring according to the XaaS stack; adopting cloud paradigms; structuring cloud services and components; middleware and communication; management and security.
  • Deployment/operation architecture: geo-location check (legal/political — e.g., government data and mail servers must stay within the country’s territory); operation and monitoring.

Layered view

  • Bottom: storage and infrastructure → middle: middleware/platform (cloud runtime, libraries) → top: applications → client infrastructure interacts with applications.
  • Stakeholder views: IaaS → IT architects/IT operations; PaaS → software architects/developers; SaaS → end users/application administrators (e.g., CRM).
  • Microsoft Azure vs Amazon EC2 mapping: both split into infrastructure (Azure: Windows servers; Amazon: Windows/Linux + S3, SimpleDB), middleware/platform, and applications; client via browser (and Silverlight for Azure — historical).
  • Management, security (and QoS) are vertical stacks — they cut across all layers, so they need cross-layer consideration. How much the provider manages depends on the service model (IaaS: up to infrastructure; SaaS: up to the application).

Classic XaaS stack (bottom → top)

Networking · Storage · Servers (bare metal) → Virtualization (of machines, network, storage) → OS → Middleware → Runtime → Data → Applications

  • This is a logical representation (like OSI/TCP-IP), not a strict physical layering. Storage is often treated separately from other infrastructure because storage management is different.

Elasticity: scale up vs scale out (L4)

Vertical scale-up Horizontal scale-out
How Add more resources to the same box (more blades in a chassis, more RAM/CPU) Add more boxes/machines
Cost Probably cheaper for small scenarios Only solution for large scenarios — one 64-way server is much more expensive than 64 one-way servers
Failure Single box can be a single point of failure Failure of some nodes → work continues at lower performance

Legacy IT vs simplified (cloud) IT stack

  • Legacy: end-user devices, applications and dedicated infrastructure tightly coupled (application sized for the infrastructure).
  • Simplified/cloud: loosely bound layers → better resource utilization, better ROI, many services on a common resource base (e.g., pool idle lab PCs after hours).
  • Classical model: licensed software, hardware products, people-based services → XaaS model.

Broader cloud-service view (L5)

Infrastructure/operations (compute, network, storage) → services (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS) → business processes → presentation (user interfaces, APIs). Cross-cutting: integration (service orchestration/execution engine), QoS, information (service dissemination), governance (management + legal/policy compliance with federal laws).

Networking in cloud (L5)

  • Network is critical — blade/rack servers rely on highly redundant, high-speed backbone networks.
  • Network resources can be provisioned dynamically; the whole network can be virtualized (e.g., set up a virtual network for an event, then release it).
  • Concepts forming the core: VLAN, VPN, protocol layers; tools: OpenSSH, OpenVPN.
  • Network Function Virtualization (NFV): implement network functions in software running on industry-standard servers/switches/storage (possibly in data centers) that can be moved or instantiated at various locations without installing new equipment — consolidates many network equipment types.

MCQ traps (1.7)

  • Management and security are vertical/cross-layer, not confined to one layer.
  • “Scale-up is the only solution for large-scale scenarios” → False (scale-out is).
  • Geo-location check belongs to the deployment/operation architecture, not the technical architecture.
  • Claims-based authentication, stateless design, loose coupling, caching = architectural tactics, not quality attributes. Elasticity, availability, interoperability = quality attributes. TCO, market share = business goals.
  • NFV = network functions in software on standard hardware, not on new proprietary appliances.

Quick revision (1.7)

  • Business goals → quality attributes → architectural tactics.
  • Scale-up (vertical, cheaper small) vs scale-out (horizontal, only solution large; 64×1-way ≪ one 64-way).
  • Provider responsibility on OSI: IaaS → data link; PaaS → presentation/session; SaaS → all.
  • NFV = network functions as software on commodity servers.

Week 1 — High-yield takeaways

  1. NIST: 5 characteristics (on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service), 3 service models, 4 deployment models.
  2. Utility computing = concept (metered, pay-per-use); cloud = practical implementation.
  3. Cluster = interconnected stand-alone computers as one resource; Grid = harness unused cycles / single system image; analogy = electric grid.
  4. Client–server has no virtualization; cloud’s core is virtualization and it is (theoretically) infinitely scalable.
  5. SaaS not for real-time/extremely fast processing; PaaS has vendor lock-in risk; IaaS not when highest dedicated performance or regulation forbids outsourcing.
  6. Responsibility: IaaS provider up to virtualization; PaaS up to runtime; SaaS up to application.
  7. Scale-out beats scale-up for large systems; management and security are vertical stacks.

Week 2 — Deployment Models, Virtualization, XML, Web Services & SOA (Lectures 6–10)

Source: L6 Architecture – Deployment Models · L7 Virtualization · L8 XML Basics · L9 XML Basics (contd.) · L10 Web Services, Service Oriented Architecture

2.1 Deployment models in detail (L6)

🎯
Your practice set for L6 (your file w11): 50 questions · 11 easy · 27 medium · 12 hard · 1 with ⚠️ notes. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 2.

Public cloud

  • Infrastructure provisioned for open use by the general public; owned/managed/operated by a business, academic or government organization, or a combination.
  • Exists on the premises of the cloud provider (CSP).
  • Provider’s computing and storage resources are potentially large; communication is over the public Internet; serves a diverse pool of clients — some may be attackers.
  • Examples (lecture): Google App Engine, Microsoft Azure, IBM Cloud, Amazon EC2.

Characteristics / considerations of public cloud | Point | Explanation | |—|—| | Workload locations hidden from clients | You don’t know where your VM/data reside or with whom | | Risks from multi-tenancy | A single machine may be shared by workloads of any combination of subscribers — your workload may be co-resident with a competitor or adversary → reliability and security risk | | Network dependency | Always-available connectivity required | | Limited visibility and control over data (security) | You rely on SLA/MoU promises | | Elasticity: illusion of unlimited resource availability | Theoretically infinite scale up/down | | Low up-front cost to migrate into the cloud | Pay and use; nothing to buy/install | | Restrictive default SLAs | Small users must accept provider’s standard terms (large deployments may negotiate) |

Private cloud

  • Provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization comprising multiple consumers (e.g., business units).
  • May be owned, managed and operated by the organization, a third party, or a combination; may exist on or off premises.
  • “Contrary to popular belief, a private cloud may exist off premises and can be managed by a third party.”
  • Examples / software (lecture): Eucalyptus, OpenStack, Ubuntu Enterprise Cloud, Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud), VMware Cloud Infrastructure Suite, Microsoft ECI data center; IIT KGP’s Meghamala.
  • Two scenarios: on-site private cloud (at the customer’s premises — the “de facto” one) and outsourced private cloud (server side outsourced to a hosting company).

On-site private cloud

  • Security perimeter extends around both the subscriber’s on-site resources and the private cloud’s resources. The perimeter does not guarantee control over private-cloud resources, but the subscriber can exercise control over them.
  • Considerations: network dependency (on-site) · subscriber still needs IT skills · workload locations hidden from clients · risk from multi-tenancy (among the organization’s own units) · data import/export and performance limitations (bulk import/export limited by on-site network capacity; real-time critical processing may be problematic) · potentially strong security from external threats (inherits the organization’s network security, e.g., Meghamala inside IIT KGP’s network) · significant-to-high up-front costs to migrate · limited resources — a fixed computing and storage capacity sized for anticipated workloads (e.g., buy 1.5× expected need and you are capped at 1.5×).

Outsourced private cloud

  • Has two security perimeters — one implemented by the subscriber, one by the provider — joined by a protected communication link. Security depends on the strength and availability of both perimeters and of the link.
  • Considerations: network dependency · workload locations hidden · risk from multi-tenancy (provider may host others’ private clouds) · data import/export & performance limitations · potentially strong security from external threats · modest-to-significant up-front costs · SLA must be negotiated with the provider · extensive resource availability (provider has a large back-end pool).

Community cloud

  • Provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organizations with shared concerns (mission, security requirements, policy, compliance considerations).
  • Owned/managed/operated by one or more community organizations, a third party, or a combination; may be on or off premises.
  • An organization can belong to several communities (like being in both an office group and a residential community); communities can form and dissolve over time.
  • Participant organizations are connected via links between boundary controllers, allowing access through their security perimeters.
  • Access policy can be complex (prevent leakage between communities) → policy specification techniques: RBAC (role-based access control) and ABAC (attribute-based access control).
  • On-site community considerations: network dependency · subscribers still need IT skills · workload locations hidden · data import/export & performance limitations · potentially strong security from external threats · highly variable up-front costs.
  • Outsourced community considerations: network dependency · workload locations hidden · risk from multi-tenancy · data import/export & performance limitations · potentially strong security from external threats · modest-to-significant up-front costs · extensive resource availability.

Hybrid cloud

  • Composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private, community or public) that remain unique entities but are bound together by standardized or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability.
  • Why: classify data/applications by sensitivity — e.g., keep student records/exam data private, run practice lab sessions on public cloud; or temporarily rent public capacity when the private cloud is short (buying for a private cloud takes a long time). (The second pattern is commonly called “cloud bursting” — clarification, term not used in lecture.)
  • Portability/interoperability of data and applications across the constituents must be handled (applications may need resizing).
  • Examples (lecture): Windows Azure (capable of hybrid), VMware vCloud.
  • Considerations: significant variation in performance, reliability and security depending on constituent clouds · can be extremely complex · may change over time as constituent clouds join or leave (subscriptions end, pricing changes, providers disappear).

Choosing a deployment model

Depends on requirements: small organizations/individuals → public cloud is often fine; mission-critical clients (financial, defence) may demand private infrastructure; or classify applications/data into categories and place each in private/public/community accordingly (managing this is itself a challenge).

Comparison table (high-yield)

Model Up-front cost to migrate Resource availability Security from external threats Typical location
Public Low Illusion of unlimited (elastic) Multi-tenancy risk; limited visibility Provider’s premises
On-site private Significant to high Limited (fixed capacity) Potentially strong Customer’s premises
Outsourced private Modest to significant Extensive Potentially strong (two perimeters + link) Hosting company
On-site community Highly variable Limited Potentially strong Participant premises
Outsourced community Modest to significant Extensive Potentially strong Third party
Hybrid Depends on constituents Mix Varies — can be extremely complex Mix

MCQ traps (2.1)

  • “A private cloud must be on-premises and managed by the organization” → False.
  • “Extensive resource availability” is a property of outsourced private/community clouds, not on-site private clouds (those have limited resources).
  • Low up-front cost belongs to public cloud; on-site private has significant-to-high.
  • Outsourced private cloud = two security perimeters.
  • Workload locations are hidden from clients in all these models (even on-site private — hidden from the organization’s own client units).
  • RBAC/ABAC are mentioned for community cloud access policies.
  • Hybrid constituents remain unique entities — they are not merged into one cloud.

2.2 IaaS and virtualization architecture (L7)

What an IaaS subscriber gets and pays for

  • Gets: access to virtual computers, network-accessible virtual storage, network infrastructure components (e.g., firewalls, configuration services).
  • Pays (typically): per CPU-hour, per GB of data stored per hour, network bandwidth consumed, network infrastructure used (e.g., IP addresses), and value-added services (monitoring, automatic scaling).
  • Providers keep a large pool of VMs in a few flavours (e.g., Meghamala offers three: IITKGP — 4 GB RAM, 20 GB disk; IITKGP Large — 8 GB RAM; IITKGP Extra Large — larger RAM). The mix of flavours depends on back-end capacity and the type of requests received. Different clients get disjoint VMs (A: VM1–VM2, B: VM3, C: VM4–VM6; provider retains VM7–VMn for others).

IaaS component stack and scope of control

  • Stack: hardware → operating system → middleware → applications.
  • The OS level is split into two: the lower, most privileged layer is the VMM/hypervisor; the higher layer is the guest OS running inside a VM.
Layer Cloud provider Cloud subscriber
Hardware Total control No control
Hypervisor (VMM) Administrative control Makes requests (e.g., for VMs)
Guest OS No control Total control (can load any OS the provider supports)
Middleware (e.g., Java) No control Total control
Applications (mail, CRM…) No control Total control

Rule: control of upper layers moves to the subscriber; control of lower layers stays with the provider.

  • The hypervisor uses the hardware to synthesize one or more VMs — each an “efficient, isolated duplicate of a real machine.” To the subscriber the VM appears as actual hardware that can be powered on/off and have peripherals configured via commands sent over the network.

IaaS cloud architecture — 3-level hierarchy (very examinable)

Cloud Manager (top) → Cluster Managers (middle) → Computer Managers (bottom, one per computer, running the hypervisor + VMs) Supporting stores: Data Object Storage (DOS) at the cloud-manager level; Persistent Local Storage (PLS) at the cluster-manager level.

Component Level Responsibilities
Cloud Manager (CLM) Top — central control Public access point of the cloud; subscribers sign up for accounts and manage rented resources; authenticates subscribers; generates/validates access credentials used to communicate with VMs; top-level resource management — decides whether the cloud has enough free resources for a request; maintains metadata. Can be geographically distributed.
Data Object Storage (DOS) With cloud manager Stores subscriber metadata (user credentials, OS images, etc.); usually a single DOS service per cloud — acts like the cloud’s registry/catalogue
Cluster Manager (CM) Middle Operates a collection of computers connected by a high-speed LAN (clusters may be geographically distant from each other); receives allocation commands/queries from the cloud manager and calculates whether part or all of a command can be satisfied by its cluster; queries computer managers for availability and reports back; instructs computer managers to allocate, reconfigure, de-allocate resources
Persistent Local Storage (PLS) Connected to cluster manager Provides persistent, disk-like storage to VMs — data survives VM shutdown/de-provisioning
Computer Manager Bottom — runs on each computer Uses virtualization to provide VMs to subscribers; maintains status (e.g., how many VMs are running); uses the command interface to the hypervisor to start, suspend and reconfigure VMs

Flow: subscriber queries/commands enter at the top and are forwarded down the layers, which answer queries or execute commands.

⚠️ Transcript slip: one line of L7 says “cloud manager runs on each computer system”; from context (and the slide it describes) this is the computer manager. Use: computer manager runs on each computer.

Virtualization — core concept

  • Virtualization is not new (VLAN, VPN, running Linux on Windows); cloud exploits it.
  • Definition (lecture): virtualization allows one computer to do the job of multiple computers by sharing the resources of a single hardware across multiple environments.
  • Non-virtualized: a single OS controls all hardware platform resources. Virtualized: multiple virtual containers run on a single physical platform.
  • Virtualization vs dual boot: in dual boot only one OS runs at a time; with virtualization all OSs run simultaneously and are completely isolated from each other.
  • A hypervisor runs the guest OS directly on the CPU — this works if the guest uses the same instruction set as the host; otherwise instruction translation is needed.

Popek and Goldberg (1974) — requirements for virtualization

Three goals of a virtual machine architecture: | Property | Meaning | |—|—| | Equivalence | The VM should be indistinguishable from the underlying hardware | | Resource control | The VM (VMM) should be in complete control of the virtualized resources | | Efficiency | Most VM instructions should execute directly on the underlying CPU without involving the hypervisor |

Instruction classification:

  • Privileged instructions — cause a trap if executed in user mode.
  • Sensitive instructions — change underlying resources (e.g., do I/O, change page tables) [control-sensitive], or observe information indicating the current privilege level / that the guest isn’t on bare metal [behaviour-sensitive].

Theorem (key result): A VMM with all three properties can be built if the set of sensitive instructions is a subset of the set of privileged instructions.

  • Intuition: every sensitive instruction then traps to the VMM, which can emulate it safely; everything else runs directly (efficiency).
  • Lower privilege rings (ring 0) are closer to bare metal; the higher the level at which virtualization operates, the more translation and latency.

Approaches to (server) virtualization — the three generations

Full virtualization (1st gen) Para-virtualization (2nd gen) Hardware-assisted virtualization (3rd gen)
Technique Binary rewriting / dynamic binary translation; software-based; all hardware emulated, including the CPU Cooperative virtualization; guest OS is modified Silicon-based; VMM uses processor extensions (Intel VT, AMD-V) to intercept privileged operations
Guest OS Unmodified Modified — kernel recompiled; para-virtualized drivers installed; guest runs kernel at ring 1 (or 3) and is aware of virtualization; uses a specialized API to talk to the VMM Unmodified; guest OS runs at ring 0
Examples VMware, Microsoft; emulators QEMU, Bochs VMware, Xen VMware and Xen on virtualization-aware hardware
Pros Emulation layer isolates VMs; total VM portability (only the VMM needs to understand it) Better performance — privileged-instruction translation by VMM no longer necessary Runs unmodified OS; removes many problems of writing a VMM
Cons Performance price of hardware emulation; x86 kernels expect ring 0 Requires modifying/recompiling the OS kernel Speed and flexibility issues; loses VM portability (VM tied to hardware that supports the extensions)

Network virtualization (L7)

  • Emulate one or more virtual networks over a given physical network.
  • Why: the Internet is “ossified” (hard to change); hard to design a one-size-fits-all architecture → instead let “all sizes fit into one”; provides a test bed for future networking research.
  • Not new: builds on VPNs, active and programmable networks, overlay networks.
  • Characterization: networking technology (IP-based, ATM-based), layer of virtualization, architectural domain (network resource management, spawning networks), level of virtualization (node level, full virtualization).
  • Business model players: infrastructure providers, service providers, end users, brokers (complex relationships; same model applies to other virtualization). Several service providers (SP1, SP2) can create different virtual networks on one infrastructure provider’s network.
  • Server-level (IaaS) virtualization + network virtualization together → a virtualized IT infrastructure (e.g., a geographically spread test with its own network).

MCQ traps (2.2)

  • Para-virtualization modifies the guest OS; hardware-assisted does not; full virtualization does not (it translates binaries instead).
  • Popek–Goldberg condition is sensitive ⊆ privileged (not the reverse).
  • Equivalence = indistinguishable from hardware; efficiency = most instructions run directly on the CPU.
  • QEMU and Bochs are emulators / full-virtualization tools (lecture).
  • Full virtualization gives total VM portability; hardware-assisted loses portability.
  • In IaaS the provider has administrative control over the hypervisor and total control over hardware; the subscriber has total control over guest OS and above.
  • DOS = metadata store, usually one per cloud (at cloud-manager level); PLS = persistent disk-like storage for VMs (at cluster level). Don’t swap them.

Quick revision (2.2)

  • IaaS billing: CPU-hour, GB-stored-hour, bandwidth, infrastructure (IPs), value-added services.
  • Hierarchy: Cloud manager (authenticate, credentials, top-level allocation, DOS) → Cluster manager (cluster-level feasibility, instructs computer managers, PLS) → Computer manager (one per machine; starts/suspends/reconfigures VMs via hypervisor).
  • Generations: full (binary translation) → para (modified guest, faster) → hardware-assisted (Intel VT/AMD-V, unmodified guest, ring 0).

2.3 XML basics (L8–L9)

Why XML matters for cloud

Cloud services (XaaS) must interoperate regardless of where/how they are hosted → web services/SOA, whose basic building block is XML. SOAP, WSDL and UDDI are all XML documents.

Core properties of XML (eXtensible Markup Language)

Property Meaning
Data transformation / exchange language Unlike HTML (data display/presentation), XML represents and transforms data to achieve interoperation
Text-based syntax Written in printable Unicode characters; no explicit binary data
Extensible You define your own elements/tags (HTML has a fixed, predefined tag set) — within syntax rules
Universal format Syntax rules ensure all XML processing software handle a given XML data identically — if you can read/process it, so can everyone else
Hierarchical, structured Forms an XML tree
Strict syntax To eliminate syntax errors
Self-describing data Tags describe the data
Designed for distributed environments Data from many sources can be mixed (e.g., combine academic-section and activity data to find the best all-rounder)

Parsing: well-formed vs valid

  • An XML parser extracts the information for the XML-based application (parser → parser interface → application).
  • Well-formed = syntactically correct. This is the minimum requirement to be XML. If the data is not well-formed, the parser must stop processing and throw an exception to the application.
  • Valid = well-formed AND conforms to a DTD or XML Schema. → All valid XML documents are well-formed; not all well-formed documents are valid.
  • DTD (Document Type Declaration/Definition): declares the document’s structure (like a relational table schema).
  • Internal entities (defined in the document’s DTD) vs external entities (referenced by a URL). The parser checks each entity is well-formed, then replaces every entity reference by the referenced entity, recursively, and hands the resolved data to the application.
  • What if an external entity can’t be found (e.g., firewall blocks it)? Depends on the parser type:
Parser type Behaviour
Validating parser Must retrieve all entities and process all DTD content; stops and indicates failure if it cannot
Non-validating parser Tries to retrieve entities, but ceases processing DTD content at the first entity it cannot find
  • Validating parsers are slower than non-validating ones (must check conformance first).
  • Character-set rules: XML specifies which characters may be whitespace (e.g., EBCDIC NEL cannot be used as whitespace); mechanisms exist to include characters outside the encoding.

DTD vs XML Schema (XSD)

DTD XML Schema (XSD)
Origin Part of core XML spec New specification (2001)
Written in Non-XML syntax Written in XML itself — schema handled like XML data
Power Structure only More powerful — data types (integer, date, real…), type validation, relating database schemas to XML models
Entities Can declare entities Cannot declare entities (only DTD can)
  • Both specify allowed elements and attributes, hierarchical nesting rules, element content and type restrictions. They contain no XML data — only structure.
  • Exchanging structure, not data: two organizations (e.g., IIT KGP and a bank) first agree on the schema — no privacy/maintenance issues of sharing data — then interoperate (even auto-create DB tables from the schema).

XML namespaces

  • Because tags are user-defined, the same name can mean different things — “table” (furniture vs word-processing), “key” (security key vs database key).
  • A namespace is a mechanism for identifying different spaces for XML names (element and attribute names) — a way of identifying different language dialects with specific semantics.
  • Declared with the special xmlns attribute; the namespace is given as a URL string, but the URL does not reference anything in particular (may point to nothing).
  • Prefixes let you mix dialects in one document (e.g., db:key vs sec:key; a prefix bound to the MathML namespace to embed MathML elements).

XML parser APIs (L9)

Parser Model Advantages Disadvantages
SAX (Simple API for XML) Event-based: reports events (tags, attributes, text nodes, unresolved external entities); programmer attaches event handlers Simple; very fast (as fast as you can stream data); low memory footprint; widely available Doesn’t do much for you; not useful for dynamically modifying a document in memory
DOM (Document Object Model) Object/tree-based: builds an in-memory tree of the whole document; methods to access and modify it Dynamic modification and access; querying that depends on tree structure; same interface for many languages (C++, Java) Slow; memory-intensive; programming interface not straightforward
JDOM (Java DOM) Java-based, object-oriented in-memory tree Like DOM, plus a much nicer OO interface Can be slow; Java only
DOM4J Java framework to read, write, navigate, edit XML Access to SAX, DOM, JDOM, XSLT; mixed SAX/DOM parsing; open-source (Apache-style licence) Java only; open-source concerns

Others: Xerces, XML Toolkit, XML for C++. Parser benchmarks compare speed, memory, stream processing.

XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations)

  • An XML language for processing XML data — tree transformation: takes XML + XSLT stylesheet → produces a new XML document with a different structure (filtering, extracting a sub-tree).
  • XML + styling ≈ displayable output (even HTML).
  • Pros: very useful for tree transformations. Cons: slow for large documents/stylesheets, difficult to debug, poor error detection.

XML messaging

  • Use XML as the format for messages between systems. Pros: common syntax, self-describing, easier to parse, can use existing transport mechanisms (HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP).
  • XML needs a carrier protocol; “transport” here means the carrier (e.g., HTTP), not the TCP/IP transport layer.
  • The XML message is embedded in an HTTP POST (HTTP is the envelope, XML the payload).
  • Message format standards: XML-RPC — very simple encoding of function/method calls; SOAP — more complex wrapper: specify schemas for interfaces, rules for handling and proxying messages; primarily used in web services/SOA.
  • XML family: XSL, XSLT, XPath, XPointer; dialects such as MathML, SVG (graphics); web-service protocols SOAP, WSDL, UDDI.

MCQ traps (2.3)

  • XML is not primarily a display language (that’s HTML); XML tags are user-defined.
  • Valid ⇒ well-formed, not the converse.
  • XSD is written in XML; DTD is not. XSD cannot declare entities.
  • A namespace URL need not point to any real resource.
  • SAX = event-based, fast, low memory, no in-memory tree; DOM = in-memory tree, slow, memory-hungry, good for modification.
  • Non-validating parser stops processing DTD content at the first unresolvable entity; validating parser fails.
  • XSLT produces XML (a transformed tree), not binary.

Quick revision (2.3)

  • Well-formed (syntax) → valid (+ DTD/XSD).
  • DTD (entities, non-XML) vs XSD (2001, XML, data types, no entities).
  • xmlns + prefixes resolve name clashes.
  • SAX (events) vs DOM (tree) vs JDOM (Java OO tree) vs DOM4J (Java, mixed).

2.4 Web services and Service-Oriented Architecture (L10)

Definitions of a web service (all three are used in MCQs)

  1. W3C: a software application identified by a URI, whose interfaces and bindings are capable of being defined, described and discovered as XML artifacts.
  2. Microsoft: programmable application logic accessible using standard Internet protocols.
  3. An interface that describes a collection of operations that are network-accessible through standardized XML messaging; software components that can be spontaneously discovered, combined and recombined to provide a solution to the user’s problem/request.

Common thread: XML-based, message-exchange, accessible by URI, loosely coupled (client–server is more tightly bound). The caller only cares where the service is and how to talk to it, not how it works internally — which also lets legacy applications talk to others.

Genesis

Structured programming → object-oriented programming; distributed computing; Electronic Data Interchange (EDI); World Wide Web.

  • Problem in distributed computing: interoperability (communicate and share data with software from different vendors/platforms) was limited in conventional proprietary technologies.

EDI (Electronic Data Interchange)

  • Computer-to-computer exchange of business data and documents between companies using standard formats recognized nationally and internationally. The format is agreed by both companies beforehand.
  • Advantages: lower operating cost, less human error/more accuracy (no re-entry), increased productivity, faster trading cycle.

What web services add

  • Exploit OOP: build applications from existing software components in a modular way; transform the Internet into a library of programmatic components.
  • Example — online travel booking: the travel portal (a broker) owns no flights or hotels; it calls airline services, shows options, then calls card/net-banking services — multiple services choreographed to execute one job; neither the airline nor the bank knows the whole picture.
  • Improve interoperability through open, non-proprietary standards.
  • Like EDI but simpler and less expensive to implement; can be configured to work with EDI or to phase it out.
  • Unlike the WWW, separate visual from non-visual components; interaction via browser or desktop clients (Java Swing, Python, Windows).

Three problems web services address | Problem | How | |—|—| | Interoperability | Lack of interoperability standards in distributed object messaging → open XML standards | | Firewall traversal | Runs over HTTP (port 80), which most firewalls allow; CORBA and DCOM used non-standard ports | | Complexity | Developer-friendly, open text-based standards; components in different languages/platforms can communicate; can be implemented incrementally (lower cost, less disruption); legacy software keeps running behind a WS interface |

Summary of how web services work: communicate via open standards (HTTP, SMTP, other TCP/IP application protocols) · process XML messages framed using SOAP · describe messages using XML Schema · provide an endpoint description using WSDL · publish and discover using UDDI.

SOA — the service triangle

  • IBM created the model showing web-service interaction, called Service-Oriented Architecture, as a relationship between three entities:
    • Service provider — owner of the service; platform hosting access to it.
    • Service requestor (consumer) — business requiring the service.
    • Service registry (broker) — searchable registry of service descriptions where providers publish.
  • Three operations: Publish (provider → registry), Find (requestor → registry, using WSDL and UDDI), Bind (requestor ↔︎ provider).
  • Analogy: telephone directory / yellow pages.

Interaction sequence: client queries the registry to locate services → registry refers to the WSDL document → client accesses the WSDL (data needed to interact) → client sends a SOAP request to the provider → service returns a SOAP response.

Web-service stack (bottom → top): network (TCP/IP, HTTP) → XML-based messaging (SOAP) → service description (WSDL) → service publication & discovery (UDDI — static or dynamic) → service flow (WSFL). Vertical: Quality of service, management, security.

The core standards

Standard Full form Role
XML eXtensible Markup Language (evolved from SGML) Uniform data representation and exchange; separates content from presentation; structure via DTD/XSD
SOAP Simple Object Access Protocol Messaging protocol — format for sending messages over the Internet; XML-based, W3C compliant, stateless, one-way; uses mainly HTTP as the (carrier) transport
WSDL Web Services Description Language XML-based, W3C-compliant meta-language to describe the services offered — port types, messages, bindings
UDDI Universal Description, Discovery and Integration Framework to define XML-based registries — mechanism to register and locate web-service applications

SOAP details

  • Building blocks (outside → in): transport protocol → MIME header → SOAP envelope → SOAP header + SOAP body (+ fault handling). All XML-based.
  • The SOAP envelope piggybacks as the payload of the transport (HTTP POST for request; HTTP response for reply — e.g., “get stock price of IBM”).
  • Why SOAP: platform-neutral; simple XML wire format; places no restriction on endpoint implementation technology (legacy systems can participate).
  • Characteristics: extensible, neutral, independent.
  • Usage models: RPC-like message exchange; or any kind of body content (document style).

UDDI benefits: registry data in a standard, searchable format; discover the right business among millions online; define how to enable connectivity/commerce with the preferred business.

Web-service security (vertical): WS-Policy, WS-Trust, WS-Privacy, WS-SecureConversation, WS-Federation, WS-Authorization. Management and QoS are also vertical.

Link to cloud: IaaS/PaaS/SaaS/XaaS are all built on the web-service publish–find–bind idea (who provides, where the service is, how to bind) — web services and SOA made cloud computing viable.

MCQ traps (2.4)

  • SOAP = messaging; WSDL = description; UDDI = registry/discovery. Classic matching question.
  • SOAP is stateless and one-way; “transport” for SOAP means HTTP/SMTP as carrier, not TCP.
  • Web services traverse firewalls because they use HTTP/port 80; CORBA/DCOM used non-standard ports.
  • SOA operations are publish, find, bind — not “register, request, respond”.
  • The registry is the broker; the consumer does find, the provider does publish.
  • EDI requires a pre-agreed format; web services are a simpler, cheaper alternative that can coexist with EDI.

Quick revision (2.4)

  • W3C definition: URI + interfaces/bindings defined, described, discovered as XML artifacts.
  • SOA triangle (IBM): provider, requestor, registry; publish–find–bind.
  • XML → SOAP → WSDL → UDDI → WSFL; QoS/management/security vertical.

Week 2 — High-yield takeaways

  1. Public: low up-front cost, multi-tenancy risk, restrictive default SLAs, illusion of unlimited resources.
  2. On-site private: limited resources, significant–high up-front cost, strong external security; outsourced private: two perimeters, extensive resources, negotiated SLA.
  3. Community → RBAC/ABAC; hybrid → constituents remain unique, portability, complexity, members join/leave.
  4. IaaS hierarchy: Cloud manager (+DOS) → Cluster manager (+PLS) → Computer manager (per machine).
  5. Popek–Goldberg: equivalence, resource control, efficiency; VMM possible if sensitive ⊆ privileged.
  6. Full (binary translation, QEMU/Bochs, portable, slow) / Para (modified guest, ring 1, Xen) / Hardware-assisted (Intel VT, AMD-V, unmodified guest, ring 0, less portable).
  7. XML: well-formed vs valid; DTD vs XSD; namespaces via xmlns; SAX (event) vs DOM (tree); XSLT transforms trees.
  8. Web services: SOAP (messaging, stateless, one-way, over HTTP), WSDL (description), UDDI (registry); SOA publish–find–bind.

Week 3 — SLA, Cloud Economics, Managing Data, MapReduce, OpenStack (Lectures 11–15)

Week 3 — SLA, Cloud Economics, Managing Data, MapReduce, OpenStack (Lectures 11–15)

Source: L11 Service Level Agreement (SLA) · L12 Economics · L13 Managing Data · L14 Introduction to MapReduce · L15 OpenStack

Numerical-heavy week. Formulas you must be able to apply: coefficient of variation and the 1/n​ smoothing rule, utility-pricing condition U<P/A, penalty ∫∣D(t)−R(t)∣dt, system-failure probability 1−(1−p)N, Dynamo quorum R+W>N, parallel efficiency T1​/(pTp​), word-count efficiencies 1/p vs 1/(1+2p/nf), MapReduce efficiency 1/(1+2cσ/w).

3.1 Service Level Agreement (L11)

🎯
Your practice set for L11 (your file w12): 50 questions · 14 easy · 26 medium · 10 hard · 2 with ⚠️ notes. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 3.

Core concept

  • SLA = a formal contract between the service provider and the service consumer.
  • It is the foundation of the consumer’s trust in the provider, and lets consumers compare providers.
  • Purpose: to define a formal basis for the performance and availability the provider guarantees to deliver (e.g., “uptime ≥ 95 %”).
  • There is still no standard format for SLAs; consumers usually click-accept the provider’s terms.
  • Applies to every service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, data services…).

Terminology hierarchy: KPI → SLO → SLA

Term Meaning Examples
KPI (Key Performance Indicator) Low-level resource metric, measured directly from the system downtime, uptime, bytes in, bytes out, packet size
SLO (Service Level Objective) Objectively measurable condition for the service; encompasses multiple QoS parameters. Multiple KPIs are composed, aggregated or converted into high-level SLOs availability of service = 99.9 %; response time of a DB query between 3 and 5 s; throughput of a server at peak = 0.875
SLA Multiple SLOs are integrated into the agreement the whole contract
Service Level Management Monitoring and managing service performance based on SLOs Provider: decisions from business objectives + technical realities; Consumer: decisions about how to use cloud services
  • SLOs vary from consumer to consumer (an academic institute may accept 95 % uptime but want high data persistence; another may need ≥ 99 % uptime but keep its own backups) and over time (≥ 99 % at peak hours, ≥ 90 % off-peak).
  • QoS parameters inside SLOs: availability, serviceability, billing, throughput, response time, quality.

KPI → SLO mapping example given in the lecture: Availability=1−uptimedowntime​

⚠️ Flag: the lecture slide writes downtime/uptime. The standard definition is Availability=uptime+downtimeuptime​=1−total timedowntime​. For small downtimes the two are almost equal. If an MCQ reproduces the slide formula, choose it; for numerical availability problems use downtime/total time (as in the SLA tutorial, Week 5).

Typical contents of an SLA (list question)

  1. Set of services the provider will deliver.
  2. Complete, specific definition of each service.
  3. Responsibilities of the provider and the consumer.
  4. Set of metrics to measure whether the provider is offering the services as guaranteed.
  5. Auditing mechanism to monitor the services (possibly a third-party auditor).
  6. Remedies available to consumer and provider if the terms are not satisfied (penalty/compensation for not providing guaranteed service).
  7. Whether/how the SLA will change over time.

Web-service SLAs (cloud SLAs evolved from these)

  • WS-Agreement: an XML-based language and protocol for negotiating, establishing and managing service agreements at runtime; specifies the nature of the agreement template; facilitates discovering compatible providers; interaction is usually request–response; SLA violations dynamically managed and verified.
  • WSLA (Web Service Level Agreement framework): formal XML-schema-based language to express SLAs + a runtime interpreter; measures and monitors QoS parameters and reports violations; weakness: lack of formal definitions for the semantics of the metrics.

Traditional web-service SLA vs cloud SLA (classic comparison)

Aspect Traditional web services Cloud
QoS parameters Response time, SLA violation rate for reliability, availability, cost of service Security, privacy, trust management have more importance
Automation SLA negotiation, provisioning, service delivery, monitoring are not automated SLA automation required for highly dynamic, scalable services
Resource allocation UDDI used for advertising and discovering services Resources allocated and distributed globally without any central directory

Types of SLA

Type Description
Off-the-shelf / non-negotiable / “direct” SLA Provider creates an SLA template defining all criteria (contract period, billing, response time, availability…). Followed by present-day (public) clouds. Not conducive for mission-critical data or applications. Suits small requirements.
Negotiable SLA Negotiated via an external agent, or via multiple external agents (when combining several services). Suits large requirements (like booking a whole hotel vs one room).

Considerations for SLAs (L11 lists)

  • Business-level objectives.
  • Responsibilities of provider and consumer — balance varies with service type (e.g., consumer must not send data faster than the agreed rate, or it may cause violations of the provider’s other SLAs).
  • Business continuity and disaster recovery — consumer should ensure adequate protection against natural/man-made disasters and system failure.
  • System redundancy — many providers use massively redundant systems.
  • Maintenance of cloud infrastructure (affects every offering, hardware and software).
  • Location of data — if regulations require data to stay in a jurisdiction (e.g., within India), the consumer must be able to audit the provider to prove compliance.
  • Seizure of data — if law enforcement targets one consumer’s data, multi-tenancy makes it likely that other consumers are affected too.
  • Failure of the provider.
  • Jurisdiction (where litigation is handled).

Further SLA requirements:

  • Security — data encryption, key management (where keys reside, how communicated).
  • Privacy — isolation of consumer data in a multi-tenant environment.
  • Data retention and deletion.
  • Hardware erasure/destruction — provider must zero out memory when a consumer powers off a VM, and zero out disk platters before disposal/recycling.
  • Regulatory compliance, transparency, certification.
  • Monitoring — to eliminate conflict of interest, a neutral third-party organization is the best solution (hard to implement in practice).
  • Auditability — consumers are liable for breaches, so they must be able to audit provider systems/procedures; the SLA should say how and when. Audits are disruptive and expensive, so providers will limit them or charge for them.

Metrics for monitoring and auditing

Throughput · availability · reliability · load balancing (when elasticity boots/terminates VMs) · durability (how likely data is to be lost) · elasticity · linearity (how the system performs as load increases — linear growth is easy to chase; non-linear/exponential is hard) · agility · automation · customer service response time · service level violation · transaction time · resolution time. Different metrics matter for IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS.

Example provider SLAs cited

Provider Service Availability in SLA (as cited)
Amazon EC2 IaaS 99.5 % (service year 365 days; annual percentage uptime; region)
Amazon S3 Storage ~99 % (defined via error rate, monthly uptime percentage)
Microsoft (Azure) IaaS/PaaS 99.9 % (monthly connectivity uptime service level)
Google, Salesforce, Zoho, Rackspace, Terremark Various listed

⚠️ Lecture vs today: these figures are historical and differ from current SLAs. Use them only if an MCQ quotes the lecture table.

⚠️ Practice-set clash: your L11 practice set (file w12, Q40) keys “S3 — storage as a service, 99.9 %”. The lecture actually says 99 % for S3; 99.9 % is the Microsoft/Google/Salesforce line. If both values appear as options, go with the lecture’s 99 %.

  • Availability ≠ durability:
    • Availability asks whether the service is reachable now.
    • Durability asks how likely the stored data is to be lost.
    • So 99 % availability with 99.9999 % durability = “may be down for a while, but the data is almost never lost”.
  • Who is at fault? The SLA divides responsibilities. Downtime from the consumer’s own code, unpatched OS (IaaS) or bad configuration is not a provider violation.

MCQ traps (3.1)

  • KPI is the lowest level; SLOs are built from KPIs; the SLA integrates SLOs. Don’t reverse it.
  • Off-the-shelf SLAs are not suitable for mission-critical applications.
  • In cloud SLAs, security/privacy/trust gain importance and automation is required; in traditional WS SLAs, monitoring/negotiation is not automated.
  • WSLA = XML-schema language + runtime interpreter; its weakness = no formal semantics of metrics.
  • Best monitor = neutral third party (not the provider, not the consumer).

Quick revision (3.1)

  • SLA = formal contract; foundation of trust.
  • KPI → SLO → SLA; SLM manages it.
  • 7 SLA contents; 2 SLA types; cloud vs WS SLA on QoS, automation, resource allocation.

3.2 Cloud economics — “cloudonomics” (L12)

Economic properties of cloud

Property Economic meaning
Common infrastructure Pooled, standardized resources, with benefits generated by statistical multiplexing
Location independence Ubiquitous availability meeting performance requirements; benefits from latency reduction and better user experience
Online connectivity An enabler of the other attributes; affects service cost and performance via network architecture
Utility pricing Pay-as-you-go (like electricity)
On-demand resources Scalable, elastic resources provisioned and de-provisioned without delay or costs associated with the change

Why owning is wasteful: we size for peak load (e.g., a lab of 55 PCs for 50 M.Tech seats, used ~8 h/day; a 24-port 100 Mbps switch with a 1 Gbps uplink is “blocking” but a 2.4 Gbps uplink would be over-provisioning, because all users rarely peak together). Overheads (AC, power/UPS, AMC, staff) can exceed equipment cost, and hardware becomes obsolete within 2–3 years (certainly within 5).

Value of common infrastructure:

  • Economies of scale: reduced overhead costs; buyer power through volume purchase.
  • Statistics of scale:
    • For infrastructure built to peak: multiplexing demand → higher utilization → lower cost per delivered resource than unconsolidated workloads.
    • For infrastructure built to less than peak: multiplexing demand → fewer unserved demands → lower loss of revenue / fewer SLA-violation payouts.

Coefficient of variation — the smoothness measure

Formula: Cv​=∣μ∣σ​

  • Symbols: σ = standard deviation of demand; μ = mean demand.
  • Purpose: statistical measure of the dispersion of a data series around its mean; lets you compare the variability of two series even if their means differ greatly. Used in investing to compare volatility (risk) against expected return.
  • Interpretation: lower Cv​ ⇒ smoother demand ⇒ better risk–return trade-off; a smoother curve has a large mean for a given σ or a small σ for a given mean.
  • Not the same as variance or correlation coefficient.
  • Importance of smoothness: a facility with fixed assets servicing highly variable demand achieves lower utilization than a similar one servicing relatively smooth demand.

Multiplexing independent demands (key result): If X1​,…,Xn​ are independent demands each with mean μ and s.d. σ:

  • Aggregate mean =nμ; aggregate variance =nσ2 ⇒ aggregate s.d. =n​σ Cv​(aggregate)=nμn​σ​=n​1​Cv​
  • Adding n independent demands reduces Cv​ by a factor 1/n​ → penalty for insufficient/excess resources shrinks.
  • Example: aggregating 100 independent workloads → 1/100​=0.1 → the penalty falls to 10 % of the original (the lecture phrases this as “bring the penalty down by 10 percent”; mathematically it is reduced to one-tenth).

Other correlation cases: | Demand relationship | Result | |—|—| | Negatively correlated (e.g., X and 1−X; day-time vs night-time customers) | Sum is constant → Cv​=0; choose customer segments with complementary demand | | Perfectly correlated (n copies of X) | Mean nμ, variance n2σ2, s.d. nσ → Cv​ unchanged (no smoothing) | | All peak at the same time | Congestion (e.g., all classes ending on the hour) — worst case |

Implications:

  • With correlated demands, private, mid-size and large providers see similar statistics of scale.
  • With independent demands, a mid-size provider can achieve statistical economies similar to an infinitely large provider (benefit grows like n​ and saturates).
  • Evidence on economies of scale for large providers is mixed: all use the same COTS components; large ones locate near cheap power; early entrants’ automation tools soon become available from third parties.

Value of location independence

  • Earlier we went to the computer; now applications/services come to us (thin client + network).
  • Latency matters: human response 10–100 ms; latency grows with distance and hops; speed of light in fibre ≈ 124 miles per millisecond; VoIP becomes hard beyond **200 ms**; users are unhappy if search takes more than a couple of seconds.
  • Serving a global user base requires a dispersed service architecture — with coordination issues of consistency, availability, partition tolerance — which has investment implications.

Utility pricing — when is cloud cheaper? (core numerical)

“Cloud services do not need to be cheaper to be economical.” Car analogy: buying/leasing vs renting — renting is cheaper if you need the car only occasionally; buying is cheaper for daily long commutes.

Symbols | Symbol | Meaning | |—|—| | D(t) | Demand for resources over 0≤t≤T | | P=maxt​D(t) | Peak demand | | A=T1​∫0T​D(t)dt | Average demand | | B | Baseline (owned) unit cost | | C | Cloud unit cost | | U=C/B | Utility premium (how much more a unit of cloud costs than an owned unit) |

Costs Cloud cost CT​=∫0T​U⋅B⋅D(t)dt=U⋅B⋅A⋅T Owned (baseline) cost BT​=P⋅B⋅T(you must own enough for the peak) Cloud is cheaper when CT​<BT​⟺UBAT<PBT⟺ U<AP​​ Utility premium less than the peak-to-average ratio ⇒ cloud is cheaper than owning.

  • Interpretation: spiky demand (high P/A) favours cloud; flat demand (P/A→1) favours owning unless U<1.
  • Car example (lecture numbers): own/lease ≈ 500 per day, rent ≈ 5000 per day ⇒ U=5000/500=10. Demand when needed = 1 car, so P=1; if you need it on a fraction f of days, A=f ⇒ rent if 1/f>10, i.e., need the car on fewer than 10 % of days.
  • Worked example: peak P=100 servers, average A=25 ⇒ P/A=4. If cloud costs $0.30/server-h and owning $0.10/server-h, U=3<4 ⇒ cloud cheaper (cloud: 0.30×25=7.5/h vs own: 0.10×100=10/h).
  • Real world: demand is spiky (news stories, promotions, product launches, Internet flash crowds, seasonal — Christmas, tax). A hybrid model is often best — own a car for the daily commute, rent one for trips (own the baseline, rent the peaks). The key factor is still peak-to-average ratio, but also consider network costs (fixed and usage), interoperability overhead, reliability, accessibility.
  • Common mistakes: using U=B/C (wrong — it’s cloud ÷ owned); comparing U with A/P; forgetting owned cost scales with peak, cloud cost with average.

Value of on-demand services — penalty of mis-provisioning
