When you own resources, you pay a penalty whenever resources R(t) don’t match demand D(t): either pay for unused resources or suffer the penalty of missing service delivery. Penalty∝∫0T​​D(t)−R(t)​dt | Demand pattern | Consequence | |—|—| | Flat | Penalty = 0 (provision exactly) | | Linear | Periodic provisioning is acceptable (gap stays bounded) | | Exponential D(t)=et | With provisioning delay tp​, R(t)=D(t−tp​)=et−tp​, so D(t)−R(t)=et(1−e−tp​)=k1​et ⇒ penalty cost ck1​et grows exponentially — you fall exponentially behind unless you over-provision (also hard) |

  • Lecture exercise (solved in Week 5, L22): peak demand 120 units, given D(t), R(t)=D(t−δ) with provisioning delay δ, cost 0.9 units per resource-unit-time — compute penalty.

MCQ traps (3.2)

  • Cloud cheaper iff U<P/A (peak/average), not average/peak.
  • Cv​ reduction is 1/n​, not 1/n.
  • Perfectly correlated demands do not smooth (Cv​ constant); negatively correlated demands can give Cv​=0.
  • “Cloud must be cheaper per unit to be economical” → False (it can cost more per unit, U>1, and still win if demand is spiky).
  • Exponential demand + provisioning delay ⇒ exponentially growing penalty; linear ⇒ periodic provisioning OK.

Quick revision (3.2)

  • 5 economic properties: common infrastructure, location independence, online connectivity, utility pricing, on-demand resources.
  • Cv​=σ/∣μ∣; n independent ⇒ Cv​/n​.
  • U=C/B; cloud cheaper iff U<P/A; owned cost =PBT, cloud cost =UBAT.
  • Penalty ∝∫∣D−R∣dt.

3.3 Managing data in the cloud (L13)

Why a new approach

Conventional relational/object models work for small instances, but large-scale read/write and huge volumes need parallel, distributed, fault-tolerant designs. Suitable for large-volume massively parallel text processing and enterprise analytics on distributed data stores (retail chains, banks, meteorological/climatological data). (Book followed: Gautam Shroff, Enterprise Cloud Computing.)

Relational database recap

  • Applications interact via SQL; the RDBMS parser transforms queries into memory/disk operations and optimizes execution time (e.g., doing selections before a join shrinks tuples from millions to thousands — same result, far less time).
  • Disk space management layer: stores records on pages of contiguous memory blocks to minimize disk movement; pages fetched with pre-fetching and page-replacement policies.
  • Database file system layer: independent of the OS file system (full control of pages in memory); files may span multiple disks; uses parallel I/O, RAID (RAID-1, 5, 6…) for redundancy/fault tolerance.

Row vs column storage | | Row-oriented | Column-oriented | |—|—|—| | Stores | Tuples (rows of same schema) in contiguous pages | Columns (projections) stored separately, sorted by dimension values | | Best for | Write-oriented transaction processing (OLTP) | Data-warehouse workloads — aggregation of measure columns by dimension columns | | Access | Indexes, B+-tree on primary key | Join indexes needed to link projections |

Parallel database architectures

Architecture Description
Shared memory Servers with multiple CPUs share one memory address space, managed by an SMP OS; schedules processes in parallel
Shared disk Hybrid — independent servers share storage via a high-speed network (NAS or SAN) over Ethernet, Fibre Channel, InfiniBand
Shared nothing Cluster of independent servers, each with its own disk, connected by a high-speed network

Parallel relational DB features: efficient SQL execution over multiple processors; in shared-nothing, tables partitioned and distributed across processors; SQL optimizer handles distributed joins; distributed two-phase commit (2PC) locking for transaction isolation; fault tolerance by transferring control to a standby system. Examples: Oracle, DB2, SQL Server (transaction processing); Vertica, Teradata, Netezza (data warehouses).

Cloud file systems: GFS and HDFS

  • GFS (Google File System): manages relatively large files using very large distributed clusters of commodity (Linux) servers connected by high-speed networks; handles failures even during reads/writes of individual files; supports parallel reads, writes and appends by multiple simultaneous clients.
  • HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System): open-source implementation of the GFS architecture (available on Amazon EC2).

Why fault tolerance is a necessity — the formula: P(system failure)=1−(1−P(component failure))N

  • N = number of components; system fails if any component fails.
  • As N grows this probability approaches 1 — e.g., p=0.001, N=1000: 1−0.9991000≈1−e−1≈0.63.

⚠️ Flag: the transcript says “if N is pretty large … the risk of failure is minimum”, which is the opposite of what the formula shows. With large N, some failure is almost certain, so fault tolerance is mandatory. Answer numerical MCQs using the formula.

GFS vs HDFS terminology (matching question) | GFS | HDFS | Role | |—|—|—| | Master | NameNode | Single (logical) master controls the namespace (metadata) | | Chunk server | DataNode | Commodity Linux servers storing the data | | Chunk | Block | Large files are broken into these | | Replication | Replication | Each chunk/block replicated 3 times on different physical racks and network segments |

Read operation (GFS): Client → master: full path + offset → master → client: metadata for ONE of the replicas → client caches metadata → client reads directly from that chunk server.

Write/append operation (GFS):

  1. Client sends full path to master.
  2. Master replies with metadata for ALL replicas.
  3. Client sends the data to be appended to all chunk servers; they acknowledge receipt.
  4. Master designates one chunk server as primary.
  5. Primary chooses an offset and appends its copy (may append beyond EOF to account for multiple simultaneous writers).
  6. Primary sends the offset to the replicas; if not all replicas succeed at that offset, the client retries (so all replicas hold the data at the same offset).

Fault tolerance in GFS: master exchanges heartbeat messages with chunk servers; on failure, chunk-server metadata is updated; if the primary fails, the master assigns a new primary; clients occasionally retry the failed server, update metadata from the master, and retry.

BigTable (Google)

  • Distributed structured storage system built on GFS.
  • Data accessed by row key, column key, timestamp.
  • Each column stores arbitrary name–value pairs in the form column-family:label.
  • Set of column families is fixed when the table is created; labels within a family can be created dynamically at any time.
  • Each cell can store multiple versions of data in decreasing timestamp order.
  • Tables are split into row ranges called tablets, each managed by a tablet server, which stores each column family for a row range in a separate distributed file called an SSTable.
  • A single metadata table is managed by metadata servers; because metadata can be very large it is itself split into tablets, with a root tablet pointing to the other metadata tablets.
  • Supports large parallel reads and inserts, even simultaneously on the same table; inserts are done in sorted fashion → more work than a simple append.

Dynamo (Amazon)

  • Supports large volumes of concurrent updates, each small in size (contrast: BigTable supports bulk reads/writes).
  • Data model: simple key–value pairs (values are arbitrary byte arrays) — well suited to web-based e-commerce.
  • Not dependent on an underlying distributed file system — handles failure, conflict resolution, etc. itself.
  • Uses MD5 to generate a 128-bit hash; the hash range is mapped to virtual nodes arranged in a ring; each physical node manages several virtual nodes at distributed ring positions (load balancing for transient failures, network partitions).
  • An object is replicated at its primary virtual node plus N−1 additional virtual nodes (lecture: “N is the number of physical nodes”; effectively N = number of replicas).
  • A write executes at one virtual node, which forwards the request to all nodes holding replicas; a quorum protocol maintains eventual consistency under many concurrent reads/writes.
  • Distributed object versioning: each write creates a new version with its local timestamp.

Quorum consistency rule (numerical!): R+W>N⇒quorum-consistent

  • R = number of replicas read; W = number of replicas that must acknowledge a write; N = number of replicas.
  • Intuition: every read set overlaps every write set, so a read sees the latest write.
  • Trade-off: efficient writes (small W) ⇒ a large number of replicas must be read (large R); efficient reads (small R) ⇒ large number written (large W).
  • Example: N=3: (R,W)=(2,2) ✓ consistent; (1,3) ✓ (fast reads); (3,1) ✓ (fast writes); (1,1) ✗ (may read stale).
  • Node-level storage engines: Berkeley DB (used by Amazon), MySQL.

Datastores (Google App Engine Datastore, Amazon SimpleDB)

  • Simple key–value database stores; all entities (objects) reside in one big table.
  • Exploit column-oriented storage — store data as column families (vs row/tuple-based RDBMS).
  • Multiple index tables support efficient queries; the big table is horizontally partitioned (“sharded”) across disks, stored lexicographically by key → enables prefix and range queries.
  • Entities are grouped for transactions.
  • Indexes: automatically created single-property indexes and a “kind” index (efficient lookup like “select all of a kind”); configurable (composite) indexes; query execution chooses the index with the highest selectivity.

MCQ traps (3.3)

  • GFS read: metadata for ONE replica; write: metadata for ALL replicas.
  • Master = NameNode, chunk server = DataNode, chunk = block; default replication 3.
  • In GFS append, the primary chunk server chooses the offset (not the master, not the client).
  • BigTable: column families fixed at creation; labels dynamic; versions in decreasing timestamp order; tablets → tablet servers → SSTables.
  • Dynamo = key–value, small concurrent updates, MD5 ring, quorum, eventual consistency, no dependence on a DFS; BigTable = built on GFS, bulk reads/writes.
  • Quorum consistency requires R+W>N (strictly greater).
  • Row-store → OLTP (write-heavy); column-store → warehouse analytics.

Quick revision (3.3)

  • P(fail)=1−(1−p)N → fault tolerance necessary.
  • GFS/HDFS: master/NameNode, chunk servers/DataNodes, 3× replication on different racks, heartbeats.
  • BigTable: (row, column, timestamp); column-family:label; tablets & SSTables; root tablet.
  • Dynamo: key–value, MD5 128-bit, ring of virtual nodes, N replicas, R+W>N.
  • Datastore: one big table, sharded, lexicographic, kind index, highest-selectivity index.

3.4 MapReduce (L14)

Core concept

  • Programming model developed at Google to implement large-scale search and text processing on massively scalable web data stored in BigTable and GFS.
  • Designed for processing and generating large volumes of data via massively parallel computation using tens of thousands of processors.
  • Fault tolerant: computation progresses even if processors or the network fail.
  • Hadoop: open-source implementation of MapReduce, initially developed at Yahoo; available as pre-packaged AMIs on Amazon EC2.
  • Parallel computing began for compute-intensive science, later used in databases; MapReduce programs run over shared-memory / shared-disk / shared-nothing configurations.

Parallel efficiency (needed for all MapReduce numericals)

  • Ideal: a task taking time T on one processor takes T/p on p processors — only if the work has inherent parallelism.
  • Sources of inefficiency: synchronization among processors, message-communication overhead, imbalance in work distribution. ε=pTp​T​
  • Scalable if ε remains constant as data size grows with a proportional increase in processors.
  • For a scalable algorithm, ε increases with data size for a fixed number of processors.

Word-count efficiency analysis (classic derivation — know the results)

Setup: n documents, m distinct words; each word occurs f times per document on average; time to read a word = time to send a word to another processor = c; adding to running totals is negligible. Distributed memory with a shared disk (no contention).

  • Single processor: T1​=nmfc.
Approach Work per processor Parallel efficiency Scalable?
1. Split the words: each processor counts m/p words over all n documents Reads up to nmf words (the whole collection) ε=p⋅nmfcnmfc​=p1​​ No — falls as p grows; most reads are wasted (no hit)
2. Split the documents: each processor counts all m words over n/p documents, then partial counts are exchanged and summed Read: pn​mfc; write partial counts: cm; communicate to p−1 processors & add p sub-vectors (to build 1/p of the final vector): ≈cm ε=1+nf2p​1​ Yes — constant when n and p grow proportionally; → 1 for fixed p as n grows; since p≪nf, ε≈1
  • Intuition: in approach 2 every read is useful (contributes to the result); in approach 1 each processor scans all words but only 1/p of them matter.
  • Numerical check: n=104 docs, f=1, p=10: approach 1 → ε=0.1; approach 2 → ε=1/(1+20/104)≈0.998.
  • Approach 2 is exactly the MapReduce pattern (local map counts → shuffle → reduce/sum).

The MapReduce model

  • Two phases: Map and Reduce. A configurable number of M mapper and R reducer processors; computation coordinated by a single master process.

Map phase

  • Each mapper reads ≈ 1/M of the input from the global file system.
  • Map transforms one set of key–value pairs into another: map:(k1​,v1​)→[(k2​,v2​)].
  • Each mapper writes its results into one file per reducer, sorted by key, on its local file system. The master keeps track of the locations of these files.

Reduce phase

  • The master informs reducers where the partial results are stored (on mappers’ local disks).
  • Reducers make remote procedure calls (RPC) to the mappers to fetch the files.
  • Each reducer groups results by key and applies a function f: (k2​,[v2​])→(k2​,f([v2​])) (e.g., f = sum for word count).
  • Final results are written back to GFS.

Input (GFS) → M mappers [(k1,v1)→(k2,v2), one sorted file per reducer, local disk] → master tells reducers file locations → R reducers fetch via RPC, group by key, apply f → output (GFS)

Word-count example (3 mappers, 2 reducers): each mapper emits (wi​,count in its documents) and writes one file for each reducer (e.g., reducer 1 handles w1​,w2​; reducer 2 handles w3​,w4​); reducers sum counts, e.g., w1​=7, w2​=15.

Fault tolerance in MapReduce

  • Heartbeat messages from workers.
  • If communication exists but no progress, the master duplicates those tasks onto processors that have finished or are free.
  • Mapper fails: the master reassigns its key-range to another node for re-execution (its local outputs are lost).
  • Reducer fails: only the remaining (unfinished) tasks are reassigned, because completed reduce outputs are already written to GFS.

Efficiency of MapReduce (formula)

Setup: uniprocessor time wD for data volume D (reading, computing, writing); c = time to read/write one word.

  • Map stage: time cm​D, output σD; Reduce stage: time cr​σD, output σμD.
  • No decomposition overhead: wD=cm​D+cr​σD.
  • With P processors acting as both mappers and reducers, the extra cost is that each mapper writes σD/P to local disk and each reducer reads σD/P remotely (it reads σD/P2 from each of the P mappers). This adds 2cσD/P per processor. εMR​=P(PwD​+P2cσD​)wD​=1+w2c​σ1​​
  • Interpretation: efficiency is independent of P ⇒ scalable; it decreases as the map output ratio σ or I/O cost c grows relative to the work w.

Applications

  • Indexing a large collection of documents (Google’s main motivation): map emits (word, document/record-id) pairs for each word; reduce groups pairs by word and creates an index entry (list of documents).
  • Relational operations with MapReduce: execute SQL-like joins and group-by on large data — adding large-scale fault tolerance to parallel-database-style processing.

MCQ traps (3.4)

  • Each mapper produces one output file per reducer (not one file overall); files are sorted by key and stored locally, not in GFS.
  • Reducers pull data via RPC after the master tells them where it is.
  • Mapper failure ⇒ re-execute its whole task; reducer failure ⇒ only unfinished tasks (finished output already in GFS).
  • Approach 1 (split words) has efficiency 1/p — not scalable; approach 2 (split documents) → 1/(1+2p/nf) — scalable.
  • MapReduce efficiency 1/(1+2cσ/w) does not depend on P.
  • Hadoop came from Yahoo (lecture), MapReduce from Google.

Quick revision (3.4)

  • ε=T/(pTp​); scalable = constant ε when data and processors grow together.
  • map: (k1​,v1​)→[(k2​,v2​)]; reduce: (k2​,[v2​])→(k2​,f([v2​])).
  • One single master; M mappers; R reducers; mapper output per reducer, local, sorted.
  • εMR​=1/(1+2cσ/w).

3.5 OpenStack (L15; demo in Week 4, L16)

Core concept

  • OpenStack is a cloud operating system that controls large pools of compute, storage and networking resources throughout a data center, all managed through a dashboard that gives administrators control while empowering users to provision resources through a web interface.
  • Open source; primarily used for IaaS (can be installed on blade servers or even a couple of PCs/laptops — good for lab experiments in resource/power management, green cloud).
  • IIT KGP’s Meghamala is built on OpenStack (blade servers).
  • Capabilities: VMs on demand (provisioning and snapshotting), networking, storage for VMs and arbitrary files, multi-tenancy (quotas per project; a user can belong to multiple projects).
  • History: started as a collaboration between NASA and Rackspace (~2010); regular releases named alphabetically — Austin (first) … Newton, Pike, Queens.

Components (very high-yield matching question)

Service Project name Role
Compute Nova Manages the life cycle of compute instances — spawning, scheduling, decommissioning VMs on demand; VM flavours; ephemeral + persistent storage attached
Networking Neutron Network connectivity as a service for other OpenStack services (e.g., Nova); API for users to define networks and attachments; pluggable architecture supporting many vendors/technologies; internal (cloud-internal) and external networks
Object storage Swift Stores/retrieves arbitrary unstructured data objects via a RESTful, HTTP-based API; highly fault tolerant via replication and scale-out; not a file server with mountable directories; writes objects to multiple devices across the cluster
Block storage Cinder Persistent block storage for running instances; pluggable driver architecture for creating/managing block devices
Identity Keystone Authentication and authorization for other OpenStack services; catalogue of endpoints of all services
Image Glance Stores and retrieves VM disk images; used by Nova during instance provisioning
Telemetry Ceilometer Monitors and meters the cloud for billing, benchmarking, scalability and statistical purposes (realizes “measured service”; helps plan capacity)
Dashboard Horizon Web-based self-service portal — launch instances, assign IP addresses, configure access control; admin front end

⚠️ Transcript slip: L15 says “project newton … networking” — the networking project is Neutron (Newton is a release name).

Sub-components: Glance — database, registry, API, storage adapter. Cinder — database, scheduler, API, volume, backup service. Keystone — policy backend, token backend, catalogue service, identity service, assignment backend, credentials backend. Neutron — API, scheduler, plugins, queues. Nova — API, scheduler, conductor, compute nodes, message queue. Clients: CLI (nova, neutron, swift…), cloud management tools (e.g., RightScale), GUI tools (dashboard, Cyberduck).

Storage types in OpenStack (classic comparison)

Ephemeral Block Object
Persists Until the VM is terminated Until specifically deleted by the user Until specifically deleted
Accessed From within the VM as a local file system Within the VM as a block device From anywhere (REST/HTTP)
Used for Running the OS and scratch space Adding additional persistent storage to a VM Storing files, including VM images
Managed by Nova Cinder Swift

Workflow — launching a VM (sequence question)

  1. User logs in to Horizon, specifies VM parameters (name, flavor, keys…) and clicks create.
  2. Horizon sends an HTTP request to Keystone (credentials in header); Keystone authenticates and returns a temporary token.
  3. Horizon sends a POST request to the Nova API; Nova API validates the token with Keystone.
  4. Nova initiates provisioning and saves state to the database; nova-api makes an RPC cast to the scheduler via the message queue.
  5. Nova scheduler fetches cluster info from the DB, filters and selects a compute node (host), publishes to the compute queue.
  6. nova-compute picks up the message, makes RPC calls to nova-conductor (DB access).
  7. Neutron configures networking; Cinder provides block devices.
  8. Image URI looked up through Glance; image retrieved via Swift.
  9. The VM is rendered by the hypervisor.

Short form: Horizon → Keystone (auth) → Nova (provision, DB) → Nova scheduler (host) → Neutron (network) → Cinder (block) → Glance (image URI) → Swift (image) → hypervisor (VM). Token flow: user → Keystone → Nova → Glance → Neutron.

MCQ traps (3.5)

  • Swift = object storage; Cinder = block storage (commonly swapped).
  • Glance = images (not storage of user files); Ceilometer = telemetry/metering; Keystone = identity; Horizon = dashboard; Nova = compute; Neutron = networking.
  • Ephemeral storage disappears with the VM (managed by Nova).
  • OpenStack began with NASA + Rackspace.
  • Swift is not a file server with mountable directories.

Quick revision (3.5)

  • Nova, Neutron, Swift, Cinder, Keystone, Glance, Ceilometer, Horizon — know each role.
  • Ephemeral (Nova, dies with VM) / Block (Cinder, persistent device) / Object (Swift, anywhere, VM images).
  • VM launch: Horizon → Keystone → Nova → scheduler → Neutron → Cinder → Glance/Swift → hypervisor.

Week 3 — High-yield takeaways

  1. KPI → SLO → SLA; off-the-shelf vs negotiable SLA; cloud SLA needs automation, security/privacy/trust focus; neutral third-party monitoring.
  2. Cv​=σ/∣μ∣; n independent workloads → Cv​/n​ (100 workloads → 10 %); negative correlation → 0; perfect correlation → unchanged.
  3. Cloud cheaper iff U=C/B<P/A; penalty ∝∫∣D−R∣; exponential demand → exponential penalty.
  4. P(fail)=1−(1−p)N; GFS/HDFS master/NameNode, chunk server/DataNode, 3× replicas, read = one replica’s metadata, write = all replicas, primary picks offset.
  5. BigTable (row, column, timestamp; tablets; SSTable) vs Dynamo (key–value, MD5 ring, quorum R+W>N, eventual consistency).
  6. Parallel efficiency T/(pTp​); word count: 1/p (not scalable) vs 1/(1+2p/nf) (scalable); MapReduce 1/(1+2cσ/w).
  7. Mapper → one sorted local file per reducer; reducer pulls via RPC; master tracks; mapper failure = redo all, reducer failure = redo remaining.
  8. OpenStack: Nova/Neutron/Swift/Cinder/Keystone/Glance/Ceilometer/Horizon; NASA + Rackspace.

Week 4 — OpenStack Demo, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform (Lectures 16–20)

Week 4 — OpenStack Demo, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform (Lectures 16–20)

Source: L16 Open Source Cloud: OpenStack Demo · L17 Case study with a commercial cloud: Microsoft Azure · L18 Azure Demo · L19 Case Study: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) · L20 Demo on GCP

This week is mostly demonstrations. Click-by-click steps are omitted; what is kept is what MCQs can test: which service does what, which model (IaaS/PaaS) each product belongs to, the order of steps, key terms (flavor, security group, floating IP, web role/worker role, resource group, app service plan, bucket, app.yaml).

4.1 OpenStack demo — Meghamala, IIT Kharagpur (L16)

🎯
Your practice set for L16 (your file w1): 50 questions · 16 easy · 23 medium · 11 hard · 11 with ⚠️ notes. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 4.

What Meghamala is

  • IIT KGP’s experimental private IaaS cloud built on OpenStack (on blade servers), used by faculty and research scholars; reachable only inside the IIT KGP network.
  • Other services built on top of Meghamala: Meghadoop — a Hadoop cluster service; Meghadata — a personal cloud storage service (“Dropbox-like”).
  • Three VM flavours: IITKGP Regular (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, ephemeral disk ≈ 45 GB as stated in the demo), IITKGP Large, IITKGP Extra Large; persistent volumes (e.g., 20 GB or 60 GB) on request.
  • Three OS images offered: Ubuntu, CentOS, Fedora.
  • Users request a VM through a request form; the admin provisions it.

What the OpenStack dashboard (Horizon) shows

Dashboard item OpenStack service behind it
Overview — vCPUs, RAM, disk in use, vCPU-hours (e.g., 134 vCPUs, 316 GB RAM, 2945 GB disk at demo time) Nova (compute) + Ceilometer (usage)
Instances — running VMs Nova
Volumes and snapshots Cinder
Images Glance
Networks (IPv4; internal and external) Neutron
Hypervisors — physical compute nodes (demo: 3 physical machines, 48 vCPUs each) Nova compute
Access & Security → Security groups Firewall rules for VMs
  • Security group = a firewall-like set of rules defining which incoming and outgoing traffic (by port/service) is allowed for a VM. Assign a security group when creating a VM and its firewall rules apply automatically — no per-VM firewall configuration needed.
  • The admin is also a tenant: the dashboard has a Project view (tenant) and an Admin view (e.g., hypervisors list).

Launching and using a VM (sequence)

  1. Instances → Launch Instance.
  2. Availability zone (only one in Meghamala: “nova”), instance name, flavor (e.g., IITKGP Regular), instance count.
  3. Boot source = image (e.g., CentOS) — fetched via Glance.
  4. Security group (one default group), network (choose the internal network).
  5. Optional post-creation script; disk partition automatic → Launch.
  6. Status goes Build → Active; power state Running.
  7. The VM first gets an internal IP; to reach it from outside the cloud, allocate and associate an external (“floating”) IP from the pool.
  8. Connect through a GUI client (x2go, XFCE desktop) using the public IP and credentials; the VM behaves like any normal machine (Internet access, YouTube, terminal).
  9. Terminate instance → deletes the VM and releases all its resources. (Other admin actions: shut down, view log.)

MCQ traps (4.1)

  • Security groups control both incoming and outgoing traffic; they are assigned per VM to avoid configuring each firewall individually.
  • A VM gets an internal IP automatically; external access requires associating an external (floating) IP.
  • Terminate ≠ shut down: terminate deletes the VM and frees resources.
  • Meghadoop = Hadoop service; Meghadata = personal storage (Dropbox-like).

Demo details your practice set asks about (4.1)

  • Who and what: the demo is run by Rajesh, the Meghamala administrator.
    • The VM created is named “nptel”, uses the CentOS image and goes on the internal network.
    • The single availability zone is “nova”. Status goes Build → Active, with power state Running.
    • Login is through X2Go (GUI remote-desktop client, XFCE session). He then opens a terminal and a browser, checks the internet, and plays YouTube.
  • Admin overview shows usage graphs at a glance (vCPU-hours etc.). The Hypervisors tab is admin-only: 3 physical machines, 48 vCPUs each, e.g. 14 instances on one. An instance = a VM.
  • Ephemeral vs persistent:
    • The ephemeral disk comes with the flavour and is deleted when the VM is terminated.
    • A persistent volume (Cinder, typically 20 GB on request) survives termination.
    • vCPU = virtual CPU.
  • Terminate vs shut down: shut down only powers the VM off, and it keeps its allocation. Terminate deletes the VM and frees its CPU, RAM and disk.
  • External IPs come from a pre-allocated pool. Associate one so that people outside the cloud can reach the VM.
  • Professor’s takeaway: set up your own small OpenStack cloud. It is a good exercise for seeing both the admin and the user side. “Realised” = how compute, storage and image services are actually implemented in a working system.

Beyond the lecture (general OpenStack facts the practice set also tests):

  • A snapshot of a VM is stored as a new Glance image.

  • A VM can boot from an image or from a volume.

  • nova-scheduler picks the hypervisor; if no host has room for the flavour, the launch fails (ERROR state).

  • A released floating IP goes back to the pool.

  • A security group that allows only port 22 inbound lets SSH in and blocks everything else inbound (outbound is allowed by default).

  • View Log shows the VM’s console output.

  • Real OpenStack can also resize a VM to another flavour. The lecture’s route is simply to request a VM with a bigger flavour.

4.2 Microsoft Azure (L17–L18)

Core concept

  • Described in the lecture as popular mainly as a PaaS, maintained by Microsoft with data centers across the globe.
  • Definition (Microsoft): a growing collection of integrated cloud services which developers and IT professionals use to build, deploy and manage applications through a global network of data centers. Developers can build and deploy wherever they want with tools, applications and frameworks of their choice; can run in the cloud or on-premises (hybrid).

Azure platform components (lecture version)

Component Role
Windows Azure Windows-based environment for running applications and storing data on servers in Microsoft data centers
SQL Azure Data services in the cloud based on SQL Server
AppFabric Cloud services for connecting applications running in the cloud or on premises

Windows Azure: compute, storage, fabric

Part Role
Compute Runs applications; supports apps with a very large number of simultaneous users that scale out
Storage Storing and accessing data — simple blobs, more structured tables, and queues for exchanging data between parts of an application
Fabric Manages the underlying resources (bare metal across data centers) and gives a common way to manage and monitor applications

Web role and worker role (very examinable)

Role Purpose
Web role A running environment that users access over the Internet — the web application service (front end, behind a load balancer)
Worker role An environment for running processing — handles distributed or complex tasks in the background
  • Any service must include at least one role of either type, but may have any number of web roles or worker roles.
  • Worker roles communicate with web roles through Azure storage queues.
  • Each VM contains an agent that lets the application interact with the Azure fabric.
  • Flow: user → Internet → load balancer → web role → (queue) → worker role → results back.

Azure offerings highlighted

  • Deploy anywhere with your choice of tools; consistent hybrid capabilities — build apps your own way, connect on-premises data and apps, extend the cloud on-premises; uses open-source technologies too.
  • Protect assets: security, privacy, compliance and transparency.
  • Accelerate app innovation: build simple-to-complex projects in a consistent portal; build quickly, manage proactively, deliver mobile apps seamlessly.
  • Analytics and data services: detect anomalies, predict behaviours, recommend actions.

Azure demo — deploying a Python (Flask) web app (L18)

  1. Log in at portal.azure.com → open Cloud Shell (terminal in the browser).
  2. git clone a sample “Hello World” Flask app; install Flask (Python micro web framework); run locally and test at localhost:5000.
  3. Create a deployment user (az webapp deployment user set) — needed for FTP and local Git deployment.
  4. Create a resource group (az group create) — a logical container into which Azure resources (web apps, databases, storage accounts) are deployed and managed.
  5. Create an App Service plan (az appservice plan create) — specifies the location, size and features of the web server that hosts the app.
  6. Create the web app (az webapp create) — provides hosting space and a URL: <appname>.azurewebsites.net.
  7. Configure Python version (az webapp config set …) — uses the platform’s default container.
  8. Configure local Git deployment, git remote add azure <url>, then git push azure master (asks for the deployment user’s password).
  9. Edit main.py → git commit → git push azure master → refresh to see the change (“Welcome to the NPTEL course on cloud computing”).
  • App Service supports deployment via FTP, local Git, GitHub, Visual Studio Team Services, etc.

MCQ traps (4.2)

  • Web role = user-facing front end; worker role = background processing. They communicate via storage queues.
  • A service needs at least one role (of either type), not one of each.
  • Resource group = logical container; App Service plan = location/size/features of the hosting server; web app = hosting space + URL.
  • AppFabric connects cloud and on-premises applications; SQL Azure = SQL Server data services.
  • The lecture classes Azure as PaaS.

4.3 Google Cloud Platform (L19–L20)

Core concept

  • GCP = a set of (modular) cloud services that enables developers to build, test and deploy applications on Google’s reliable infrastructure — from a simple website to complex applications.
  • Infrastructure is spread over regions, each with zones; resources can be global, regional or zonal.
  • Motto: Build, Store, Analyze.
  • Runs on the same infrastructure Google uses for its own products (lecture figures: billions of search results in milliseconds, ~6 billion hours of YouTube per month, ~425 million Gmail users) — globally connected, highly redundant (fault tolerant).
  • Developer focus: rapidly develop, deploy and iterate without worrying about system administration; Google manages application, database and storage servers; managed services, developer tools/SDKs, console and administration.
  • Mix and match services: VMs, managed platform, blob storage, block storage, NoSQL datastore, MySQL databases, big-data analytics.
  • Scale to millions of users: apps scale up automatically under heavy load and scale down when traffic subsides; pay only for what you use. Managed services such as App Engine and Cloud Datastore provide auto-scaling.
  • Performance: consistent CPU, memory and disk performance; global network and edge caches; transparent maintenance; support from community, partners and premium packages.

GCP services (lecture grouping)

Category Services Model
Compute App Engine PaaS — focus on your code, no patching/maintenance
Compute Engine IaaS — raw, flexible VMs
Storage Cloud Storage Flexible object storage with global edge caching
Cloud SQL MySQL (relational)
Cloud Datastore NoSQL
Persistent disk Block storage for VMs
App services BigQuery, Cloud Endpoints, caching, queues APIs to add functionality quickly instead of building from scratch
  • Migrate web apps to App Engine; scale apps using Cloud Endpoints; integrate Google services using Google APIs.

GCP demo 1 — hosting a static website on Cloud Storage (L20)

  1. Log in to the GCP console.
  2. Storage → Create bucket (give a name, choose storage class, e.g., Regional, asia-east1).
  3. Upload the site’s files/folders — a site needs index.html (home page) and a 404.html (not-found page).
  4. Share the files publicly (tick public link for every file, including those inside folders).
  5. Open the public link — served from storage.googleapis.com/<bucket>/index.html. → Uses only GCP storage services.

GCP demo 2 — building a web app with App Engine (L20)

  1. Create a new project (gets a globally unique project ID).
  2. Activate Cloud Shell; git clone Google’s sample apps.
  3. Two key files:
    • app.yaml — configuration file: runtime python27, threadsafe: true (the app can handle many simultaneous requests), URL handlers (any URL matching the regex is handled by main.app).
    • main.py — the app (Flask), prints “Hello World”.
  4. Start the local development server → check via Web preview → edit the message → restart and re-check.
  5. Deploy: gcloud app deploy (choose the region) → files uploaded to Cloud Storage → app deployed to App Engine.
  6. View: gcloud app browse (URL contains the project ID). The project can later be shut down.

MCQ traps (4.3)

  • App Engine = PaaS; Compute Engine = IaaS.
  • Cloud SQL = MySQL; Cloud Datastore = NoSQL; Cloud Storage = object storage.
  • Static website hosting uses Cloud Storage buckets (not App Engine) and needs files to be publicly shared.
  • app.yaml is the configuration file; threadsafe: true ⇒ concurrent requests.
  • Deployment command: gcloud app deploy; open in browser: gcloud app browse.

Week 4 — High-yield takeaways

  1. OpenStack dashboard maps to services: instances→Nova, volumes→Cinder, images→Glance, networks→Neutron; security groups = per-VM firewall rules (in/out); external access needs a floating IP; terminate releases resources.
  2. Meghamala: 3 flavours (Regular/Large/Extra Large), 3 OSs (Ubuntu/CentOS/Fedora), Meghadoop (Hadoop), Meghadata (personal storage).
  3. Azure (PaaS in lecture): Windows Azure + SQL Azure + AppFabric; compute/storage/fabric; web role (front end) vs worker role (processing) via storage queues; agent in each VM talks to fabric.
  4. Azure deploy flow: deployment user → resource group → App Service plan → web app → config Python → git push.
  5. GCP: App Engine (PaaS), Compute Engine (IaaS), Cloud Storage (object), Cloud SQL (MySQL), Datastore (NoSQL), BigQuery/Endpoints; auto-scaling via managed services.
  6. GCP demos: bucket + index.html/404.html + public sharing; App Engine with app.yaml + main.py → gcloud app deploy.

Week 5 — Tutorials (SLA, Economics, MapReduce) and Resource Management (Lectures 21–25)

Week 5 — Tutorials (SLA, Economics, MapReduce) and Resource Management (Lectures 21–25)

Source: L21 SLA – Tutorial · L22 Economics Tutorial · L23 MapReduce – Tutorial (titled “Lecture 24” in the transcript) · L24 Resource Management – I · L25 Resource Management – II

This is the most numerical week of the course. Each tutorial problem below is solved step by step, followed by a reusable template and the traps. Theory for these tools is in Week 3 (§3.1 SLA, §3.2 economics, §3.4 MapReduce).

5.1 SLA tutorial (L21)

🎯
Your practice set for L21 (your file w2): 50 questions · 10 easy · 27 medium · 13 hard · 7 with ⚠️ notes. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 5.

Availability formulas used in the tutorial

Availability (%)=(1−Expected service timeDowntime​)×100(Azure: Max available minutesMax available minutes−Downtime​×100)

  • Expected service time = days in period × service hours per day (only the hours the service is supposed to run).
  • SLA is violated if measured availability < guaranteed availability.
  • Service credit = percentage of the bill refunded, chosen from the credit table using the measured availability.
  • Effective cost payable = total cost − service credit.

⚠️ Flag on the formula: in Problem 1 the lecture divides downtime by the uptime (360 − 10.75 h), giving 96.92 %; in Problem 2 it divides by the total expected time (360 h), giving 97.385 %. The total-time version is the standard one (and Azure’s definition). The verdict is the same either way in both problems. In an MCQ, compute both if options are close and pick the one that matches.

Problem 1 — Was the availability guarantee violated?

Given: guaranteed availability 99 %; application runs 12 h/day; over one month (30 days) total outage = 10.75 h.

  1. Expected run time = 12 × 30 = 360 h.
  2. Service (up) duration = 360 − 10.75 = 349.25 h.
  3. Lecture: availability = (1 − 10.75/349.25) × 100 = 96.92 %. (Standard: (360 − 10.75)/360 = 97.01 %.)
  4. 96.92 % < 99 % ⇒ the provider violated the SLA.

Problem 2 — Effective cost after service credits

Given: | SLA term | Value | |—|—| | Availability guarantee | 99.95 % of service period | | Service period | 30 days | | Max service hours per day | 12 h | | Cost | $50 per day | | Service credit | 10 % if 99 % ≤ monthly uptime < 99.95 %; 25 % if uptime < 99 % | | Outages observed (different days) | 5 h 30 min, 1 h 30 min, 15 min, 2 h 25 min |

Solution (lecture):

  1. Expected service time = 30 × 12 = 360 h; total cost = 50 × 30 = $1500.
  2. Total downtime — lecture total = 9 h 25 min (= 9.4167 h).
  3. Availability = (1 − 9.4167/360) × 100 = 97.385 %.
  4. 97.385 % < 99 % ⇒ credit = 25 % of $1500 = $375.
  5. Effective cost payable = 1500 − 375 = $1125.

⚠️ Arithmetic flag: the four listed outages add up to 9 h 40 min, not 9 h 25 min (the lecture total equals the sum without the 15-minute outage). With 9 h 40 min, availability = 1 − 9.667/360 = 97.31 %. This is still < 99 %, so the credit (25 %) and the payable amount ($1125) are unchanged.

Reusable template — SLA availability / service-credit questions

  1. Expected time T = days × hours/day (convert to minutes if the table uses minutes).
  2. Downtime d = sum of outages (watch h/min conversion: 25 min = 0.4167 h).
  3. Availability =(1−d/T)×100.
  4. Compare with guarantee → violated or not.
  5. Find the credit band that contains the measured availability → credit % × bill.
  6. Payable = bill − credit.
  • Variant to practise: guarantee 99.9 %, 24 h/day, 30 days ⇒ T=720 h; outages total 2 h ⇒ availability = 1 − 2/720 = 99.72 % → falls in the “≥ 99 % but < 99.9 %” band.
  • Allowed downtime for a target availability: dmax​=(1−A)T — e.g., 99.95 % over 360 h ⇒ 0.18 h ≈ 10.8 min; 99.9 % over 30 days of 24 h ⇒ 0.72 h = 43.2 min.

Time-varying availability (L21)

Availability requirements can vary over time with business needs — e.g., a bank needs 99.9 % during peak hours (9:00–17:00), 99 % in shoulder hours, 97 % overnight; an institute needs high availability during lab hours. More guaranteed availability ⇒ higher price.

SLA definitions used by commercial clouds (Microsoft Azure example)

Term Meaning
Applicable monthly period Calendar month for which a service credit is owed (days you were a subscriber)
Applicable monthly service fees Fees paid for the service in that month
Downtime Defined per service in service-specific terms
Error code Indication that an operation failed, e.g., HTTP 5xx
Success code e.g., HTTP 2xx
External connectivity Bidirectional network traffic over supported protocols (HTTP/HTTPS) that can be sent/received from a public IP
External connectivity incident Any single incident or set of incidents resulting in downtime
Management portal Web interface through which the customer manages the service
Service credit % of fees credited back when the service level is not met
Service level Performance metric(s) the SLA sets out
Support window Period during which a service feature/compatibility with a separate product is supported
Availability set Two or more VMs deployed across different fault domains to avoid a single point of failure
Fault domain Collection of servers sharing common resources such as power and network connectivity
Update domain Set of instances to which platform updates are applied concurrently
Cloud services Compute resources used for web and worker roles
Tenant One or more roles, each with one or more role instances, deployed in a single package
VNet Virtual (private) network
  • Monthly uptime % = (Maximum available minutes − Downtime) / Maximum available minutes × 100, where maximum available minutes = total accumulated minutes in the billing period (for cloud services: all Internet-facing roles with ≥ 2 instances in different update domains). Credit rules like < 99.95 % → 10 %; < 99 % → 25 % (same pattern as Problem 2).

CSCC — 7 steps for evaluating cloud SLAs (Cloud Standards Customer Council, April 2012)

  1. Identify the cloud actors — per NIST: consumer, provider, carrier, broker, auditor (5 actors).
  2. Evaluate business-level policies — data policies, guarantees, services not covered, excess usage, payment and penalties, sub-contracted services, licensed software, industry-specific standards.
  3. Understand service and deployment model differences — SaaS/PaaS/IaaS and public/private/hybrid; SLA terms depend on the complexity of the control variables the provider exposes.
  4. Identify critical performance objectives — which metrics (availability, response time…) and how often they are collected.
  5. Evaluate security and privacy requirements — asset sensitivity, legal/regulatory requirements (e.g., data must stay within a geographic boundary), provider’s security capabilities.
  6. Identify service management requirements — what to monitor and report (load, application performance), what to meter, how rapid provisioning should be (speed, testing, demand flexibility), how resource changes are managed.
  7. Prepare for service failure management — remedies (service credits), liability limitations, how the disaster recovery plan works, and an exit clause (every cloud SLA should have one, for either party to terminate).

MCQ traps (5.1)

  • Use only scheduled service hours (12 h/day × 30 days = 360 h), not 24 × 30.
  • Credit is chosen by which band the measured availability falls in — 97 % is < 99 %, so it gets the larger (25 %) credit, not 10 %.
  • NIST cloud actors are five: consumer, provider, carrier, broker, auditor.
  • Fault domain = shared power/network; update domain = updated together; availability set = VMs across fault domains.

5.2 Economics tutorial (L22)

Problem 1 — Penalty with provisioning delay

Given: peak demand 120 units; D(t)={50sint,20sint,​0≤t≤π/2π/2<t≤π​ Resources provisioned with delay: R(t)=D(t)+δdtdD(t)​, delay δ=π/12; cost of one unit of cloud resource per unit time = 0.9; minimum demand 0. Find the penalty.

Lecture solution:

  1. ∫0π​Ddt=50[−cost]0π/2​+20[−cost]π/2π​=50(1)+20(1)=70.
  2. ∫0π​δD′(t)dt=δ(∫0π/2​50costdt+∫π/2π​20costdt)=δ(50−20)=30δ.
  3. ∫R=70+30π/12, so ​∫R−∫D​=30π/12≈ 7.85 (lecture: 7.86) — reported as the penalty (resource provisioned exceeds demand, so it is paid-for unused resource).
  • Multiplying by the unit cost (0.9) would give ≈ 7.07 cost units — the lecture stops at 7.86.

⚠️ Method flag: the formula ∫∣D−R∣dt takes the absolute value inside the integral. Here R−D=δD′ is positive on [0,π/2] (over-provisioning) and negative on (π/2,π] (under-provisioning, i.e., missed demand). The strict value is δ(50+20)=70π/12≈18.33 (×0.9 ≈ 16.5). The lecture’s 7.86 nets the two parts against each other. For assignment/exam questions modelled on this tutorial, expect the lecture’s answer (≈ 7.86). Know that the strict method gives 18.33.

Problem 2 — Is cloud cheaper than owning over 100 time units?

Given: peak demand 100 units; demand D(t)=50(1+e−t) (so D(0)=100 = peak, decaying towards 50); baseline (owned) unit cost B=120; cloud unit cost C=200; period T=100.

  1. Owned: BT​=P⋅B⋅T=100×120×100=1,200,000.
  2. Cloud: CT​=∫0100​CD(t)dt=200×50[t−e−t]0100​=10,000×(100−e−100+1)≈ 1,010,000.
  3. Ratio CT​/BT​≈1,010,000/1,200,000≈ 0.84 < 1 ⇒ cloud is cheaper.
  • Cross-check with the rule: U=C/B=200/120=1.67; A=5050/100=50.5; P/A=100/50.5=1.98; U<P/A ✓.

⚠️ Flags: (i) the transcript calls the 0.84 ratio the “utility premium” — strictly, the utility premium is U=C/B=1.67; 0.84 is the cost ratio CT​/BT​. (ii) The slide had a typo and the transcript reads the demand once as 50(1−e−t); only 50(1+e−t) matches the stated peak of 100 and the lecture’s 1,010,000. With 1−e−t you get CT​≈990,000 (ratio 0.825), and the cloud is still cheaper.

Problem 3 — In-house server vs cloud server (core-hour economics)

Given: | | In-house server | Cloud server | |—|—|—| | Purchase cost | ₹6,00,000 (over a 3-year life) | Nil | | CPU cores | 12 | 8 | | Cost per hour (3-year span) | — | ₹42 | | Efficiency (utilization) | 40 % | 80 % | | Power & cooling per hour | ₹22 | Nil | | Management cost per hour | ₹6 | ₹1 |

(a) Price of a core-hour

  • In-house cost per hour = 600000 / (3 × 365 × 24) = 600000/26280 = ₹22.83/h → per core = 22.83/12 = ₹1.90.
  • Cloud per core = 42/8 = ₹5.25.

(b) Cost per effective hour (divide by efficiency)

  • In-house = 22.83/0.40 = ₹57.08 (lecture: 57.075).
  • Cloud = 42/0.80 = ₹52.50.

(c) Total cost per effective hour and ratio

  • In-house = 57.075 + 22 (power & cooling) + 6 (management) = ₹85.075.
  • Cloud = 52.5 + 1 = ₹53.50.
  • Ratio in-house : cloud = 85.075/53.5 = 1.59 → cloud is cheaper.

⚠️ Transcript slips: it writes 87.075 once (the correct sum is 85.075) and 53.25 once (it should be 53.5).

(d) What if in-house efficiency rises?

  • At 70 %: 22.83/0.7 = 32.61 → total = 32.61 + 28 = ₹60.61 > 53.5 → cloud still cheaper.
  • At 90 %: 22.83/0.9 = 25.37 → total = 25.37 + 28 = ₹53.37 < 53.5 → in-house becomes (slightly) cheaper.
  • Break-even efficiency (my extension): 22.83/e+28=53.5⇒e≈0.895 (≈ 89.5 %).
  • Lesson: under-utilized in-house infrastructure loses to cloud; heavily utilized (≈ 90 %) in-house infrastructure can beat cloud. It depends on demand pattern and duration.

Reusable templates — economics numericals

  • Own vs cloud (utility pricing): compute U=C/B and P/A; cloud cheaper iff U<P/A. Or compute BT​=PBT and CT​=C∫Ddt directly.
  • Core-hour comparison: hourly cost = capex/(years × 8760); per core = hourly ÷ cores; per effective hour = hourly ÷ efficiency; total = per-effective-hour + power/cooling + management (per hour); compare.
  • Penalty with delay: R(t)=D(t)+δD′(t) ⇒ ∫(R−D)=δ[net change in D] — lecture nets the pieces; strict = δ∫∣D′∣.

MCQ traps (5.2)

  • Owned cost uses peak P; cloud cost uses actual demand (average).
  • Effective cost divides by efficiency (40 % → ×2.5).
  • Remember to add power/cooling and management to in-house per-hour cost; cloud has only management.
  • 3 years = 3 × 365 × 24 = 26,280 h.

5.3 MapReduce tutorial (L23)

Problem 1 — HDFS blocks with replication

Given: HDFS block size 64 MB, replication factor 3; files of 64 KB, 65 MB, 127 MB. | File | Blocks = ⌈size / 64 MB⌉ | |—|—| | 64 KB | 1 | | 65 MB | 2 (64 + 1) | | 127 MB | 2 (64 + 63) | | Total | 5 blocks |

  • With 3 replicas: 5 × 3 = 15 blocks stored.
  • (Clarification:) a block smaller than the block size (e.g., the 64 KB file) occupies only its actual size on disk; the count of blocks is still 1.

⚠️ Lecture vs today: the lecture uses 64 MB (Hadoop 1.x / GFS chunk size). Hadoop 2.x+ defaults to 128 MB. Use whatever block size the question states. With 128 MB: 64 KB → 1, 65 MB → 1, 127 MB → 1 ⇒ 3 blocks, 9 with replication.

Template: blocks per file = ⌈file size / block size⌉ (convert units first: 1 MB = 1024 KB in HDFS); total blocks = Σ blocks × replication factor; raw storage ≈ Σ file sizes × replication factor.

Problem 2 — Average of integers with MapReduce

Given: A = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; 3 mappers, 1 reducer. Master splits: M1 = {10, 20}, M2 = {30, 40}, M3 = {50}.

  • Map: each mapper emits (local average, count) to its local file system: M1 → (15, 2), M2 → (35, 2), M3 → (50, 1).
  • Reduce: total = Σ(avg × count) = 15×2 + 35×2 + 50×1 = 150; count = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 ⇒ average = 150/5 = 30. The result is written back to GFS/HDFS.
  • Trap: the average of the mappers’ averages (15 + 35 + 50)/3 = 33.3 is wrong. Mappers must emit the count (or the sum and count) so the reducer can weight correctly.
  • Pseudocode idea: map(l): sum the chunk, emit sum*1.0/len(l), len(l) (use float division). reduce: accumulate avg*count and count, then emit total/count.

Problem 3 — Total and average salary grouped by gender

Input tuples: (name, gender, salary), e.g., (John, M, 10000), (Martha, F, 15000).

  • Map: split each line on commas; drop the name; emit key = gender, value = salary → (M, 10000), (F, 15000).
  • Reduce: group by key (dictionary keyed by gender); for each gender, total = Σ salaries, average = total / count; emit (gender, total, average) to HDFS/GFS.
  • Pattern = SQL GROUP BY with SUM and AVG done in MapReduce.

General MapReduce-design checklist (from the tutorial)

  1. Identify the key you group by (word, gender, “all” for a global aggregate).
  2. Mapper: transform input records into (key, value) pairs; emit enough info for the reducer (e.g., counts).
  3. Master assigns ≈ 1/M of the input to each mapper and tracks the intermediate files.
  4. Reducer: apply the aggregate function f (sum, count, average…) per key.
  5. Number of mappers ≈ number of input splits/blocks; number of reducers is chosen by the developer.

5.4 Resource management in the cloud (L24–L25)

Why resource management

  • Consumer’s view: the cloud is an infinite, scalable resource pool, pay-as-you-go.
  • Provider’s view: finite resources that must serve as many consumers as possible, maximize profit without compromising QoS or violating SLAs, under energy and environmental (carbon footprint) limits.
  • Definition: resource management refers to the operations used to control how capabilities provided by cloud resources and services are made available to other entities — users, applications, services — in an efficient manner. (“Efficient” may mean profit, energy, SLA or QoS.)

Types of resources | Physical | Logical | |—|—| | CPU/compute, memory, storage/disk, databases (hardware), network, scientific instruments, workstations, sensors/actuators | OS, applications, communication protocols, energy management, network throughput/bandwidth, load balancing mechanisms, information security, delays, APIs, monitoring and management tools |

  • Resources exist at every layer — infrastructure, platform, application — but IaaS (infrastructure) is the main focus, because other layers are dictated by the underlying hardware. Physical and logical resources are intermingled (a fast CPU with little memory, or fast storage with a slow network, doesn’t help).

Data-center power — the motivation for green cloud (L24)

  • Servers consume about 0.5 % of the world’s electricity (lecture’s figure; likely higher now).
  • A data center = compute infrastructure (servers, storage, network) + environment/logistics (power supply/UPS, air conditioning/cooling, space). The environment part consumes roughly as much power as the compute part ⇒ total data-center consumption can exceed 1 % of world electricity.
  • Server energy demand is doubling every ~5–6 years; large CO₂ footprint (mostly fossil fuel power); sustainable sources not yet ready for such loads.
  • Economic aspects: new data centers run at megawatt scale and cost millions to operate; even with money, the electricity supplier may not have surplus power (e.g., state electricity board) ⇒ peak capacity can’t simply be expanded.
  • Performance per watt does not follow Moore’s law.
  • Goal: reduce energy use with minimal (or no) performance loss — “green data centers.”

How to conserve energy — Green Cloud framework

Area Techniques
VM control — scheduling Power-aware and thermal-aware VM scheduling
VM control — management VM image design (minimal images), VM migration/consolidation, dynamic shutdown of idle servers
Data-center design Server and rack design, air-conditioning recirculation, confined/integrated rack cooling (cool only the rack enclosure, not the whole room)
  • Also: minimize operating inefficiencies for non-essential tasks (don’t run unneeded packages/services); optimize data-center design.

Power-aware VM consolidation (worked example, L24)

Key observation: the relationship between the number of processors (cores) in use and power consumption is non-linear — power rises steeply from idle and then flattens. An idle server still burns a large base power. ⇒ It is better to pack VMs onto as few servers as possible and put the rest into low-power/hibernate mode.

Example: 4 identical nodes; idle = 105 W; fully loaded with 8 VMs = 170 W; 8 VMs to run. | Placement | Power | |—|—| | All 8 VMs on one node, other 3 idle | 170 + 3 × 105 = 485 W | | Spread 2 VMs per node (each node ≈ 138 W) | 4 × 138 = 552 W | | All 8 on one node and the 3 idle nodes shut down/hibernated | 170 W |

  • Greedy scheduling: schedule as many VMs as possible on a multi-core node, keep track of the free cores on each node, and match each VM’s requirements to node capacity.
  • Catch: migration has a cost, and VMs differ in size, so not all VMs can be packed onto one node — monitor load before consolidating.
  • Operating policy: monitor cloud usage and load → when load decreases, live-migrate VMs to more utilized nodes and shut down unused nodes → when load increases, use Wake-on-LAN to start waiting nodes and schedule new VMs on them. (Many hypervisors support live migration; it also helps when a server is failing.)
  • (Clarification:) a commonly used linear approximation is P(u)=Pidle​+(Pmax​−Pidle​)u. With this example’s figures, 2/8 load would give 121 W, but the lecture’s measured 138 W shows the curve is non-linear (concave), which makes consolidation even more attractive.

Minimizing VM images (L24)

  • Default VM images carry unwanted packages and services; clouds are service-oriented ⇒ build customized lightweight (Linux) VM images per service; smaller images reduce network latency (and migration cost).
  • Example procedure: start from Ubuntu 9.04 → remove unneeded packages (X11, window manager…) → read-ahead profiling (reorder the boot sequence and prefetch boot files to cut I/O wait) → optimized Linux kernel for Xen DomU (no 3D graphics, no sound).
  • Results: boot time 38 s → 8 s; image size 4 GB → ~600 MB. Small per-VM savings add up to a large impact (a cloud creating 100 or 1000 images per hour).
  • Summary: green cloud framework = power-aware VM scheduling + advanced VM/infrastructure management + specialized VM images; combining methods has a larger impact than each alone. Research directions: combined power- and thermal-aware scheduling; integrated server/rack/cooling; better VM image minimization; customer profiling.

Resource-management goals and challenges (L25, based on a survey paper)

Broad objectives: preserve scalability · preserve QoS · optimal utility · reduced overhead (heavy RM algorithms hurt performance) · improved throughput · reduced latency · specialized environments · cost effectiveness (for provider and consumer) · simplified interface (ease of use).

IaaS resources include compute (VMs), raw storage, firewalls, load balancers and network devices. Key challenge: manage them optimally with minimal energy while maximizing provider profit and utilization and still meeting QoS/SLA.

Resource-management aspects — definitions (classic matching question)

Aspect Definition
Resource provisioning Allocation of the provider’s resources to a customer (user or process)
Resource allocation Distribution of resources economically among competing groups of people, programs or processes
Resource adaptation Ability/capacity of the system to adjust resources dynamically to fulfil users’ requirements
Resource mapping Correspondence between the resources required by users and the resources available with the provider
Resource modelling Based on detailed information about network elements, resources and entities; describes the attributes, states, transitions and outputs of resource management in a given environment (e.g., state charts)
Resource estimation A close guess of the actual resources an application requires, usually with some thought or calculation (a priori/meta information)
Resource discovery and selection Identify the list of authenticated resources available for job submission and choose the best among them
Resource brokering Negotiation of resources through an agent to ensure the necessary resources are available at the right time (and price) to complete the objective
Resource scheduling A timetable of events and resources — resources available at certain times, events planned for those times (durations, predecessor relationships, start/end)

These aspects are inter-linked; their emphasis depends on the application.

Approaches named in the lecture (recognition level)

Aspect Approaches
Provisioning Nash equilibrium / game theory (runtime IaaS allocation considering heterogeneous resources, rational selfish users, incomplete information, successive allocation) · network queuing model (queues represent application tiers; session workloads, concurrency limits, caching) · prototype provisioning using k-means clustering to find the workload mix + queuing model to predict server capacity · VM provisioning on Xen with an earliest-deadline-first (EDF) scheduler implementing weighted fair sharing of CPU among VMs · adaptive resource provisioning (detect and resolve bottlenecks) · SLA-oriented methods · dynamic/automated frameworks · optimal cloud provisioning under demand and price uncertainty
Allocation Market-oriented allocation (model predictive control) · intelligent multi-agent model (virtualization for mobile devices) · energy-aware allocation · measurement-based performance analysis · dynamic and real-time allocation (helps small/medium IaaS providers) · dynamic scheduling and consolidation
Mapping Symmetric mapping pattern (users and providers match and enter resource-supply agreements; users place tasks in subscribed resource containers; providers place supplied containers on physical resources) · load-aware mapping (simplify VM image management, multicast file transfer, image caching) · iterated-local-search request partitioning across eligible cloud providers · mapping a virtual network onto a substrate network
Adaptation Reinforcement-learning-guided control policy · web-service-based prototypes · virtual networks · DNS-based load balancing · hybrid approaches

Performance metrics for judging resource-management techniques

Reliability · ease of deployment · QoS · delay · control overhead. Different applications weight them differently (some are delay-sensitive, some accuracy-sensitive). A bad RM technique can undermine cloud’s basic benefits (scalability, the “infinite resources” illusion).

MCQ traps (5.4)

  • Provisioning = giving resources to a customer; allocation = distributing among competing users economically; mapping = matching required to available; brokering = negotiation via an agent; discovery = find and choose authenticated resources; estimation = guess requirements; adaptation = dynamic adjustment.
  • Power vs processors is non-linear ⇒ consolidate VMs and shut down/hibernate idle servers. Spreading VMs evenly is less energy-efficient.
  • Migration has a cost; VMs are heterogeneous.
  • The environment/cooling side of a data center uses about as much power as the compute side.
  • Performance per watt does not follow Moore’s law.
  • k-means → workload mix; Nash equilibrium → game theory provisioning; EDF → VM CPU sharing on Xen.

Week 5 — High-yield takeaways

  1. SLA numericals: Availability = 1 − downtime/expected time (12 h × 30 d = 360 h); 10.75 h outage → 96.92 % < 99 % ⇒ violated; 9 h 25 min → 97.385 % → 25 % credit → $1125 payable on $1500.
  2. CSCC 7 steps; NIST 5 actors (consumer, provider, carrier, broker, auditor); fault domain vs update domain vs availability set.
  3. Economics numericals: penalty example ≈ 7.86 (lecture; strict 18.33); 50(1+e−t) example: BT​ = 1.2 M vs CT​ ≈ 1.01 M → cloud cheaper (ratio 0.84); core-hour: ₹1.90 vs ₹5.25; effective ₹57.08 vs ₹52.5; totals ₹85.075 vs ₹53.5 (ratio 1.59); in-house wins only at ≈ 90 % efficiency.
  4. HDFS: 64 KB, 65 MB, 127 MB with 64 MB blocks → 5 blocks, ×3 = 15.
  5. MapReduce average: mappers emit (avg, count); reducer Σ(avg×count)/Σcount = 150/5 = 30. Salary by gender: key = gender, value = salary.
  6. Green cloud: consolidate VMs (485 W vs 552 W; 170 W if idle nodes off); Wake-on-LAN; minimal VM images (38 s → 8 s, 4 GB → 600 MB).
  7. RM aspects: provisioning, allocation, adaptation, mapping, modelling, estimation, discovery, brokering, scheduling; metrics: reliability, ease of deployment, QoS, delay, control overhead.

Week 6 — Cloud Security I–IV and Broker for Cloud Marketplace (Lectures 26–30)

Week 6 — Cloud Security I–IV and Broker for Cloud Marketplace (Lectures 26–30)

Source: L26 Cloud Security – I (security basics) · L27 Cloud Security – II (cloud-specific issues) · L28 Cloud Security – III (case study: “Hey, You, Get Off of My Cloud”) · L29 Cloud Security – IV (collaborative SaaS cloud security) · L30 Broker for Cloud Marketplace

High-yield: CIA triad; the 4 attack types; 4 threat classes; passive vs active attacks; policy vs mechanism; secure/precise/broad; Gartner’s 7 cloud risks; RPO vs RTO; co-tenancy; the EC2 co-residency case study (placement + extraction, Dom0, co-residency checks); IDRM, SoD, cyclic inheritance; fuzzy broker.

6.1 Security fundamentals (L26)

🎯
Your practice set for L26 (your file w3): 50 questions · 11 easy · 27 medium · 12 hard · 1 with ⚠️ notes. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 6.

CIA triad

Component Meaning
Confidentiality Keeping data and resources hidden from unauthorized parties
Integrity Data integrity (what A sends is what B receives) and origin/source integrity (authentication of the source)
Availability Enabling access to data and resources — most attacks (DoS/DDoS) target this

A security attack = any action that compromises the security of information (violates CIA).

Four basic attack types (source S → destination D, intruder I)

Attack What happens Attack on
Interruption Communication path is broken Availability
Interception I listens to the message Confidentiality
Modification I intercepts, changes message m→m′, forwards it; D thinks it came from S Integrity
Fabrication I pretends to be the source Authenticity

Classes of threats (a threat is a possible violation, not an attack)

Threat class Examples
Disclosure Snooping
Deception Modification, spoofing, repudiation of origin, denial of receipt
Disruption Modification
Usurpation Modification, spoofing, delay, denial of service

Policies and mechanisms

  • Policy says what is and what is not allowed; it defines the security of a site/system. Policies are usually formulated centrally, but implemented in a distributed way (switches, routers, firewalls across departments) — the challenge is to guarantee the implementation conforms exactly to the policy (an active research problem).
  • Mechanisms enforce policies.
  • Composition of policies: conflicts/discrepancies (one allows a traffic class, another denies an overlapping class; local vs global policies) can create security vulnerabilities.

Goals of security

Goal Meaning
Prevention Prevent attackers from violating security policies
Detection Detect attackers’ violations of policy — the earlier the better (late detection = post-mortem)
Recovery Stop the attack, assess and repair damage, continue to function correctly even if the attack succeeds (redundancy, logging) — at a cost

Trust and assumptions

  • Underlie all aspects of security. Assumptions: policies unambiguously partition system states (secure vs non-secure) and correctly capture security requirements; mechanisms are assumed to enforce policies; support mechanisms work correctly.
  • Types of security mechanisms (set view): let R = set of reachable states, Q = set of secure states.
    • Secure: R⊆Q — every reachable state is secure.
    • Precise: R=Q.
    • Broad: some reachable states are not secure.

Assurance, operational and human issues

  • Assurance = specification (requirements analysis, statement of desired functionality) → design (how the system will meet the specification) → implementation (programs/systems that carry out the design).
  • Operational issues: cost–benefit analysis (is it cheaper to prevent or to recover? e.g., a teaching lab that stores no data can just be reimaged; research data must be protected) · risk analysis (should we protect something, and how much?) · laws and customs (are desired measures legal? will people follow them?).
  • Human issues: organizational problems (responsibility, authority) and people problems. Example: an employee tricked by a phishing mail into revealing a password (social engineering).
  • Why this matters for cloud: mission-critical data, e.g. banking data, defence data, even academic data such as students’ results. The lecture says these generic security concepts carry over to cloud in the same or different forms.
  • Goals of security = prevention, detection, recovery (only three; “retaliation” is a common distractor).
  • Tying it together: threats → policy → specification → design → implementation → operation, with operational issues fed back into each stage.

Passive vs active attacks

Passive Active
Nature Obtain information being transmitted (eavesdropping) Modify the data stream or create a false stream
Types Release of message contents; traffic analysis (infer activity from volume/timing — e.g., heavy traffic ⇒ video call) Masquerade (one entity pretends to be another) · Replay (passive capture and later retransmission to produce an unauthorized effect) · Modification of a legitimate message · Denial of service
Detection Difficult to detect (no direct harm) Easier to detect, hard to prevent

Security services / role of security infrastructure

Confidentiality (protect against loss of privacy) · integrity (against alteration/corruption) · availability (against DoS) · authentication (identify legitimate users) · authorization (whether an operation is allowed for a user) · non-repudiation (“the order is final” — you can’t later deny an online fund-transfer instruction you gave) · access control (prevent misuse of resources; e.g., RBAC) · safety (against tampering, damage, theft). Common attacks listed: social engineering, phishing, password attacks, buffer overflow, command injection, viruses deleting files (non-availability).

Network security process

  1. Determine the security policy — a full security roadmap; network design must reflect it.
  2. Implement the policy — install/configure firewalls, IDS, DMZ, NAT, dual firewalls; honeypots/honeynets (deliberately vulnerable systems that attract attacks so their signatures can tune IDS/firewall rules).
  3. Reconnaissance — learn about the network (host IPs, key servers with critical data): passive (undetectable) or active (often not detected by IDS).
  4. Vulnerability scanning — e.g., Nessus, nmap (open ports, possible vulnerabilities); exploitation frameworks such as Metasploit; vulnerability databases such as NVD (National Vulnerability Database); scanners must be updated like antivirus signatures.
  5. Penetration testing — safe “self-attack” to find how far the system can be penetrated, then patch.
  6. Post-attack investigation — forensics, guided by law; retain the chain of evidence.

MCQ traps (6.1)

  • Interception ⇒ confidentiality; modification ⇒ integrity; fabrication ⇒ authenticity; interruption ⇒ availability.
  • Snooping = disclosure; delay/DoS = usurpation; repudiation of origin, denial of receipt = deception.
  • Traffic analysis is passive; replay is active.
  • Passive attacks are difficult to detect.
  • Policy = what is allowed; mechanism = enforcement.
  • Secure: R⊆Q; precise: R=Q; broad: R⊆Q.

6.2 What is different about cloud security (L27)

Why security is the top barrier

  • Cloud = elastic (theoretically infinite) resource scalability + on-demand, just-in-time provisioning + pay-as-you-go. Economic benefits: consumer has no upfront cost and scales as required; provider increases data-center utilization — a win-win.
  • So why isn’t everyone on cloud? Clouds are still subject to traditional confidentiality, integrity, availability and privacy issues, plus some additional attacks.
  • IDC Enterprise Panel (2008): security was the top challenge/issue, followed by performance and availability. It’s not only that cloud is insecure — it’s hard to define security precisely and to trust the provider.

New threats introduced by cloud

  • Traditional security focuses on keeping attackers out; an attacker must compromise authentication/access control or impersonate a user.
  • In cloud:
    • Co-tenancy: multiple independent users share the same physical infrastructure → an attacker can legitimately use the same physical machine as the target.
    • Customer’s lack of control over its own data and applications (they sit on the provider’s premises).
    • Reputation fate-sharing: tenants sharing infrastructure share each other’s fate (e.g., one tenant’s misbehaviour gets a shared IP blacklisted).
  • Responsibility shift: IaaS → consumer bears most security responsibility (everything above the infrastructure); moving towards SaaS → provider’s responsibility increases.
  • Scenarios: in a private cloud, business units A and B may share a physical host; in a public cloud, different customers share hosts and a channel between them may exist (e.g., via a compromised VMM) — beyond the consumer’s control, who can only rely on SLAs and provider reports.

Gartner’s seven cloud computing security risks (list question)

Risk Key point
1. Privileged user access Sensitive data processed outside the enterprise bypasses the organization’s physical, logical and personnel controls → ask providers about hiring and oversight of privileged administrators and controls over their access
2. Regulatory compliance and audit Traditional services undergo external audits/certification; a provider refusing scrutiny is fit only for trivial functions; usually no customer-side audit facility; a trusted third-party auditor may be needed
3. Data location Customer often has no clue where data is stored; data centers in different jurisdictions → whose law applies?
4. Data segregation Data sits in a shared environment with other customers’ data; encryption is effective but not a cure-all; data in transit must be decrypted for processing; need a secure key store; encryption schemes should be designed and tested by experts
5. Recovery What happens to data and services in a disaster/outage; replication and redundancy for fault tolerance
6. Investigative support Investigating inappropriate or illegal activity may be impossible in cloud (little customer-side control/monitoring)
7. Long-term viability How do you get data back (in an importable format) if the provider goes bankrupt, shuts the service, raises prices, degrades quality or has a business dispute? Main obstacle to switching: vendor lock-in

RPO and RTO (recovery metrics)

Metric Definition
RPO — Recovery Point Objective Maximum amount of data that may be lost following an interruption or disaster
RTO — Recovery Time Objective Time period allowed for recovery — time allowed to elapse between the disaster and activation of the secondary site

Additional cloud security issues

(a) Virtualization (VMM/hypervisor is the key):

  • Recap: full virtualization — VMs run on the hypervisor, which interacts with the hardware; para-virtualization — VMs interact with the host more directly (modified guest). Main functionality: resource isolation.
  • Hypervisor vulnerabilities: shared clipboard technology can transfer malicious programs from VMs to the host; keystroke logging — some VM technologies log keystrokes and screen updates passed across virtual terminals.
  • Hypervisor risks: rogue hypervisor rootkits (initiate a rogue hypervisor, hide from normal malware detection, create a covert channel to dump unauthorized code); external modification of the hypervisor; VM escape; improper VM configuration; denial of service.
  • Threats: unauthorized access to virtual resources; loss of confidentiality, integrity, availability. If the VMM is compromised, all VMs on it are potentially compromised.

(b) Access control and identity management: proper access control (RBAC, MAC, DAC) for CIA; prevention of identity theft — privacy threats via massive data mining; identity management authenticates users and services based on credentials and characteristics.

(c) Application security: cloud apps are mostly web-based → injection attacks, XML signature element wrapping, cross-site scripting (XSS), flooding, DNS poisoning, phishing, metadata (WSDL) spoofing; insecure communication channels → interruption, eavesdropping.

(d) Data life-cycle management:

  • Confidentiality — will sensitive data stay confidential? Will the cloud leak client data? Will the provider itself be honest and not peek?
  • Integrity — how do I know the provider computed correctly and stored data without tampering?
  • Availability — will critical systems go down if the provider suffers DoS, or goes out of business?
  • Data location — all copies/backups only where the contract/SLA/regulation allows.
  • Archive access latency.

(e) Inter-cloud communication: a process in cloud 1 → cloud 2 → cloud 3 → back may let a user access data that would otherwise be denied — violating access control.

(f) Choosing providers: trust, competence, risk of each provider.

MCQ traps (6.2)

  • Gartner list has seven items (privileged user access, regulatory compliance & audit, data location, data segregation, recovery, investigative support, long-term viability). “Pricing” or “performance” is not one of them.
  • RPO = data loss tolerance; RTO = time to restore.
  • Co-tenancy lets an attacker be on the same machine legitimately (no break-in needed).
  • IaaS consumer has more security responsibility than a SaaS consumer.
  • Encryption is “effective but not a cure-all” (data must be decrypted for processing).

6.3 Case study: “Hey, You, Get Off of My Cloud” (L28)

Paper

Ristenpart et al., ACM CCS 2009 — “Hey, You, Get Off of My Cloud: Exploring Information Leakage in Third-Party Compute Clouds.” Claimed to be the first work on cloud cartography; experiments on Amazon EC2; achieved about 40 % success in getting co-resident with a target VM. (Purpose in the course: show new cloud risks, not to criticize a provider.)

New risks highlighted

  • Trust and dependency — customer must trust the provider to respect data privacy and integrity of computations.
  • Multi-tenancy — multiplexing VMs of disjoint customers on the same physical machine; you cannot prevent your instance from being co-resident with an adversary.
  • Side-channel exploitation — cross-VM information leakage due to shared physical resources; potential to extract RSA and AES secret keys.
  • Vulnerable VM isolation — a vulnerability may allow an escape to the hypervisor.
  • Lack of control over who you share the server with.

Attack model — two steps

  1. Placement: the adversary arranges to place a malicious VM on the same physical machine as the target customer.
  2. Extraction: extract confidential information via a side-channel attack.

Threat model (assumptions)

  • Provider and infrastructure are trusted. No attacks that subvert administrative functions; no exploitation of VMM vulnerabilities.
  • Adversaries are non-provider-affiliated malicious parties (ordinary customers) who can run and control many instances.
  • Victims run confidentiality-requiring services.
  • Two attack kinds: on some known hosted service, or on a particular victim’s service (targeted).

The four questions the study answers

  1. Can one determine where in the cloud infrastructure an instance is located? (cartography)
  2. Can one easily determine if two instances are co-resident on the same physical machine?
  3. Can an adversary launch instances that will be co-resident with a target’s instances?
  4. Can an adversary exploit cross-VM information leakage once co-resident?

EC2 background (as of 2009)

  • Three degrees of freedom when launching: instance type, region, availability zone.
  • Instance types: m1.small, c1.medium (32-bit), m1.large, m1.xlarge, c1.xlarge (64-bit). Regions: US, EU, Asia; regions split into availability zones with separate power and network (independent failures).
