  • Customers are assigned to a physical machine based on instance type, region and zone choices; an instance stays on one physical machine for its lifetime.
  • EC2 uses the Xen hypervisor. Dom0 = the privileged VM that manages guest images, provisions physical resources and access-control rights, routes packets to guests and appears as a hop in traceroute.
  • Each instance has an internal and an external IP address and domain name; inside the cloud both names resolve to the internal IP; outside, the external name maps to the external IP.

Q1 — Cloud cartography

  • Amazon doesn’t disclose placement; map EC2 to find where potential targets are and which creation parameters (zone, type) are needed for co-residence.
  • Hypothesis: different availability zones and instance types correspond to different internal IP address ranges.
  • Network probing with open-source tools nmap, hping, wget on ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS). External probe: from outside EC2 to an EC2 instance. Internal probe: from one EC2 instance to another. DNS lookups translate public IPs/names to internal IPs (~14,000 unique internal IPs found).
  • Findings: EC2’s internal address space is cleanly partitioned between availability zones, and instance types occupy disjoint ranges; assumption: internal IPs are statically assigned to physical machines (eases routing). So picking the same zone/type as the target likely lands you in the same IP block.

Q2 — Checking co-residency

Network-based checks — instances are likely co-resident if they have:

  1. Matching Dom0 IP address (first traceroute hop);
  2. Small packet round-trip times;
  3. Numerically close internal IP addresses (typically within 7).
  • Verified using a hard-disk-based covert channel (if two self-controlled instances can communicate over it, they are co-resident).
  • Efficient check against a target: compare internal IPs; do a TCP SYN traceroute to an open port and see if there’s a single hop (Dom0). Needs at most two TCP SYN packets, no full TCP connection → very quiet (victim unaware).

Q3 — Achieving co-residency

  • Brute-force placement: launch numerous probe instances and keep those that land co-resident.
  • Target recently launched instances: EC2 tends to assign fresh instances to a small set of machines.
  • Placement locality:
    • Instances launched simultaneously from the same account do not run on the same machine.
    • Sequential placement locality: two instances run sequentially are often assigned the same machine.
    • Parallel placement locality: two instances (different accounts) run at roughly the same time are often on the same machine.
    • Instance flooding: launch many instances in parallel in the right zone and type.

Q4 — Exploiting co-residency (cross-VM attacks)

  • Learn about resource usage of other instances; create/use covert channels to leak information intentionally.
  • Load-based co-residence check via cache usage (no network needed once co-resident); estimating traffic rates of a co-resident web server; keystroke timing attacks (infer passwords from timing).

Countermeasures discussed

Attack step Countermeasure Catch
Mapping Randomize IP allocation; block probing tools (nmap, traceroute) Randomization may hurt the provider’s resource optimization
Co-residency checks Prevent identification of Dom0 —
Co-location Don’t allow co-residence at all Good for users, inefficient for providers
Side channels — Information leakage via side channels remains a big challenge

Summary: shared physical infrastructure creates new risks absent from traditional computer/network security; practical attacks were demonstrated, along with countermeasures.

MCQ traps (6.3)

  • The two steps are placement then extraction (side channel).
  • The threat model trusts the provider and does not exploit VMM bugs; adversaries are ordinary customers.
  • Co-residency indicators: same Dom0 IP, small RTT, internal IPs within ~7.
  • Simultaneous launches from the same account → different machines; parallel launches by different accounts at the same time → often the same machine.
  • Probing used ports 80 and 443, tools nmap, hping, wget.
  • Disallowing co-residence is inefficient for the provider.

6.4 Security in collaborative SaaS clouds (L29)

Context

  • Cloud-unique issues: co-tenancy and lack of control over outsourced data and applications; general concerns: inadequate policies and practices, insufficient security controls.
  • Trust must go both ways — the provider must also be wary of malicious customers who use the platform to attack or peep into others’ data.
  • Provider security responsibility: IaaS → up to the hypervisor; PaaS → up to the platform/solution stack; SaaS → up to the application interface (SaaS consumers depend most on the provider).
  • Collaboration types: tightly coupled (federated) vs loosely coupled. Existing security mechanisms are mainly for tightly coupled systems; existing authentication/authorization in cloud is restrictive → securing loosely coupled collaboration is a major problem.
  • Motivation: SaaS has the maximum lack of control; no active data streams, audit trails or outage reports directly available; cloud marketplaces with many providers, inconsistent service guarantees and non-standard SLA clauses → choosing an ideal provider is hard.
  • Goal: select an ideal SaaS provider and secure loosely coupled collaboration (dynamic information sharing among e.g., sellers, payment providers, couriers).

The four-part framework (Dr. Nirnay Ghosh’s work)

Objective Approach Key points
1. Select a trustworthy and competent collaboration service provider (SelCSP) Model trust, reputation and competence of providers (interaction ratings + temporal metrics → trust & reputation → trustworthiness; recommendations + standard security controls in SLAs → competence; plus risk estimation) Present-day SLAs mostly guarantee availability only and have non-standard clauses on assurance and compensation → need a standard set of SLA parameters to reduce the perceived risk of outsourcing
2. Recommend access requests from anonymous users for authorization Risk-based access control using a fuzzy inference system (inputs: requester’s reputation, local object security level) → grants a subset of the requested permissions Gives access even when subjects lack proper permissions (with bounded risk); balances access risk vs security uncertainty due to information sharing; more flexible than binary MLS; challenge: computing security uncertainty; quantifying operational need
3. Map authorized permissions into local roles Inter-Domain Role Mapping (IDRM) — find a minimal set of roles that encompasses the requested permission set No polynomial-time solution (NP-hard) → greedy search heuristics (sub-optimal); multiple minimal role sets may exist, or none may match exactly; variants IDRM-safety and IDRM-availability; aim: minimal excess permissions (e.g., give read only if only reading is needed)
4. Dynamically detect and remove access conflicts Distributed secure collaboration framework using only local information Conflicts: cyclic inheritance conflict (a role gains write access via a cycle across domains that it should not have) and SoD (separation of duty) constraint violation (e.g., the person who issues a demand draft must not verify it); removal: if an exactly matching role set exists → RBAC hybrid hierarchy; otherwise create a virtual/collaborating role

MCQ traps (6.4)

  • Existing security mechanisms target tightly coupled (federated) systems; the hard problem is loosely coupled collaboration.
  • IDRM = map requested permissions to a minimal set of local roles; it is NP-hard, so use greedy heuristics.
  • SoD = one person must not perform two conflicting duties (issue and verify).
  • Risk-based access control is more flexible than binary MLS.
  • The provider’s SaaS responsibility extends up to the application interface.

6.5 Broker for cloud marketplace (L30)

Why a broker

  • Rapid growth of cloud services: many providers with varying QoS and many customer use cases with different requirements (e.g., Amazon VMs created per day grew enormously 2007–2011).
  • Need a middleman — an (intelligent) agent/broker that suggests the best provider for a customer and safeguards the customer’s interest.
  • Motivation: flexible provider selection · trustworthiness of providers · monitoring of services · avoiding vendor lock-in.

Objectives

  1. Select the most suitable provider satisfying the customer’s QoS requirements.
  2. Calculate the degree of SLA satisfaction and the provider’s trustworthiness.
  3. Decision support for dynamic service migration (move the application to another provider) based on experienced QoS.
  4. Handle the fuzziness of user requirements (they are rarely crisp).

Related approaches: CloudCmp (a tool that compares cloud providers’ QoS to help users choose) · fuzzy provider selection · a framework measuring satisfaction with a provider given fuzzy requirements · selection based on trustworthiness and competence.

QoS parameters: IaaS — 24×7 availability, bandwidth; SaaS — uptime, response time; also storage, security, trust, competence, risk, cost. Providers publish promised QoS values (e.g., 99.99 % uptime). Trust values are kept per parameter (e.g., trust 0.8 on availability), computed from history or third-party monitoring.

Marketplace broker architecture

Module Role
Provider selection decider Fuzzy inference engine: inputs = QoS offered by a provider + its trustworthiness; output = suitability of the provider for the customer; request dispatched to the provider with maximum suitability
Monitoring module Monitors QoS experienced by VMs (availability, bandwidth vs promised values) → computes SLA satisfaction per VM per parameter → feeds the provider trust calculator
Migration module (migration decider) Fuzzy inference engine: output = degree of SLA satisfaction for a service instance; if below a threshold → migrate; target provider chosen like in provider selection
  • Customer side: input membership functions built on the fly from user requirements, plus a rule list. Provider side: offerings are fuzzified → rules evaluated → defuzzified → provider fitness.
  • Linguistic levels: extremely poor, very poor, poor, medium, good, very good, excellent.

Evaluation (simulation)

  • 10 providers, 500 requests, simulated over 365 days; some providers degrade, with degraded QoS following a Gaussian distribution; compared with a conventional minimum-cost crisp broker.
  • Result: the fuzzy broker tracks user requirements better than the crisp broker on average availability, bandwidth, cost per VM-hour (IaaS) and response time, cost (SaaS) — “likely better, not always”.
  • Future scope: flexible QoS specification, production workloads, customer classes, extend to XaaS.

MCQ traps (6.5)

  • The fuzzy selection engine’s inputs are QoS offered + trustworthiness; its output is suitability.
  • The migration engine outputs the degree of SLA satisfaction; migration happens when it is below a threshold.
  • CloudCmp compares providers’ QoS.
  • The baseline compared against is a minimum-cost crisp broker.

Week 6 — High-yield takeaways

  1. CIA; interruption→availability, interception→confidentiality, modification→integrity, fabrication→authenticity.
  2. Threat classes: disclosure (snooping), deception (spoofing, repudiation, denial of receipt), disruption, usurpation (delay, DoS).
  3. Passive (release of contents, traffic analysis; hard to detect) vs active (masquerade, replay, modification, DoS).
  4. Policy vs mechanism; goals prevention–detection–recovery; secure R⊆Q, precise R=Q, broad otherwise.
  5. Cloud-specific: co-tenancy, lack of control, reputation fate-sharing; IDC 2008: security is the top concern.
  6. Gartner’s 7 risks; RPO (data loss) vs RTO (recovery time); hypervisor risks (rootkits, VM escape, shared clipboard, keystroke logging).
  7. EC2 study: placement + extraction; Dom0; co-residency = same Dom0, small RTT, IPs within 7; ~40 % success; countermeasures and their costs.
  8. Collaborative SaaS: SelCSP, risk-based access (fuzzy), IDRM (NP-hard, greedy), conflicts (cyclic inheritance, SoD).
  9. Broker: fuzzy selection (QoS + trust → suitability), monitoring → trust, migration when SLA satisfaction < threshold; beats crisp min-cost broker.

Week 7 — Mobile Cloud Computing, Fog Computing, Geospatial Cloud (Lectures 31–35)

Week 7 — Mobile Cloud Computing, Fog Computing, Geospatial Cloud (Lectures 31–35)

Source: L31 Mobile Cloud Computing – I · L32 Mobile Cloud Computing – II · L33 Fog Computing – I · L34 Fog Computing – II · L35 Use Case: Geospatial Cloud

High-yield: MCC definition, profiler/solver/synchronizer, MAUI vs COMET, cloudlet, the offloading energy formula (numerical!), cloud vs fog comparison table, fog enablers, fog use cases, geospatial cloud architecture and SDI.

7.1 Mobile Cloud Computing — basics (L31)

🎯
Your practice set for L31 (your file w4): 50 questions · 14 easy · 25 medium · 11 hard. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 7.

Why MCC

  • Huge growth of smartphones and smart applications; devices more resourceful; easy, low-cost high-bandwidth Internet access.
  • But resource challenges remain for resource-hungry apps: battery life, storage, bandwidth (and processing).
  • Cloud offers infrastructure, platform and software at low cost, elastically, on demand → combine them: Mobile Cloud Computing (MCC).

Definitions

  • MCC = a combination of cloud computing, mobile computing and wireless networks to bring rich computational resources to mobile users.
  • MCC provides mobile users with data storage and processing services in the cloud — moving computing power and data storage away from the mobile device.
  • Benefits mobile users, network operators and cloud providers (a “win” for all).
  • Mobile Backend as a Service (MBaaS): gives app developers a way to connect their apps to backend cloud storage and processing, abstracting away the complexity of launching and managing their own infrastructure, so they focus on front-end development; supports multiple apps, backends, developers, platforms, third-party integrations (APIs, SDKs, enterprise connectors).
  • Examples of mobile + cloud: Amazon Silk (a split browser), Apple Siri, Apple iCloud, image-recognition apps for augmented reality.

Why MCC — three reasons

Reason Meaning
Speed and flexibility Mobile apps can be built or revised quickly using cloud services; e.g., a new shortest-path heuristic is changed in the cloud, front end unchanged
Shared resources Apps running in the cloud are not constrained by device storage and processing; data-intensive processing runs in the cloud while user engagement continues on the device
Integrated data Quickly and securely collect and integrate data from various sources wherever it resides (e.g., disaster management with mobile sensors)

Key features: delivers apps quickly and securely with capabilities beyond local resources; uses fewer device resources (less battery, heat); supports many development approaches and devices (reusability/standardization); devices connect through an API architecture; improves reliability — information backed up in the cloud.

Architecture and offloading

Smart Mobile Device (SMD) ⇄ wireless network (service provider) ⇄ computational cloud

  • MCC = a framework to augment resource-constrained mobile devices to execute parts of a program on cloud-based servers.
  • Pros: saves battery; makes execution faster. Cons: must send program state/data to the cloud server — consumes battery; network latency can delay execution.
  • Network side: mobile devices connect to mobile networks via base stations; requests go to the operator’s central processors/servers; subscriber requests reach the cloud through the Internet; in the cloud, cloud controllers process requests and provide the services.

Dynamic runtime offloading — tricky issues:

  1. Dynamic application profiling and solver on the SMD.
  2. Runtime application partitioning.
  3. Migration of computation-intensive components.
  4. Continuous synchronization for the entire duration of runtime execution.

Key components (very examinable) | Component | Job | |—|—| | Profiler | Monitors application execution to collect data on time to execute, power consumption and network traffic | | Solver | Selects which parts of an app run on the mobile device and which on the cloud | | Synchronizer | Collects the results of split execution, combines them, and makes execution details transparent to the user | (Also: SMD synchronizer, mobile load manager, cloud data center.) Requirements: simple APIs (no knowledge of underlying network technology needed), web interface, Internet access to remotely stored applications.

Advantages of MCC

  1. Extending battery lifetime — computation offloading of heavy work to resourceful servers; remote execution can save significant energy.
  2. Improving data storage capacity and processing power.
  3. Improving reliability and availability — data/apps in the cloud reduce loss; comprehensive data security model possible (e.g., protecting copyrighted digital content, virus scanning, malicious-code detection in the cloud); always available while moving.
  4. Dynamic provisioning · scalability · multi-tenancy · ease of integration (services from different providers integrated through the cloud).

Challenges

  • Security and privacy: two categories — security of mobile users and securing data in the cloud. Mobile devices face malicious code; GPS/location-based services leak private info (location, mobility footprints). Approaches: move threat detection to the cloud — a host agent on the device inspects file activity while attack detection runs on a remote server; the smartphone records only a minimal execution trace and sends it to the cloud security server.
  • Context-aware mobile cloud services — use local context (data types, network status, device environment, user preferences) to improve QoS.
  • Network access management — improve link performance and optimize bandwidth usage.
  • Quality of service.
  • Pricing — multiple parties (mobile service provider + cloud provider) → business model and price sharing are tricky.
  • Standard interfaces.
  • Service convergence — services differentiated by type, cost, availability, quality; mobile users should be able to use multiple clouds in a unified fashion.

7.2 Mobile Cloud Computing — partitioning and offloading (L32)

Key challenge

  • Dynamically partition an application to optimize energy saving and execution time; middleware must decide which parts run locally and which remotely — a classic optimization problem; can be static (a priori) or dynamic (data/condition dependent), and needs synchronization, scheduling and resource management across different authorities (device owner, network operator, cloud provider).

MAUI vs COMET (classic comparison)

MAUI — Mobile Assistance Using Infrastructure COMET — Code Offload by Migrating Execution Transparently
Granularity Method-level Thread-level
Source code Programmer annotates each method as remoteable or not (needs source) Works on unmodified applications — no source code needed, only program binaries
Rules Native methods cannot be remoteable Executes multi-threaded programs correctly
Mechanism MAUI framework uses annotations to decide at runtime whether a method runs on the cloud server to save energy and time; MAUI client (mobile) + MAUI server (cloud); profiler + solver; RPC Distributed Shared Memory (DSM) in the runtime engine lets threads migrate between machines depending on workload; DSM = physically separate memories addressed as one logically shared address space; sends only modified parts of the heap to reduce traffic

Task-partitioning problem (formalization)

  • Input: a call graph of the application’s methods (edges = call/execution sequence).
  • Node attributes: energy to execute the method on the mobile device, and energy to transfer the program state to the remote server. (Energy for executing in the cloud is treated as negligible from the device’s view.)
  • Output: partition methods into two sets — executed on the mobile vs on the cloud.
  • Goal: minimize energy consumed (maximize energy saved = local energy avoided − transfer energy).
  • Constraints: total execution time/latency ≤ threshold (T or L); some (native) methods must execute on the device (highlighted nodes v1​,v4​,v9​ in the lecture’s example); total monetary cost limit; dependencies respected.
  • Static partitioning: when the app is launched, invoke an ILP solver (or heuristics) to decide where each method runs. Dynamic/adaptive partitioning: for long-running programs, conditions vary (bandwidth, remote availability, input-dependent energy) → re-partition.
  • Related approaches: estimate energy before execution; dynamic optimal partitioning from the communication vs computation trade-off; profiling at procedure-call level → cost graph → branch-and-bound to minimize total energy and data.

Challenges

  • Mobile communication issues: low bandwidth (radio resources are scarcer than wired; also varies over time), service availability (congestion, network failure, weak signal), heterogeneity (always-on connectivity, on-demand scalability, energy efficiency across heterogeneous networks).
  • Computing/offloading issues: offloading is not always effective in saving energy; it is critical to decide whether to offload and which portion of the code.

Cloudlet

  • A cloudlet is a trusted, resource-rich computer or cluster of computers that is well connected to the Internet and available for use by nearby mobile devices.
  • Middle tier of a 3-tier architecture: mobile device → cloudlet → cloud.
  • Decreases latency by using a single-hop network and can lower battery consumption using Wi-Fi/short-range radio (vs multi-hop WAN to a distant cloud).

When to offload — the energy formula (numerical!)

Symbols | Symbol | Meaning | |—|—| | Pc​ | Power (energy per second) of the mobile while computing (W) | | Pi​ | Power of the mobile while idle (waiting for the cloud) (W) | | Ptr​ | Power of the mobile while transmitting data (W) | | C | Number of instructions of the computation | | M | Speed of the mobile (instructions/s) | | S | Speed of the cloud (instructions/s); S=F⋅M | | F | Speed-up factor — how many times faster the cloud is | | D | Data to transmit (bytes/bits) | | B | Bandwidth (same unit per second) |

Energy saved by offloading: Esaved​=Pc​MC​−Pi​SC​−Ptr​BD​ Substituting S=FM: Esaved​=MC​(Pc​−FPi​​)−Ptr​BD​​

  • Interpretation: term 1 = energy you would spend computing locally; term 2 = energy spent idling while the cloud computes; term 3 = energy spent sending data.
  • Offload only if Esaved​>0. This happens when D/B is sufficiently small compared to C/M and F is sufficiently large ⇒ offloading is beneficial when a large amount of computation C is needed with relatively small data communication D.
  • Not all applications are energy-efficient when migrated to the cloud. Mobile cloud services must differ from desktop cloud services because they must save energy. Energy overheads of privacy, security, reliability, data communication are not included in this simple model.

Worked example (practice): C=109 instructions, M=108 instr/s (10 s locally), Pc​=0.9 W, Pi​=0.3 W, Ptr​=1.3 W, F=10, B=1 MB/s.

  • Local compute energy = 0.9 × 10 = 9 J; idle while cloud computes = 0.3 × (10/10) = 0.3 J.
  • If D=10 MB: transmit energy = 1.3 × 10 = 13 J ⇒ Esaved​=9−0.3−13=−4.3 J → don’t offload.
  • If D=1 MB: transmit = 1.3 J ⇒ Esaved​=9−0.3−1.3=7.4 J → offload. Effect of parameters: ↑C or ↑F or ↑B ⇒ more favourable; ↑D or ↑Ptr​ ⇒ less favourable; if F→∞, the idle term → 0.

MCQ traps (7.1–7.2)

  • Profiler measures time/power/traffic; solver decides placement; synchronizer merges results.
  • MAUI needs annotations (source code) at method level; COMET needs only binaries, migrates threads via DSM.
  • In MAUI, native methods are never remoteable.
  • Cloudlet = single-hop, nearby, trusted, resource-rich; it is the middle tier.
  • Offloading helps for compute-heavy, data-light tasks; it is not always beneficial.
  • In the formula, the idle term uses cloud time C/S; the transmit term uses D/B.

7.3 Fog computing — concept (L33)

Problem with cloud-only computing

  • All data must be uploaded to the cloud for processing → huge volumes (IoT, sensors, multimedia), much redundant data (10 sensors in a lab all reporting ≈ 20 °C).
  • Congestion in the core network (especially during exigencies like disasters) and long response time — bad for tasks needing very low response time (e.g., accident prevention).
  • Meanwhile, intermediate/edge devices (sensor sink nodes, routers, gateways, base stations) are increasingly resourceful but used only to store-and-forward.
  • Example: a sink node of a lab’s 10 temperature sensors can send the average (or just “within 18–22 °C: yes/no”) instead of all 10 readings.
  • Must keep the cloud’s key features: dynamic scalability, (almost) no infrastructure management at the user end, metered pay-as-you-go service.

Definition

  • Fog computing (also called “fogging” or edge computing) is a model in which data, processing and applications are concentrated in devices at the network edge rather than existing almost entirely in the cloud.
  • The term was first introduced by Cisco as a new model to ease wireless data transfer to distributed devices in the IoT paradigm.
  • Cisco’s vision: enable applications on billions of connected devices to run directly at the network edge; users can develop, manage and run software on Cisco network devices (hardened routers, switches) — Cisco brings open-source Linux and the network OS together in a single network device.
  • Fog = a paradigm that extends the cloud and its services to the edge of the network; it provides data, compute, storage and application services to end users (like a small, local instance of the cloud).
  • Fog performs some transactions/resource use at the edge instead of just channelling everything to cloud storage; it reduces bandwidth need by aggregating data at certain access points → lowers cost, improves efficiency.
  • Locality matters: Kolkata’s traffic lights have nothing to do with Delhi’s — decide locally, send aggregates upward.

Three-layer view

Layer Role
Cloud (data centers) Massive parallel processing, big-data mining, machine learning — more compute power and storage
Fog (cellular base stations, routers, Wi-Fi gateways, local servers) Real-time data processing, data caching, computation offloading — closer to users, more interactive and responsive
Edge/end devices (sensors, cameras, smart vehicles, phones) Basic data processing: pre-processing, compression; human–computer interface
  • Processing close to the devices lowers response time, enabling real-time applications (e.g., traffic signals timed by camera-measured flow).
  • Motivating developments: smart grid, smart traffic lighting, connected vehicles, software-defined networks — all generate huge data.

Fog enablers (list question)

Enabler Role
Virtualization VMs can run on edge devices
Containers Lightweight virtualization reduces resource-management overhead; e.g., Docker (dependencies travel with the app)
Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) Services provided to components via a communication protocol over a network; provider–consumer–registry; loosely coupled heterogeneous parties
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) Uses open protocols (e.g., OpenFlow) to apply globally aware software control at the network edge to access switches/routers that would typically use closed, proprietary firmware

Fog is not a replacement for cloud

  • Fog offloads part of the workload from the cloud to edge devices; handshaking/synchronization between fog and cloud is needed.

Benefits/characteristics of fog: low latency and location awareness · widespread geographical distribution · mobility · very large number of nodes · predominant role of wireless access · strong presence of streaming and real-time applications · heterogeneity (different sink nodes, but aggregated data in a standard format). Distinguished from cloud by proximity to end users, dense geographical distribution and support for mobility; improves QoS for real-time apps.

Security issues in fog

  • Devices are dispersed → maintaining security protocols across many fog devices is hard (cloud is centrally managed).
  • Man-in-the-middle attacks.
  • Privacy: intermediate processing can track vehicles or a household’s consumption.
  • Smart grid example: each smart meter/appliance has an IP address → a malicious user can tamper with his own meter, report false readings, or spoof IP addresses.

7.4 Fog computing — comparison, use cases, resource management (L34)

Why fog (recap)

Cloud helps IoT through scalability, resource provisioning and data intelligence, but has limits for real-time, latency-sensitive applications (responses in seconds/ms/µs — e.g., car collision alerts in a VANET). Fog computing was coined to serve real-time, latency-sensitive applications faster, leveraging local knowledge of data. Fog devices are not as resource-rich → resource management is central.

Cloud vs fog (classic comparison table)

Requirement Cloud computing Fog computing
Latency High Low
Delay jitter High Very low
Location of server nodes Within the Internet At the edge of the local network
Distance between client and server Multiple hops One hop
Security Undefined (user has little control) Can be defined (local authority control)
Attack on data en route High probability Very low probability
Location awareness No Yes
Geographical distribution Centralized Distributed
Number of server nodes Few Very large
Support for mobility Limited Supported
Real-time interactions Supported Supported
Type of last-mile connectivity Leased line Wireless

They are companions, not competitors — the right orchestration/synchronization between them is the key.

Use cases

  • Emergency evacuation systems — real-time info on affected areas/buildings, dynamic exit-route planning (blocked exits after fire/earthquake).
  • Natural disaster management — real-time notifications about landslides, flash floods to potentially affected areas.
  • Large sensor deployments — pre-process and summarize data before sending to cloud (reduce congestion).
  • IoT/big-data applications — connected vehicles, smart cities, wireless sensor and actuator networks.
  • Applicability: smart traffic lighting, connected vehicles, smart grid, wireless sensor networks, IoT, SDN.

Connected vehicles: rich connectivity — V2V, V2I, I2I; road-side units (RSUs)/access points; applications: safety, infotainment, alerts, traffic support, analytics; local fog decisions (a crash alert to approaching vehicles) instead of a round trip to the cloud; VANET. Fog attributes that make it ideal: geo-distribution, mobility, location awareness, low latency, heterogeneity. A fog orchestration and network management layer coordinates fog nodes with the cloud; large analytics go to the cloud. Smart grid: smart meters in homes → fog/micro-grid level decisions (e.g., campus-wide consumption) → aggregated data to the cloud for long-term analytics and provisioning. IoT stack: embedded systems & sensors → multi-service edge (fog) → core network → cloud data center.

Resource management in fog — challenges

  • Proper resource allocation among applications while ensuring end-to-end latency; increase throughput with high availability and scalability.
  • Aspects: utilization of idle fog nodes, more parallel operations, load balancing, meeting delay requirements of real-time apps, crash fault tolerance, scalability.
  • Specific issues: data may not be available at the executing fog node (must fetch from sensor/data source); an executing node may become unresponsive under heavy load (latency compromised); choosing a new node for micro-service migration; migrating partially processed persistent data; delivering the final result to the client/actuator in time; deploying application components on different fog nodes meeting latency; multiple applications co-located on one fog node → one app’s data may be compromised by another (multi-tenancy, worse because fog has fewer resources).
  • Approaches in literature: migrate to the nearest available node (may not be the most suitable); minimize carbon footprint (e.g., video streaming); resource prediction, estimation, (advance) reservation and pricing for new IoT apps; Docker as an edge-computing platform (fast deployment, elasticity, good performance); pricing based on customers’ fluctuating relinquish probability; joint base-station association, task distribution and VM placement as an LP formulation + heuristics.
  • Security: fog devices can’t run resource-hungry security measures; they may be compromised and used as a platform to launch attacks.

MCQ traps (7.3–7.4)

  • Fog term introduced by Cisco.
  • Fog: one hop, low latency, location-aware, distributed, very many nodes, mobility supported, wireless last mile; cloud: multi-hop, leased line, centralized, few nodes, limited mobility.
  • Both cloud and fog support real-time interactions (per the table).
  • Fog complements cloud; it does not replace it.
  • SDN enabler uses OpenFlow; containers enabler = Docker.
  • Security in fog “can be defined”; in cloud “undefined”.

7.5 Use case: Geospatial cloud (L35)

Geospatial data — characteristics

  • Information explicitly linked to a location on the Earth’s surface (coordinate-based). Over 90 % of data relates to some location (e.g., student records: hall, department, home PIN code).
  • Static (rarely changes — state/district boundaries, a building’s footprint, lakes) or dynamic (traffic, city population by day/night, footfall in a building, electricity demand).
  • Scale varies from metres to the globe; scale vs detail (a building is a point from the sky but a polygon close up); ecological fallacy.
  • Types: legal/political boundaries, cultural, climatic, economic data. Sources: social surveys, national surveys (Survey of India maps), remote sensing (air photos, satellite images), weather stations, GPS, pollution/air-quality/temperature sensors — maintained by different organizations in proprietary formats.
  • GIS = tools/platform for capturing, storing, querying, analyzing and displaying geospatial data; components: hardware, software, data (management), people (specialists).

Why move geospatial work to the cloud

  • Data-intensive and computation-intensive (shortest path on huge road graphs, map overlays).
  • Variable load on GIS servers ⇒ dynamic scaling in/out (utility computing fits).
  • Network-intensive web services — data lies with many organizations; users want services, not raw data (e.g., “shortest route from IIT KGP to Kolkata with POIs and congestion”, or “population and farmland within a 2-km buffer of a new canal”).
  • Need homogeneity (syntactic and semantic) — same reference system (e.g., lat–long), scale, data description, standard encoding and sharing — before querying across organizations.
  • Trend: from project mode to societal mode — data (taxpayers’ money) should be available ubiquitously, subject to policy and security.
  • Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI): treat spatial data as infrastructure (like the telecom infrastructure — hook in and use) for development planning and disaster management.
  • Organizations benefit: less infrastructure and spatial-service expertise needed, avoid the 3–5-year hardware refresh, share data with security controls, pay as you go, economy of scale, green computing.

Geospatial cloud — features

Shared resource pooling for organizations with common goals · choice of deployment, service and business models · managed services prevent data/work loss from outages · controls for secure data sharing · organizations acquire web-service space as needed (harvest only the services/data needed).

Architecture (cloud actors applied)

Customer → Negotiator (optional) → Broker(s) (agents for data sets/services) → Data centers (VMs hosting organizations' spatial data and spatial web services), with an SLA manager (checks SLAs aren’t violated) and (security) auditor.

  • Interface/“Interoperable” GIS: holds no data itself; a middle tier that connects consumers to different spatial service providers (resource allocation/manipulation, data services, interface services).
  • Stack: hardware → hypervisor → VMs (guest OS) → instances of spatial web services (per organization/state/district) — analogous to instantiating your own Google Docs domain on shared infrastructure.
  • Model: web services are the key technology; integrate data from heterogeneous back-end data services (inside or outside the cloud); can run through the PaaS model (makes load balancing and scaling transparent); a coordinating cloud with a central repository/registry knows where each organization’s data is; integrate into a unified format.

IIT KGP experiment (on Meghamala)

  • Bankura district (West Bengal): national highway network (from the highway authority) and local road network (state/district) in two separate VMs → a processing service merges them on the fly → shortest-path query over the combined network.
  • Canal + river data in separate VMs → merged water network → 500 m buffer to find flood-vulnerable areas.
  • Point: separate repositories pulled in service mode to answer a business rule, without moving whole datasets.

Challenges

  • Implementing spatial databases in the cloud (data semantics), auto-scaling spatial DBs, multi-tenancy and policy management among tenants, geographically situated backups, data security.
  • Interoperability at three levels: data level, service level, security level (different security policies on different data sets).
  • Security: multi-tenancy and lack of complete control over data/apps; which assets to deploy, their value, how they can be compromised.

MCQ traps (7.5)

  • Geospatial data can be static or dynamic; scale ranges from metres to globe.
  • Interoperability levels: data, service, security.
  • SDI treats spatial data as infrastructure.
  • Users want services (answers), not raw data; web services are the key technology.
  • Interface GIS holds no data itself.

Week 7 — High-yield takeaways

  1. MCC = cloud + mobile + wireless; moves compute/storage off the device; MBaaS; examples Silk, Siri, iCloud, AR.
  2. Profiler (time, power, traffic) → solver (what runs where) → synchronizer (merge results).
  3. MAUI = method annotation, remoteable, native local, RPC; COMET = binaries only, thread migration via DSM, sends modified heap.
  4. Esaved​=MC​(Pc​−Pi​/F)−Ptr​BD​ — offload when compute-heavy and data-light.
  5. Cloudlet = trusted, resource-rich, nearby, single-hop, middle tier.
  6. Fog = Cisco’s term; extends cloud to the edge; enablers: virtualization, containers (Docker), SOA, SDN (OpenFlow).
  7. Cloud vs fog table: latency, jitter, hops, location awareness, distribution, node count, mobility, last mile.
  8. Fog use cases: evacuation, disasters, sensor aggregation, connected vehicles (V2V/V2I/I2I, RSU), smart grid; security issues: dispersed devices, MITM, privacy, smart-meter tampering.
  9. Geospatial cloud: data/computation/network-intensive; SDI; broker + SLA manager + auditor; Bankura road and water-network merge demos; interoperability (data, service, security).

Week 8 — Docker Introduction, Green Cloud, Sensor Cloud, IoT Cloud, Course Summary (Lectures 36–40)

Week 8 — Docker Introduction, Green Cloud, Sensor Cloud, IoT Cloud, Course Summary (Lectures 36–40)

Source: L36 Introduction to Docker Container · L37 Green Cloud · L38 Sensor Cloud Computing · L39 IoT Cloud · L40 Course Summary and Research Areas

High-yield: Docker philosophy (develop–ship–run anywhere), shipping-container analogy, image vs container, VM vs container, Docker components and commands; green-cloud energy figures, DC architectures, server/switch energy models, PUE; sensor-cloud definition, virtual sensors and their 4 configurations, proxies; IoT definition, IoT architecture, MQTT/CoAP/AMQP, IoT-cloud components, vehicular cloud services.

Containers, Kubernetes and Docker architecture are covered in more depth in Week 10 (L47–L50).

8.1 Introduction to Docker containers (L36)

🎯
Your practice set for L36 (your file w5): 50 questions · 13 easy · 25 medium · 12 hard. Answers checked against this lecture. Full set and answer key: chapter “Your practice sets”, Week 8.

Motivation

  • Software must be redeployed, reconfigured or recompiled every time it moves from one environment to another (laptop → server → phone → another cloud). With many apps (static websites, Python workers, user DBs, analytics DBs, queues, API endpoints, web front ends) and many targets, the “app × environment” matrix explodes. Goal: tick every cell with minimal effort — anything runs anywhere.
  • Container technology bundles the application with all its dependencies into one unit that runs wherever the container fits.
  • Cloud is a platform to host containers — containers enhance cloud; they are not a competitor to it.

Shipping-container analogy

  • Goods of every kind (boxes, cars, barrels, pianos, servers) and every transport (trucks, forklifts, cranes, trains, ships) → chaos until a standard shipping container is introduced.
  • Inside the container, the product dictates (a piano needs a different environment than a car); outside, the infrastructure dictates (standard size and handling for any carrier).
  • Docker does the same for software: inside — the app with its libraries, binaries and dependencies; outside — any host that can run the container.

Docker basics

  • Docker: an open-source container management service; initial release March 2013.
  • Motto: “Develop, Ship, Run Anywhere” — build once, run on desktops, Android/iOS, any cloud (OpenStack, Azure, Bluemix, Amazon…).
  • A buzzword in modern development, especially agile projects.
  • Features: smaller OS footprint via containers (reduces the size of development) · teams (development, QA, operations) work seamlessly across applications · deploy anywhere — physical or virtual machines and the cloud · lightweight ⇒ easily scalable.

Docker components (lecture list)

Component Purpose
Docker for Mac / Linux / Windows Run Docker containers on that OS
Docker Engine Builds Docker images and creates Docker containers (sits on the host OS — loosely analogous to a hypervisor)
Docker Hub Registry used to host various Docker images (developers submit images for others)
Docker Compose Defines an application using multiple Docker containers

Traditional virtualization vs Docker

Traditional virtualization (bottom → top) Docker (bottom → top)
Server (physical) → Host OS (Linux/Windows) → Hypervisor (VMware, Xen, KVM, Hyper-V) → VMs each with a guest OS → apps Server → Host OS → Docker Engine → containers (apps + dependencies)
  • Container = an abstraction at the application layer that packages code and dependencies together.
  • Multiple containers run on the same machine and share the OS kernel, each as an isolated process in user space.
  • Containers take less space than VMs: images typically tens of MB, start almost instantaneously.
  • VMs run a full guest OS in each box → resource-intensive; disk image and app state entangled with OS settings, installed dependencies and security patches. Any change needs a new virtualized environment.
  • Containers share a single kernel; the image holds only the executable and its package dependencies (never installed on the host) → no configuration entanglement → runs anywhere; a small change saves only the difference between container A and A′.
  • Containers run natively on the host kernel → better performance than VMs, which get virtual access to host resources through a hypervisor; each container is a discrete process using no more memory than any executable.

Image vs container (definitions)

Term Definition
Image A lightweight, stand-alone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software — code, runtime, libraries, environment variables, config files
Container A runtime instance of an image — what the image becomes in memory when executed; runs completely isolated from the host environment by default, accessing host files and ports only if configured to

Workflow and commands

  • Source repository → build on the Docker engine → container image → push to a container image registry → users search, pull and run (Docker works in a client–server mode).
  • On a cloud: infrastructure → hypervisor → guest OS (VM) → Docker → containers, i.e., IaaS VMs can host containers.
  • Image commands: images (list local images) · run (create a container from an image and execute a command) · tag · pull (download an image from a repository) · rmi (delete a local image; also removes unused intermediate images).
  • Container commands: ps (list running containers) · ps -a (all containers including stopped) · top (processes in a container) · start, stop, pause · rm (delete a container) · commit (create an image from a container).
  • Dockerfile — a build script that creates an image automatically; can be versioned in Git/SVN with its dependencies. Docker Hub (hub.docker.com) is a public repository of images and can automatically build images from Dockerfiles on GitHub.
  • Applicability: application-level virtualization; one host runs several (e.g., spatial) applications for better utilization; build once, deploy/run anywhere; better collaboration.
  • Who uses Docker for what: developers — eliminate “works on my machine” problems; operators — run and manage apps side-by-side in isolated containers for better compute density; enterprises — build agile software-delivery pipelines to ship features faster and more securely.

MCQ traps (8.1)

  • Image = static package; container = running instance of an image.
  • Containers share the host kernel; VMs each have a guest OS.
  • Docker Hub = registry; Docker Compose = multi-container apps; Docker Engine = builds images/creates containers.
  • Containers are lighter and start faster than VMs and give better performance (native kernel access).
  • rmi removes images; rm removes containers; commit makes an image from a container; ps -a includes stopped containers.
  • Docker’s first release: March 2013.

8.2 Green Cloud (L37)

Why green cloud — the “dark side” of cloud

  • Data centers consume huge energy; the cost of computing equipment ≈ cost of environmental infrastructure (space, AC, power) — roughly “x and x”.
  • Scaling may hit a hard limit: money may be available but power supply may not.
  • Carbon footprint and environmental harm grow with consumption.
  • Inefficient placement wastes energy: spreading VMs 1 per server looks “load balanced” but packing them and putting idle servers in sleep/off mode saves energy (see Week 5 consolidation example).
  • Every layer matters: an inefficient algorithm at SaaS level (extra loops, CPU time) also wastes energy in the IaaS below.

Definitions

  • Green computing: the environmentally responsible and eco-friendly use of computers and their resources; more broadly, the study of designing, manufacturing/engineering, using and disposing of computing devices in a way that reduces their environmental impact.
  • Green cloud computing: aims to achieve not only efficient processing and utilization of computing infrastructure but also minimize energy consumption.

Facts and figures quoted (recognition)

Figure Value
Gartner (2007): IT industry’s share of world CO₂ emissions 2 %
US data centers’ share of US power (≈2006–07) 1.5 %, more than doubled since 2000, cost $4.5 billion
Data-center energy per square foot vs typical office building 10–100 times more
Energy share of data-center operational cost (OPEX) ≈10 %, could rise to 50 %
Cooling system cost $2–5 million per year
Energy breakdown in a data center IT equipment 40 %, power distribution 15 %, cooling 45 %
Data-center carbon emissions worldwide more than Argentina’s and the Netherlands’ emissions
Amazon: energy-related costs 42 % of total budget (direct power + cooling amortized over 15 years)
Google, Microsoft, Yahoo Build data centers near the Columbia River for cheap hydroelectric power (less transmission loss)

Data-center network architectures

Architecture Description
Two-tier Access and core layers; full-mesh core network; load balancing using ECMP (equal-cost multi-path); layer-3 switches at core, rack (layer-2) switches to servers
Three-tier (most widely used today) Access, aggregation and core layers; hierarchical; scales to over 10,000 servers
Three-tier high-speed Increased core bandwidth, 2-way ECMP, 100 Gigabit Ethernet links (vs 1–10 GE)

⚠️ Transcript slip: it says “load balancing using ICMP protocol” — the slide’s protocol is ECMP (equal-cost multi-path routing).

  • Faster architectures also consume more energy → performance vs energy trade-off.

Energy models

  • Server energy model: an idle server consumes about 66 % of its peak power (at peak CPU frequency) — fixed power for memory modules, disks, I/O, plus a CPU part that scales with frequency/load. ⇒ Idle servers waste energy; consolidate and switch off.
  • Switch energy model: Pswitch​=Pchassis​+nlinecards​⋅Plinecard​+r∑​nports,r​⋅Pr​ Typical share: chassis ≈ 36 %, line cards ≈ 43 %, port transceivers ≈ 11 %. Load-aware traffic distribution can cut switch energy.

Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE)

(The lecture mentions PUE as a measure without a formula; the standard definition is given here.) PUE=IT equipment powerTotal facility power​DCiE=PUE1​×100%

  • Ideal PUE = 1.0 (all power goes to IT); higher = worse.
  • Example using the lecture’s breakdown: IT = 40 % of total ⇒ PUE = 100/40 = 2.5, DCiE = 40 %.
  • Trap: PUE is total ÷ IT, not IT ÷ total (that is DCiE).

Performance vs energy; provider initiatives

  • Shift the focus from optimizing resource management purely for performance to optimizing energy efficiency while maintaining high service-level performance — reduce power cost, maximize revenue.
  • Providers must keep profit margins from being eroded by energy costs (e.g., Amazon 42 %; siting near hydro power).

Green cloud architecture

  • Green Cloud Broker / allocator (acts for consumers): lease cloud services, schedule applications; analyze user requirements, calculate cost and carbon footprint of services, carbon-aware scheduling, monitor CO₂; works with green negotiator, service analyzer, consumer profiler, pricing, energy monitor, service scheduler, VM manager, accounting → QoS- and energy-aware provisioning.
  • Green middleware per layer:
    • IaaS: virtualization + energy and temperature sensors, demand predictor.
    • PaaS: green profiler, power capping, green compiler, green resource allocation.
    • SaaS: power capping, green software services.
  • Summary: clouds are data centers offering subscription services with high energy use → high operating cost + environmental impact → need a carbon-aware green computing framework; many open research issues.

MCQ traps (8.2)

  • Cooling (45 %) > IT equipment (40 %) > power distribution (15 %).
  • Idle server ≈ 66 % of peak power — idle is far from free.
  • Three-tier (access–aggregation–core) is the most widely used DC architecture.
  • PUE = total facility / IT power; ideal 1.0.
  • Green computing covers the whole life-cycle (design, manufacture, use, disposal).

8.3 Sensor Cloud (L38)

Motivation

  • Sensors are everywhere (temperature, pressure, atmospheric, cameras, RFID, mobile phones, biological/physiological). Sensors → decision support/intelligence → actuators (a modern car may soon have more sensors than mechanical parts).
  • The Internet is a real-time information source (blogs, social networks); cloud handles the big-data revolution. Combining sensor data + Internet data creates demand that cloud can meet.
  • Wireless Sensor Network (WSN): seamlessly couples the physical environment with the digital world; sensor nodes are small, low-power, low-cost with sensing, processing, memory, communication bandwidth and battery constraints; in aggregate they have substantial data acquisition and processing capability. Nodes → sink/gateway → rest of the world (paths or clusters with cluster heads). Applications: environment, healthcare, education, defence, manufacturing, smart homes/phones.

Limitations of sensor networks (list question)

  1. Very challenging to scale sensor networks to large sizes (or change granularity).
  2. Proprietary, vendor-specific designs → hard to interconnect different sensor networks.
  3. Sensor data cannot be easily shared between groups of users (proprietary formats, no sharing mechanisms).
  4. Insufficient computational and storage resources for large-scale applications.
  5. Used for fixed and specific applications that cannot easily be changed once deployed.
  6. Slow adaptation of large-scale sensor network applications.

Limitation on the cloud side: the immense power of the cloud can only be fully exploited if it is seamlessly integrated into our physical lives — i.e., provide real-world information to the cloud in real time and let the cloud act and serve us instantly; add sensing capability to the cloud. Tourist scenario: a phone records gestures/activities (camera, mic), geographic data, wearable physiological sensors (cross-checked with medical records), speech recognition, image processing of restaurant logos, social-network friends — the phone alone cannot do all of this ⇒ need real-time processing of heterogeneous data sources (body-area networks to wide-area water-quality monitoring), automatic workflow formation and service invocation in the cloud, and swift processing using cloud power.

Definition of sensor cloud

Sensor cloud: an infrastructure that allows truly pervasive computation using sensors as an interface between the physical and cyber worlds, the data-computing clusters as the cyber backbone, and the Internet as the communication medium.

  • It integrates large-scale sensor networks with sensing applications and cloud computing infrastructure; collects and processes data from various sensor networks; enables large-scale data sharing and collaboration among users and applications in the cloud; delivers cloud services via sensor-rich devices; allows cross-disciplinary applications that span organizational boundaries.
  • Users can collect, access, process, visualize, archive, share and search large amounts of sensor data; supports the complete sensor-data life cycle (collection → decision support); sensor networks spread over huge areas can be connected together and used simultaneously by multiple users on demand.

Proxies

Proxy Role
Sensor-cloud proxy Interface between sensor resources and the cloud fabric; manages sensor resources and network connectivity; data format conversion (e.g., XML), interoperability, data cleaning and aggregation, data transfer to cloud storage
Sensor-network proxy For sensor resources that do not have a direct connection to the cloud

Use case — traffic flow sensors on traffic lights give real-time flow for drivers’ route planning; augmented with cheap humidity and temperature sensors they give a local heat index that supplements the meteorological department’s precise but sparse sensors — one physical infrastructure, several virtualized views (met dept, traffic dept, drivers).

Virtual sensors (core idea)

  • A virtual sensor is an emulation of a physical sensor that obtains its data from underlying physical sensors.
  • Provides customized views to users using distribution and location transparency.
  • WSN hardware can barely run multiple tasks and cannot host multiple VMs → virtual sensors act as images in software of the physical sensors.
  • A virtual sensor holds metadata about the physical sensors and the users currently holding them.
  • Layers: physical sensors (data processing, routing, power management, clock sync, local fault detection) → virtual sensors → virtual sensor groups (per application: met, traffic, disaster…) → end users. The sensor-cloud admin registers physical sensors and manages the infrastructure (sensors may go up/down).
  • Request flow: client → portal server (provisioning, resource management, monitoring) → virtual sensor groups → virtual sensors → physical sensors.

Four virtual-sensor configurations (very examinable) | Configuration | Meaning | |—|—| | One-to-many | One physical sensor ↔︎ many virtual sensors. Users each see their own virtual image, but the physical sensor is shared; the middleware computes the physical sensor’s sampling duration and frequency considering all users | | Many-to-one | Geographical area divided into regions, each with one or more physical sensors/WSNs; when a user needs aggregate data of a phenomenon for a region, all underlying WSNs for it are switched on and the user gets the aggregated value | | Many-to-many | Combination of one-to-many and many-to-one | | Derived | A versatile virtual sensor derived from a combination of multiple (different types of) physical sensors — e.g., proximity, light, temperature, humidity → answer “Are environmental conditions safe in a wildlife habitat?”; a generalization of the other three (lies in the type of physical sensors it communicates with) |

Layered sensor-cloud architecture

WSN providers → sensor-centric middleware (WSN registration, maintenance, data collection) → virtualization middleware (virtual sensor provisioning, management, image life cycle) → user interfaces (user repository, data repository, session and membership management). Summary: sensor-cloud infrastructure virtualizes sensors and provides management for them; users create virtual sensor groups dynamically by selecting templates; focuses on sensor system management and sensor data management; takes the burden of deploying and managing the network away from the user (mediator).

MCQ traps (8.3)

  • One-to-many = one physical → many virtual (middleware sets sampling); many-to-one = many physical (regions) → aggregate; derived = combine different types of sensors, generalizes others.
  • Sensor-network proxy is for sensors without direct cloud connectivity; sensor-cloud proxy does format conversion/aggregation.
  • WSN nodes cannot run multiple VMs → hence virtual sensors in software.
  • In the definition: sensors = interface, data-computing clusters = cyber backbone, Internet = communication medium.

8.4 IoT Cloud (L39)

Internet of Things

  • IoT = extending the current Internet and providing connection, communication and inter-networking between devices (physical objects, “things”).
  • Objects or people are given unique identifiers and the ability to transfer data over a network without requiring human-to-human or human-to-computer interaction.
  • A “thing”: a person with a heart-monitor implant, a farm animal with a biochip transponder, an automobile with sensors that alert the driver when tyre pressure is low, or any natural/man-made object that can be assigned an IP address.
  • Difference from a plain sensor deployment: in IoT the thing is uniquely identifiable; in a sensor deployment we mostly care about the data.
  • IoT includes actuation too (switch on a light/fan from a phone app).
  • Slogan: “any time, any place connectivity for anyone and anything.” Example: low fuel → alert driver + locate nearest station/workshop.
  • Wireless sensor technology bridges the physical and virtual worlds; things respond to changes in their physical environment (e.g., an electronic jacket heating up when it gets cold).

Basic IoT architecture

Things → Gateway → Network/Cloud Layered: devices → communication (MQTT, HTTP) → aggregation/bus layer (Enterprise Service Bus — ESB, message broker) → event processing and analytics → web portal, dashboard, API management; vertical: device manager, identity and access management.

Characteristics/issues of IoT systems

Issue Meaning
Scalability Growing numbers of sensors/devices
Big data Huge volumes to process/analyse
Role of cloud IoT often uses cloud for large storage/processing and flexible scaling
Real time Data flows continually; timely responses to event streams
Highly distributed From a room to a campus or city
Heterogeneity Diverse devices, data formats and networks (Wi-Fi, ZigBee, Bluetooth) → interoperability; handled locally by IoT gateways (the gateway hides the room’s heterogeneity from the outside world)

Why IoT + cloud (“IoT cloud”)

  • Cloud makes applications infrastructure-free, pay-as-used and on-demand; clients upload data and applications; services used without understanding the infrastructure; economy of scale; data/services stored remotely but accessible from anywhere.
  • Wide IoT deployment (logistics, smart city, healthcare, parking) creates high demand for data storage, processing and management in cloud data centers; cloud services are mature, with elastic computation and data-management scalability.
  • Cloud acts as both a computational/data-processing platform and a management platform for IoT.
  • Two-way coordination: a cloud service can request an IoT service (e.g., to reduce the amount of sensing data), and an IoT service can request cloud services to provision more resources.

Cloud components for IoT (reference architecture)

User layer (end-user apps) → proximity network (sensors/actuators, agents, firmware, network connectivity, user interface, devices) → IoT gateway (application logic, analytics agent, device data store) → public network (peer cloud, DNS, CDN, firewall, load balancer) → provider cloud (device registry, device management, API management, application logic, analytics, data repository, cognitive/actionable insight, streaming computation) → enterprise network (user directory, enterprise apps — e.g., car anomaly → cloud analytics → car maker’s workshop → corrective action).

iCOMOT (an IoT cloud system framework)

  • Top layer: a typical IoT application across IoT and cloud — light-weight analytics and control (near the edge) + large-scale data analytics (cloud).
  • Middle layer: the software layer built on cloud services and IoT elements — sensors, gateways, load balancer, event handler, message-oriented middleware, NoSQL databases, near-real-time data processing.
  • Bottom layer: iCOMOT tools/services to deploy, configure, govern, control and monitor the software layer.

Infrastructure, protocols and platforms

Category IoT side Cloud side Purpose
Infrastructure Industrial/common IoT gateways (e.g., Intel IoT gateway), OS containers (Docker) VMs and OS containers Execute software components
Connectivity protocols MQTT (Message Queue Telemetry Transport), CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol), HTTP MQTT, AMQP, HTTP Connect IoT elements with each other and with cloud services
Platform services Light-weight data services Load balancers (e.g., HAProxy), databases Core platform services

Case: IoT-based vehicular data cloud

  • A multi-layered vehicular cloud using IoT + cloud to address transport issues; two innovative services: intelligent parking and vehicular data mining (e.g., vehicle warranty analysis).
  • Architecture: IoT devices (sensors, actuators, GPS, smartphones; street lights, utilities, smart metering, road-side infrastructure) ⇄ communication (satellite, VANET, 3G/4G, Internet) ⇄ cloud (remote diagnosis, traffic, GIS, SaaS/PaaS/IaaS).
  • Services:
    • Network and data processing as a service — vehicles provide their networking and data-processing capability to other vehicles through the cloud.
    • Storage as a service — vehicles with unused storage (in the OBU — on-board unit) share it with vehicles needing more.
    • Cooperative information services (platform/community) — traffic information, hazard-location warning, lane-change warning (safety services).
  • Intelligent parking: modules — driver module, communication module (V2I, I2I), functional module (parking management, monitoring, checking, reservation, advertisement), application module; cars (with sensors/timestamps) find vacant lots via the gateway and cloud before reaching the parking lot.

Summary

IoT is dynamic and growing (domestic, commercial, industrial, health), needing large processing/storage and facing scaling, speed, safety, security and privacy challenges; cloud offers large, flexible, scalable resources ⇒ IoT cloud is an enabling technology for future applications.

MCQ traps (8.4)

  • MQTT = Message Queue Telemetry Transport; CoAP = Constrained Application Protocol (IoT side); AMQP listed on the cloud side.
  • IoT things have unique identifiers and communicate without human interaction.
  • Gateways handle heterogeneity/interoperability locally.
  • Coordination is two-way: cloud ↔︎ IoT services request each other.
  • Vehicular cloud: storage as a service via unused OBU storage; network & data processing as a service by vehicles.

8.5 Course summary and research areas (L40)

What the course covered (recap list)

NIST definition and XaaS; characteristics, advantages, disadvantages; evolution (cluster, grid, distributed → cloud as utility computing: pay-as-you-go, metered, scalable, no infrastructure at user end); architecture and service models; foundation technologies — SOA, web services, XML; SLA (uptime like 99 %/99.9 %; critical for banks, defence, disaster management, healthcare); cloudonomics (when to go to cloud — also security/privacy policy limits, e.g., labs on cloud but not student/employee data); resource management (finite resources, energy); data management (GFS, HDFS, big data, MapReduce); security (IAM, RBAC vs risk-based access control, trust/reputation/risk/competence, authentication, key management for encrypted data — e.g., competitive exams conducted on cloud); open-source and commercial clouds (OpenStack/Meghamala, Amazon, Azure, GCP, IBM Bluemix); companion technologies (fog, sensor cloud, containers/Docker, green cloud).

Research areas (recognition list)

Area Topics
Infrastructure and services Cloud architecture, storage/data architecture, distributed & cloud networking, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, storage-as-a-service, network-as-a-service, information-as-a-service, science-as-a-service
Management, operations, monitoring Cloud composition, service orchestration, cloud federation, bridging, cloud bursting, cloud migration, hybrid cloud integration, green and energy management (stressed as a key challenge), configuration and capacity management, workload profiling and deployment control, metering, monitoring and auditing, service management
