Week 9 — Cloud–Fog–Edge Paradigm, Resource Management, Cloud Federation, VM Migration Basics (Lectures 41–45)

Week 9 — Cloud–Fog–Edge Paradigm, Resource Management, Cloud Federation, VM Migration Basics (Lectures 41–45)

Source: L41 Cloud–Fog Computing – Overview · L42 Resource Management – I · L43 Resource Management – II · L44 Cloud Federation · L45 VM Migration – Basics, Migration Strategies

High-yield: health cloud–fog case study (levels, module placement, iFogSim results); resource-management taxonomy (architecture / infrastructure / algorithms); service placement (constraints, offloading, control); federation architectures and coupling levels; reasons for VM migration; cold vs live; pre-copy vs post-copy; downtime vs migration time.

The numerical analysis of VM migration (formulas) is in Week 10, L46.

9.1 Cloud–Fog computing overview and health case study (L41)

Recap and motivation

  • Cloud = XaaS (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, storage-aaS, DBaaS…), pay-as-you-go; NIST characteristics. It feels centralized: data goes to the cloud, results come back → network delay is a problem for mission-critical applications.
  • Fog = processing and applications concentrated in devices at the network edge instead of almost entirely in the cloud; term coined by Cisco to ease wireless data transfer to distributed IoT devices (Cisco’s routers etc. have spare compute).
  • Example: 4 studios × 10 temperature sensors = 40 sensors. Instead of sending all readings to the cloud, a local node checks whether each room is within range (e.g., 20–22 °C ± 2) and transmits only “within range” or anomalies → less load. The cloud still does global analytics across rooms.
  • Vision of fog: enable applications on millions/billions of connected devices to run directly at the network edge, reducing overall network traffic → saves delay, energy and cost.
  • Fog is not a replacement for cloud — it is complementary/supportive. The cloud takes global decisions and provisions services fog can’t; fog has low resources, is near the things, has no global view, may give better security, supports mobility and low latency.

Cloud–fog–edge layers

  • Edge = the sensing devices (IoTs, body sensors) — may do trivial processing (e.g., noise reduction) so cleaner data is sent. (Fog and edge are often used interchangeably; the line is thin.)
  • Fog = cellular base stations, network routers, Wi-Fi gateways, dedicated fog nodes — run applications on spare resources.
  • Cloud = global view and heavy analytics.
  • Communication is two-way: e.g., in health, edge (body-area network: pulse, heart rate, temperature, BP) → fog (pre-processing; can alert the patient immediately) → cloud (processed data/health metrics, sampled data) and back.
  • Gains: better response time (no round trip to cloud) and less data volume to cloud → lower energy and cost; fog can also pull other data (e.g., nearby meteorological data for agriculture).
  • Cost: you need fog-capable devices; new challenges — interoperability among heterogeneous fog nodes (routers vs phones), timing relationships, overall management of data flow; must check whether it actually gains for a given application.

Limitations motivating cloud–fog–edge

Layer Limitations
Cloud High latency; not an HPC platform; large data volumes need high bandwidth; not designed for the 3 Vs (volume, variety, velocity) of IoT big data; interoperability across IoT sources
Edge/IoT devices Limited processing, storage (e.g., a pulse oximeter doesn’t store data), power (especially when mobile)
Fog (benefits) Much lower latency (real-time use) · less network congestion · reduced cost of execution in the cloud · location awareness (fog knows its own coordinates → spatio-temporal data without sending GPS each time) · better handling of the colossal data generated by sensors · can help interoperability (fog nodes follow an agreed protocol towards the cloud)

Case study — health cloud–fog framework (IIT KGP lab)

Hierarchy: Level 0 = Cloud → Level 1 = ISP → Level 2 = Area gateway → Level 3 = Mobile devices → Level 4 = Sensors (e.g., EEG). The fog may be a network of devices, not one box. Upward traffic carries more data; downward carries analysed (smaller) data. Simulation tools: CloudSim (from the University of Melbourne) and iFogSim (developed jointly by IIT Kharagpur and the University of Melbourne). Application modules (flow): EEG sensor → client module → data filtering module → data processing module → event handling module → confirmatory module (confirms the event/alert) → client module → display/actuator (inform patient).

Module placement compared | Module | Fog-based placement | Cloud-based placement | |—|—|—| | Client module | Mobile | Mobile | | Data filtering | Area gateway | Cloud | | Data processing | Area gateway | Cloud | | Event handling | Area gateway | Cloud | | Confirmatory module | Cloud (needs the global view) | Cloud |

Results (synthetic lab setup — not to be over-generalized):

  • Network usage: very low for fog (only positive/candidate cases go to the cloud’s confirmatory module); high for cloud (every module’s data travels to the cloud).
  • Cost of execution in the cloud: much higher with cloud-based placement (fog uses surplus local resources at practically no extra cost).
  • Latency: roughly stable for fog; increases for cloud as configurations scale.
  • Energy: data-center, mobile and edge energy patterns differ by placement. Prototype: wearable health bands → Raspberry Pi as fog devices → AWS or in-house OpenStack as cloud (in-house has little network delay inside the IIT KGP network); medical-domain logic decides alerts (“see a doctor”), part on the fog and part in the cloud.

MCQ traps (9.1)

  • In the fog placement, the confirmatory module stays in the cloud (global view); filtering/processing/event handling go to the area gateway.
  • iFogSim = IIT KGP + University of Melbourne; CloudSim = University of Melbourne.
  • Cloud is not an HPC platform.
  • Fog complements the cloud; communication is bidirectional.

9.2 Resource management in cloud–fog–edge — I (L42)

Why resource management at fog/edge

  • Processing IoT data directly in the cloud is inefficient for time-sensitive applications and uses a lot of network → fog/edge processing close to data sources.
  • But adding IoT devices is not automatically a win: some fog/edge resources become over-constrained while others have spare capacity → resource management is necessary (and itself costs resources and time).
  • Issues: resource allocation, workload balancing, resource provisioning, task scheduling, QoS.
  • Fog/edge benefits recap: latency (aggregate before sending; some decisions — e.g., temperature alarm — at the edge; aggregation of several sensors at fog avoids one misbehaving sensor’s false alarm), reliability, faster response, interoperability (convert °C vs °F from different sensor makes at edge/fog), and even privacy/trust (strip patient identity before sending to the cloud, re-attach on return; fog may be within your premises).

Fog environment model

  • Three layers: client (edge) layer, fog layer, cloud layer.
  • The fog layer accomplishes the clients’ resource requirements; if resources in the fog are unavailable or limited, the request is passed to the cloud layer (or to collaborating fog nodes). The cloud also handles global computations (e.g., campus-wide AC health statistics).
  • Fog server manager employs the available processors for clients; VMs on fog data servers process the data and deliver results to the fog server manager; fog servers use server virtualization. A fog layer may form a fog data center/fog network needing management. Must handle mobility (device moves from one fog node’s area to another → hand-off without losing aggregated data).
  • Scenarios: VANET — vehicles’ sensors and OBUs communicate V2V or V2I with road-side infrastructure, which connects to cloud data centers (e.g., certificate revocation, correlating slowdowns with accidents); highly mobile, frequent make-and-break. Healthcare — body-area network → nearest hop/mobile device (fog) → health cloud. Static cases — room temperature/humidity sensors.
  • Trend: dedicated micro data centers and Internet nodes (routers, gateways, switches) augmented with computing; bring computing down from the cloud towards the sensor end.

Taxonomy of resource management (survey: Hong & Varghese, 2019)

Three pillars: Architecture, Infrastructure, Algorithms.

Pillar Component Meaning
Architecture Data flow Direction of workload movement: aggregation, sharing, offloading (user → edge, or cloud → edge)
Control How resources are controlled: centralized (one controller for many edge nodes), distributed, (hierarchical)
Tenancy Whether a single application or multiple applications are hosted on an edge node
Infrastructure Hardware Small-form-factor devices: network gateways, Wi-Fi routers, set-top boxes, small home servers, edge ISP servers, cars/vehicles, drones used as compute servers
System software Runs directly on fog/edge hardware (CPU, memory, devices); manages and distributes resources — OS, virtualization software
Middleware Runs on the OS and provides complementary services not supported by system software — coordinates distributed nodes, deploys VMs and containers
Algorithms Discovery Identify edge resources onto which workloads (from cloud or user devices) can be deployed
Benchmarking Capture performance of resources (CPU, storage, network) — guides decisions
Load balancing Distribute tasks across edge data centers efficiently (optimization, search) — avoid skew
Placement Place incoming tasks on suitable resources considering availability and environmental change (dynamic-condition-aware or iterative techniques)
  • Architecture choice depends on the application: static sensors → centralized control may suffice; vehicles over a large area → distributed control.

MCQ traps (9.2)

  • Fog environment = client/edge, fog, cloud layers; fog serves requests and forwards to cloud when resources are limited.
  • Taxonomy pillars: Architecture (data flow, control, tenancy) · Infrastructure (hardware, system software, middleware) · Algorithms (discovery, benchmarking, load balancing, placement) — don’t mix components across pillars.
  • Middleware (not system software) deploys VMs/containers and coordinates nodes.

9.3 Resource management in cloud–fog–edge — II: service placement (L43)

Service placement problem

  • A fog orchestration engine/orchestrator decides placement so that load isn’t skewed and time and energy are optimized. Fog is highly virtualized, providing compute, storage and control between end users and cloud servers; it acts as an interoperability layer.
  • Key considerations: location awareness (vehicle → nearest RSU; ambulance sending patient data along its route), low latency, better bandwidth utilization, scalability, mobility support.

Survey structure (service placement — four groups)

Group Contents
Problem statement Infrastructure model, application model, deployment pattern
Service placement taxonomy Control plane design, placement characteristics, system dynamicity, mobility support
Optimization strategies Objectives (latency, resource utilization, cost, energy consumption), metrics, problem formulation, resolution strategies
Evaluation environment Analytical tools, simulators, experimental test-beds

Worked placement example — video capture & recognition (Google Glass)

Pipeline: vision capture (A) → coarse feature extraction (B) → face recognition (C) / object recognition / OCR → learning-based activity inference → rendering → display effect (H). | Component | Placed on | |—|—| | Vision capture, coarse feature extraction, display | The device (Google Glass) | | Face recognition | Local laptop/edge server via a smart Wi-Fi gateway (too heavy for the Glass) | | Object recognition | LAN router with spare compute | | OCR | Cloudlet | | Learning-based activity inference | Cloud (heavy compute; may need external data/models) | | Rendering | Smart Wi-Fi gateway | → Distributing across edge/fog/cloud gives better efficiency, lower latency, better scalability, mobility (another gateway takes over as the user moves).

Application placement — definition and constraints

  • Application placement = the mapping pattern by which application components and links are mapped onto the infrastructure graph (computing devices and physical edges/links). Requires finding available resources and their free capacity, and matching application requirements (e.g., face recognition needs ≥ 500 MB RAM).
  • A centralized or distributed/collaborative orchestration manager handles it; providers aim for optimal or near-optimal placement.
Constraint type Examples
Resource-level Finite CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth of each node
Network-level Latency, bandwidth
Application-level Locality (restrict services to a specific location — e.g., “must not leave the IIT KGP network”), delay sensitivity/deadlines

Offloading (the core mechanism)

  • Offloading = moving a server/application and its data towards the network edge; augments computing of user devices; then results must be aggregated/assembled. | Direction | Techniques | |—|—| | User device → edge (typically single hop) | Application partitioning, caching mechanisms | | Cloud → edge | Server offloading (replication of servers at the edge, or partitioning a server across edge nodes), caching (content-popularity-based, multi-layer) |

Control of placement

Control Approaches
Centralized Solver-based, graph-matching-based
Distributed Blockchain-based, game-theoretic, genetic-algorithm-based

Infrastructure, system software, middleware, algorithms (detail)

  • Hardware: fog/edge uses low-power, small-form-factor devices that already exist with spare capacity — compute devices (single-board computers, commodity products) and network devices (gateways, routers, Wi-Fi access points, edge racks) — together enabling processing of IoT and CPS data.
  • System software must support multi-tenancy and isolation:
    • System virtualization: VMs, containers, VM and container migration.
    • Network virtualization: SDN (separates control plane and data plane; modern switches are mostly SDN-enabled), NFV, overlay networks.
  • Middleware provides performance monitoring, coordination, orchestration, communication facilities and protocols — e.g., volunteer edge computing, hierarchical fog computing, mobile fog computing, cloud orchestration management.
  • Algorithms — discovery (identify edge resources; programming infrastructure, handshaking protocols, message passing), benchmarking (capture resource performance to maximize placement quality), load balancing (by priority, fairness…), placement (identify resources appropriate for a workload).

MCQ traps (9.3)

  • Optimization objectives listed: latency, resource utilization, cost, energy consumption.
  • Constraints: resource-level, network-level, application-level (locality, delay sensitivity).
  • Device→edge offloading uses application partitioning and caching; cloud→edge uses server offloading (replication/partitioning) and caching.
  • Centralized control: solver, graph matching; distributed: blockchain, game theory, genetic algorithms.
  • SDN separates control and data planes.

9.4 Cloud federation (L44)

Definition

  • Federated cloud (cloud federation): the deployment and management of multiple external and internal cloud services to match a business need. A federation is a union of several smaller parts that perform a common action.
  • Example: IIT KGP’s Meghamala (internal only) runs an exam for 2000 first-year students; if capacity is short, borrow capacity from external providers — seamlessly, with timing constraints met.
  • Collaboration between CSPs to achieve: capacity utilization (lend surplus at a price) · enhanced interoperability · cataloguing of services (a global catalogue of the federation’s services) · insight about providers and SLAs (how much each exposes depends on coupling).

Motivation

Maximize resource utilization · minimize power consumption · load balancing · global utility · expand CSPs’ footprint (each CSP effectively shares the others’ footprints → marketability, profitability).

Characteristics

  • Overcome current cloud limitations — service interruption, lack of interoperability, degradation of services (other members absorb overloads/faults).
  • Cloud federation is one of several inter-cloud organizations.
  • Voluntary participation (not regulated/forced).
  • Maximum geographical separation — ideally in different power zones, network zones, seismic zones so one disaster doesn’t hit all members (high reliability).
  • Well-defined marketing system and regulated federation agreement.
  • An environment where multiple service providers share their resources.
  • Issues to solve: portability between providers; interoperability of services and data.

Coupling levels

Coupling Interoperation Control over remote resources Monitoring info Advanced features
Loosely coupled Limited Little or none (VM placement unknown) Limited — e.g., CPU, memory, disk consumption of VMs Usually none — no cross-site networks, no VM migration
Partially coupled Via a contract/framework agreement stating terms under which one partner uses another’s resources Some — e.g., affinity rules forcing VMs onto the same physical cluster More — e.g., host of each VM, energy consumption Some advanced networking — e.g., virtual networks across site boundaries
Tightly coupled Clouds normally governed by the same administrator (same corporation) Advanced — e.g., decide exact placement of remote VMs All available monitoring info Cross-site networks, cross-site VM migration, high-availability techniques, virtual storage across sites

Federation architectures (classic matching question)

Architecture Description Coupling
Cloud bursting / hybrid Combines existing on-premise infrastructure (usually a private cloud) with remote resources from one or more public clouds to provide extra capacity for peak demand (don’t size the private cloud for the peak); local cloud OS has no advanced control over remote virtual resources beyond basic operations; supported by most existing cloud managers Loosely coupled
Broker A broker serving various users has access to several public clouds; a simple broker deploys resources in the cloud selected by the user; an advanced broker offers service management — scheduling decisions based on cost, performance, energy — and may distribute service components across clouds; the most common federation scenario (easy to implement/maintain, preserves providers’ privacy) Loosely coupled (public clouds don’t allow advanced control)
Aggregated Two or more partner clouds interoperate to aggregate their resources and present users with a larger virtual infrastructure; partners get some advanced control over remote resources; coupling is higher when partners belong to the same corporation than when different companies agree to cooperate Partially coupled
Multi-tier Two or more cloud sites, each running its own cloud OS, usually belonging to the same corporation, managed by a third (root) cloud OS instance in a hierarchical arrangement; the root has full control over the sites’ resources and exposes them as if located in a single cloud; good for corporations with geographically distributed infrastructure (uniform access) and for high availability, load balancing, fault tolerance Tightly coupled

MCQ traps (9.4)

  • Bursting & broker = loosely coupled; aggregated = partially coupled; multi-tier = tightly coupled.
  • Cross-site VM migration needs tight coupling; loosely coupled federations usually can’t migrate VMs.
  • Partially coupled ⇒ contract/framework agreement, affinity rules, energy info.
  • Broker is the most common federation scenario; multi-tier is hierarchical under a root cloud OS.
  • Federation members should be geographically separated (power/network/seismic zones).

9.5 VM migration — basics and strategies (L45)

What and why

  • VM migration: the process of moving running applications or VMs from one physical host/server to another. What moves: process (CPU) state, memory, storage, network connections (and active I/O).
  • Why migrate: | Reason | Explanation | |—|—| | Load balancing | Allocation/de-allocation leaves some servers overloaded; distribute VM load fairly | | Maintenance | Server needs maintenance → move its VMs transparently (customer only cares about SLA) | | Power management / operational parameters | Consolidate VMs on fewer servers; put underutilized servers into low-power mode | | QoS violation | If the provider fails to meet QoS, a user can migrate the VM to another provider (inter-provider) | | Fault tolerance | On (anticipated) failure, migrate VMs to another data center (proactive fault tolerance) | | Resource sharing (L46) | Relocate VMs from overloaded to under-loaded servers to relieve memory/cache/CPU contention |

Cold vs live migration

Cold / non-live migration Hot / live migration
During migration VM on the source is turned off or suspended VM continues to provide service — not suspended
User impact Downtime (may incur penalties/credits); for large VMs downtime can be very high; severe degradation for real-time apps Nearly seamless — user practically unaware
Complexity Simple, easy to implement Tricky; needs a defined process
  • Live migration moves the entire VM — all user processes and kernel state — without shutting it down.
  • Two main live-migration approaches: pre-copy and post-copy.

Costs and goals

  • Costs: communication overhead, migration time, downtime → may violate SLAs (penalty) and hurt reputation.
  • Downtime = total time during which services remain unavailable to the user. → minimize.
  • (Total) migration time = total time taken to move a VM from source to destination host (whole process). → minimize (migration is overhead).
  • Migration should not disrupt active services through resource contention (CPU, network bandwidth) at source/destination.

What must be migrated

Item Notes
CPU context of the VM Small; transferred during stop phase
Main memory contents The big one — dominates time
Disk If on NAS accessible from both hosts → just reconnect; local disk can be mirrored; disk data migration may be non-critical
Network If both hosts on the same LAN: migrate the IP, advertise the new MAC↔︎IP mapping via ARP reply, switches learn the new MAC location; packets redirected with transient losses; otherwise proxying etc.
I/O devices Virtual I/O devices are easier to migrate; direct assignment of physical devices to VMs is hard to migrate

Memory migration phases

  • Push: source VM keeps running while pages are pushed to the destination; pages modified during the process are re-sent (consistency).
  • Stop-and-copy: source VM stopped, pages copied, new VM started.
  • Pull: new VM runs; if it accesses a page not yet copied → page fault → page pulled across the network from the source.
  • Pure stop-and-copy: simple, but both downtime and total migration time ∝ VM memory size → unacceptable outage for live services.

Pre-copy live migration (iterative)

  1. (Iterative) pre-copy phase: VM keeps running at the source; all pages are copied in round 1; in later rounds, pages dirtied during the previous round are re-sent.
  2. Pre-copy termination — stop iterating when any threshold is hit:
    • number of rounds exceeds a threshold (Nmax​);
    • total memory transmitted exceeds a threshold;
    • number of dirty pages in the previous round drops below a threshold.
  3. Stop-and-copy phase: VM suspended at the source; remaining dirty pages and CPU state copied to the destination.
  4. Restart/resume phase: VM restarted at the destination.
  • Downtime ≈ stop-and-copy + restart (small if few dirty pages remain).

Post-copy live migration

  1. Stop phase: stop the source VM and copy the CPU state to the destination.
  2. Restart the destination VM (its memory is empty).
  3. On-demand copying: when the VM touches a page not yet copied, it is fetched from the source (demand paging; also active push and pre-paging). Many pages may never be used, so only what’s needed is copied.
  • Each page is transferred at most once (contrast with pre-copy where hot pages are re-sent).

MCQ traps (9.5)

  • Cold = VM off/suspended during migration; live = keeps running.
  • Pre-copy: memory first (iteratively), CPU state last; post-copy: CPU state first, memory on demand.
  • Pre-copy stops on rounds / total data / dirty pages below threshold.
  • Pure stop-and-copy: downtime and migration time both ∝ memory size.
  • Moving the IP on the same LAN uses an ARP reply to announce the new MAC mapping.
  • Downtime ≠ migration time (in live migration downtime ≪ migration time).
