Week 10 — VM Migration Analysis, Containers & Kubernetes, Docker Architecture and Demo (Lectures 46–50)

Week 10 — VM Migration Analysis, Containers & Kubernetes, Docker Architecture and Demo (Lectures 46–50)

Source: L46 VM Migration – analysis and strategies · L47 Containers, Container-based Virtualization, Kubernetes, Docker Container · L48 Docker Container – Overview, Components, Architecture · L49 Docker Container – Demo (install) · L50 Docker Container – Demo (MySQL + phpMyAdmin, ship to Windows)

Numerical alert: the pre-copy migration-time and downtime formulas (§10.1) are prime numerical-MCQ material. Basics of migration are in Week 9 (§9.5); the first Docker introduction is in Week 8 (§8.1).

10.1 VM migration — analysis and multi-VM strategies (L46)

Why migrate (recap, L46 list)

Load balancing (unbalanced hosts, impending downtime) · proactive fault tolerance (anticipate failure, guarantee critical availability/reliability) · power management (move VMs off lightly loaded servers, put those servers in sleep/off mode) · resource sharing (relieve memory/cache/CPU contention by moving VMs from overloaded to under-loaded servers) · system maintenance (upgrades without long provider downtime, which hurts credibility and revenue).

Pre-copy recap and who uses it

  1. Iterative push: all pages sent while the VM runs; pages dirtied (modified) during a round are re-sent in later rounds → frequently written pages are sent many times → long migration time.
  2. Termination when any holds: iterations exceed a limit (Nmax​) · total memory sent exceeds a threshold · dirty pages in the last round fall below a threshold.
  3. Stop-and-copy: suspend the VM at the source; send CPU state + remaining dirty pages.
  4. Commit/resume: the hypervisor resumes the VM at the destination.
  • KVM, Xen and VMware use the pre-copy technique for live migration.
  • Flow: start → select destination server → reserve resources at destination → treat whole memory as dirty and copy → iteratively copy dirty pages → (threshold met) suspend VM, transfer VM state (CPU registers, remaining memory) → resume at destination → commit.
  • Post-copy flow: start → select destination → reserve resources → capture VM state (CPU registers, I/O state) → transfer minimal state → resume VM at destination → active push of memory pages; on a page fault, copy the faulted page from the source → done when all pages are transferred. Techniques: demand paging, active push, pre-paging (prefetching).

Notation (lecture)

Symbol Meaning
Tmig​ Total migration time
Tdown​ Total downtime
Vm​ Memory size of the VM
R Transmission rate (assumed constant during migration)
P Page size
D Dirty page rate (pages dirtied per second)
r=RP⋅D​ Dirtying ratio — memory-dirtying rate ÷ transmission rate
n Number of pre-copy iterations (rounds after round 0)
Vth​ Threshold of remaining (dirty) memory at which iterations stop
Nmax​ Maximum allowed number of iterations
Tres​ Time to restart (resume) the VM at the destination

Non-live (cold) migration

Tmig​=RVm​​,Tdown​≈Tmig​ (Memory transfer dominates; CPU-state transfer is small. The VM is down for the whole transfer.)

Pre-copy live migration — derivation result

  • Round 0 sends the whole memory: T0​=RVm​​.
  • During round 0, PDT0​ bytes get dirty → round 1 takes T1​=RPD​T0​=rT0​; in general Tj​=rjRVm​​.
  • Round n (the stop-and-copy round) takes Tn​=rnRVm​​. Tmig​=j=0∑n​Tj​+Tres​=RVm​​⋅1−r1−rn+1​+Tres​​ Tdown​=rnRVm​​+Tres​​ Number of rounds: iterate until the remaining dirty memory rnVm​≤Vth​, capped at Nmax​: n=min(⌈logr​Vm​Vth​​⌉,Nmax​)

Interpretation and parameter effects

  • Needs r<1 (dirtying slower than the network) for the geometric series to shrink; if r≥1 the rounds never shrink → stop at Nmax​ (long downtime) — post-copy or throttling helps.
  • ↑ R (bandwidth) → ↓ both Tmig​ and Tdown​. ↑ dirty rate → ↑ r → more rounds, longer Tmig​, possibly larger Tdown​. ↑ Vm​ → both scale up proportionally.
  • Downtime ≪ migration time in live migration (only the last small round + restart); in cold migration they are equal.
  • Assumptions: constant R, constant dirtying rate, thresholds as given; I/O and network re-mapping ignored (they make it more complex). Why compute it: to plan maintenance windows and estimate how long fault-triggered migration takes.

Worked example: Vm​=1024 MB, R=100 MB/s, dirtying rate P⋅D=20 MB/s ⇒ r=0.2; Tres​=0.1 s.

  • Cold: Tmig​=Tdown​=1024/100=10.24 s.
  • Pre-copy with n=3: Tmig​=10.24×0.81−0.24​+0.1=10.24×1.248+0.1≈12.88 s; Tdown​=0.23×10.24+0.1=0.082+0.1≈0.18 s.
  • Rounds for Vth​=1 MB: need 0.2n≤1/1024 ⇒ n≥ln(1024)/ln(5)=6.93/1.61≈4.31 ⇒ n=5 (if Nmax​≥5).
  • Trade-off: live migration takes longer in total (12.9 s vs 10.2 s) but cuts downtime from 10.2 s to ~0.2 s.

Migrating multiple VMs (m VMs of equal size, one source → one destination)

Serial migration Parallel migration
How First VM runs its pre-copy cycle at the full rate R while the other m−1 VMs keep serving All m VMs start pre-copy simultaneously; each gets about R/m of the bandwidth
Stop phase When the first VM enters stop-and-copy, the remaining m−1 VMs are suspended (so they stop dirtying memory) and copied after it Equal sizes and rates ⇒ all VMs enter and finish stop-and-copy at about the same time
Downtime Stop-and-copy of the first VM + migration time of the other m−1 VMs + time to resume the VMs Stop-and-copy time of any one VM (at rate R/m) + resume time
  • Multiple-VM migration is typical for maintenance or fault recovery (a whole host is evacuated); single-VM migration is typical when one VM needs more resources than its host has.

MCQ traps (10.1)

  • r=PD/R; migration time is a geometric sum, downtime is only the last term (+ restart).
  • Cold: downtime = migration time = Vm​/R.
  • Pre-copy converges only if r<1.
  • KVM, Xen, VMware use pre-copy.
  • Serial: others are suspended when the first enters stop-and-copy (to stop dirtying). Parallel: each VM gets R/m.
  • Live migration increases total migration time but reduces downtime.

10.2 Containers and Kubernetes (L47)

Container — core concept

  • Shipping-container analogy: a self-contained box of standard size/shape; carriers don’t care what’s inside → large-scale interoperability.
  • A container is a lightweight virtualization technique. It packages the code and all its dependencies so the application runs quickly and reliably from one computing environment to another (Linux → Windows → Mac → cloud).
  • Containers are lightweight packages of application code together with dependencies such as specific versions of programming-language runtimes and libraries required to run the software services.
  • They share CPU, memory, storage and network resources at the OS level and offer a logical packaging mechanism in which applications are abstracted from the environment in which they actually run → decoupling → deploy easily and consistently on laptop, data center, or public cloud.
  • Supports agile development (no worry about environment dependencies), efficient operations (use just the resources needed), and run anywhere.

Three benefits (list question)

Benefit Meaning
Separation of responsibilities Developers focus on application logic and dependencies; IT operations teams focus on deployment and management, not application details
Workload portability Run virtually anywhere — Linux, Windows, Mac; VMs or physical machines; developer machines, on-premise data centers, public clouds
Application isolation Containers virtualize CPU, memory, storage and network at the OS level, giving developers a view of the OS logically isolated from other applications

Evolution of deployment (classic three-picture question)

Era Stack Properties
Traditional deployment Hardware → OS → apps No way to define resource boundaries for apps on a physical server → resource-allocation issues (one app starves others)
Virtualized deployment Hardware → OS → hypervisor → VMs (each with guest OS) → apps Apps isolated between VMs; better utilization and scalability; each VM is a full machine with its own OS
Container deployment Hardware → OS → container runtime → containers Like VMs but with relaxed isolation properties to share the OS among applications ⇒ lightweight; each container has its own file system, share of CPU, memory, process space; decoupled from infrastructure ⇒ portable across clouds and OS distributions

Containers vs VMs

  • Both package apps with libraries/dependencies in isolated environments (“containers and VMs”, not versus).
  • Containers are far more lightweight.
  • Containers virtualize at the OS level; VMs virtualize at the hardware level.
  • Containers share the host OS kernel and use a fraction of the memory VMs require.

Popular open-source implementations

  • Docker: an open platform for developing, shipping and running applications.
  • Kubernetes: an open-source system for automating deployment, scaling and management of containerized applications; originated at Google, open-sourced around 2014.

Kubernetes (K8s)

  • Definition: a portable, extensible, open-source platform for managing containerized workloads and services, that facilitates both declarative configuration and automation. Large, rapidly growing ecosystem; services, support and tools widely available.
  • Name from Greek: “helmsman” or “pilot”.
  • Operates at the container level rather than the hardware level; provides PaaS-like features — deployment, scaling, load balancing — and lets users integrate logging, monitoring and alerting.
  • Not monolithic: default solutions are optional and pluggable; provides building blocks for developer platforms while preserving user choice and flexibility.

Kubernetes components | Component | Role | |—|—| | Cluster | A set of worker machines called nodes that run containerized applications | | Worker node(s) | Every cluster has at least one worker node; nodes host the Pods | | Pod | The components of the application workload (run on worker nodes) | | Control plane | Manages the worker nodes and the Pods in the cluster; in production it runs across multiple computers and the cluster runs multiple nodes → fault tolerance and high availability | | Other parts named | Scheduler (control plane), kubelet, kube-proxy (on nodes) |

Docker container (L47 summary)

  • Docker gives a sandboxed process isolated from all other processes on the host.
  • A container is a runtime instance of an image; create/start/stop/move/delete via the Docker API or CLI; runs on local machines, VMs, clouds.
  • A Docker container image is a lightweight, standalone, executable package of software that includes everything needed to run an application: code, runtime, system tools, system libraries and settings.
  • Images become containers at runtime — Docker images become containers when they run on the Docker Engine.
  • Available for Linux and Windows; containerized software always runs the same regardless of infrastructure; containers isolate software from its environment so it works uniformly despite differences (e.g., dev vs staging).
  • Docker claims: standard (industry standard, portable), lightweight (share the machine’s OS kernel), secure (strong default isolation).

MCQ traps (10.2)

  • Containers virtualize the OS; VMs virtualize hardware.
  • Containers share the host kernel (relaxed isolation); VMs each have a guest OS.
  • Kubernetes = orchestration (deployment, scaling, management of containers); Docker = build/ship/run containers.
  • A K8s cluster has at least one worker node; Pods run on worker nodes; the control plane manages nodes and Pods.
  • Kubernetes is not monolithic; components are pluggable.
  • Kubernetes originated at Google.

10.3 Docker — overview, benefits, architecture (L48)

Docker as a platform

  • A platform that allows you to build, ship and run any app, anywhere — a standard way to solve one of the most challenging aspects of software: deployment (also development and testing).
  • Traditional pipeline: VMs, configuration-management tools, package management, complex webs of libraries and dependencies, each maintained by specialists with their own approaches → poor interoperability (moving from Ubuntu to Red Hat/CentOS needs re-engineering) — a big hindrance for large-scale deployment where the target site lacks expertise.
  • With Docker: everything goes through a common pipeline to a single output that can be used on any target — no need to maintain an array of configuration mechanisms. No need to throw away an existing (tested/certified) software stack — package it in a container as-is for others; you can still inspect how containers are built.
  • Name analogy: a docker is a laborer who moves commercial goods in and out of ships at ports — fitting odd-shaped items efficiently; software teams spend similar effort fitting “odd-shaped” software into different environments.
  • Reference book: Docker in Practice — Ian Miell and Aidan Hobson Sayers.

Before vs with Docker

Before Docker With Docker
Install, configure and maintain the complex application separately on the development machine, test server and live server (three efforts); even VMs required time to deploy, boot and manage overhead resources Install, configure and maintain the application once in a Docker image, then docker run it on the dev laptop, test server and live server
  • Configuration effort is separated from resource management; deployment becomes trivial — the environment image is pulled and run, consuming fewer resources and contained so it doesn’t interfere with other environments. It doesn’t matter whether the target runs Red Hat, Ubuntu or CentOS, as long as Docker runs on it.

Key uses/features of Docker (list question)

Feature Meaning
Replacing virtual machines When you care only about the application, not the OS; quicker to start, lightweight to move; layered file system makes sharing changes easy; command-line driven and scriptable
Prototyping software A sandbox environment almost instantly, without disturbing your setup or provisioning a VM
Packaging software A Docker image has effectively no dependencies → a great way to package software that runs on any modern Linux machine
Enabling a microservices architecture Decompose a complex system into a series of composable parts — manageable, pluggable
Modelling networks Spin up hundreds (even thousands) of isolated containers on one machine
Full-stack productivity when offline Bundle all parts of the system into containers and run them on a laptop on the move
Reducing debugging overhead State the steps to reproduce a bug clearly (even as a script) on a system with known properties
Documenting software dependencies and touchpoints Building images in a structured way forces you to document dependencies explicitly from the base
Enabling continuous delivery (CD) CD = a paradigm of software delivery based on a pipeline that rebuilds the system on every change and delivers it to production (live) through an automated or partly automated process; Docker builds are more reproducible and replicable than traditional builds

Key concepts: image, layer, container

  • Image: a collection of filesystem layers plus some metadata; taken together they can be spun up as containers. (Stored on disk.)
  • Layer: a collection of changes to files — e.g., the differences between v1 and v2 of an application are stored in a layer (on top of, e.g., a Debian base layer).
  • Container: a running instance of an image; multiple containers can run from the same image.
  • Images are found via a registry/namespace.

Key commands

Command Purpose
docker build Build a Docker image (from a Dockerfile)
docker run Run a Docker image as a container
docker commit Commit a Docker container as an image
docker tag Tag a Docker image

Docker architecture

  • Docker on a host is split into two parts: a daemon with a RESTful API, and a client that talks to the daemon.
  • You invoke the Docker client to get information from or give instructions to the daemon; the daemon is a server that receives requests and returns responses over HTTP; it in turn requests other services (registries) over HTTP to send and receive images.
  • The daemon takes care of images and containers behind the scenes; the client is the intermediary between you and the RESTful API.
  • Private Docker registry: a service that stores Docker images, on the internal network and not publicly accessible; any Docker daemon with access can request images from it.
  • Docker Hub: the public registry run by Docker Inc.; other public registries can also exist.
  • The host machine typically sits on a private network.

MCQ traps (10.3)

  • Docker architecture = client + daemon (RESTful API, HTTP); the daemon (not the client) manages images and containers.
  • Docker Hub = public (Docker Inc.); private registry = internal network, not public.
  • docker commit turns a container into an image; docker build builds an image from a Dockerfile.
  • Image = layers + metadata; layer = file changes (e.g., v1→v2 diff).
  • CD = rebuild on every change and deliver to production automatically/partly automatically.

10.4 Docker demo — install, build, ship, run (L49–L50)

Goal

Show “build once, run anywhere”: pull MySQL (relational DB) and phpMyAdmin (web-based GUI front end for MySQL) images from Docker Hub on Ubuntu, modify the database, package it, ship it to a Windows machine and run it without installing MySQL, Apache, PHP or phpMyAdmin there.

Traditional way: install MySQL, a web server (Apache), PHP and phpMyAdmin separately on every machine; to move data, back up the old MySQL, transfer, restore on the new server — needs expertise. Docker way: import MySQL and phpMyAdmin images from Docker Hub → bundle → build a Docker image at the source that includes everything (app + dependencies) → load the image at the target and run — no separate installation at the destination; only the Docker Engine must be installed there.

Steps (sequence)

  1. Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu (per docs.docker.com): apt-get update → install packages so apt can use a repository over HTTPS → add Docker’s official GPG key → set up the repository → apt-get update → install Docker Engine.
  2. Verify: sudo docker run hello-world — docker run pulls the image from Docker Hub if it is not available locally, then runs it; prints “Hello from Docker!” ⇒ installation OK.
  3. Pull images: docker pull mysql, docker pull phpmyadmin; check with docker images.
  4. Write a Dockerfile on top of the MySQL image that copies /var/lib/mysql to a custom directory and sets it as the data directory — so the data persists in images made from the container; docker build the new image.
  5. Run containers: docker run --name <mysql-name> -e <root-password env var> -d <image> (first attempt failed until the environment variable was supplied); docker ps shows running containers. Run phpMyAdmin with --link <mysql-container>:db and port forwarding -p 8080:80; open localhost:8080.
  6. In phpMyAdmin: create database → table (course id, course name, credit) → insert records (1001 Cloud Computing 3; 1002 Networking 4).
  7. docker commit <container-id> mysql_v3 — saves the running container’s state (with the new DB/table/records) as a new image.
  8. docker save mysql_v3 > myimage.tar — export the image as a tar archive.
  9. Ship the tar (Google Drive in the demo; scp/FTP also fine).
  10. On Windows (with Docker Desktop GUI showing images and containers): docker load the tar → image mysql_v3 appears → docker run --name mysql1 -d mysql_v3.
  11. Run phpMyAdmin pulled fresh from Docker Hub (unchanged, so not shipped) linked to mysql1:db, port 8080 → the same database, table and records are present. State preserved; no separate MySQL/PHP/Apache installed.

MCQ traps (10.4)

  • docker save → tar file; docker load → image from tar (not export/import in this demo).
  • docker commit captured the modified database into a new image.
  • Only the modified MySQL image was shipped; phpMyAdmin was pulled from Docker Hub at the destination.
  • docker run auto-pulls missing images from Docker Hub.
  • Destination needs only the Docker Engine (Docker Desktop on Windows).

Week 10 — High-yield takeaways

  1. r=PD/R; Tmig​=RVm​​1−r1−rn+1​+Tres​; Tdown​=rnRVm​​+Tres​; n=min(⌈logr​(Vth​/Vm​)⌉,Nmax​); cold: Tdown​=Tmig​=Vm​/R.
  2. Pre-copy used by KVM, Xen, VMware; post-copy = CPU state first + demand paging/active push/pre-paging.
  3. Multi-VM: serial (first VM at full R, others suspended at its stop-and-copy) vs parallel (each R/m, simultaneous stop-and-copy).
  4. Containers: lightweight, OS-level virtualization, share kernel; benefits = separation of responsibilities, workload portability, application isolation; traditional → virtualized → container deployment.
  5. Kubernetes (Google, Greek “helmsman”): portable, extensible, open-source, declarative config + automation; cluster → worker nodes → Pods; control plane; not monolithic.
  6. Docker: build/ship/run anywhere; uses (replace VMs, prototyping, packaging, microservices, network modelling, offline full stack, debugging, documenting dependencies, CD); image = layers + metadata; container = running instance; build/run/commit/tag; architecture = client + daemon (REST over HTTP) + private registry + Docker Hub.
  7. Demo: install engine → hello-world → pull MySQL/phpMyAdmin → Dockerfile (persistent datadir) → run with --link and -p 8080:80 → commit → save (tar) → ship → load → run on Windows; data intact.

Week 11 — Dew Computing, Serverless Computing I–II, Sustainable Cloud Computing I–II (Lectures 51–55)

Week 11 — Dew Computing, Serverless Computing I–II, Sustainable Cloud Computing I–II (Lectures 51–55)

Source: L51 Dew Computing · L52 Serverless Computing – I · L53 Serverless Computing – II · L54 Sustainable Cloud Computing – I · L55 Sustainable Cloud Computing – II

High-yield: dew’s two features (independence, collaboration) and its service categories (IaD, SiD, PiD, storage-in-dew, WiD, DBiD), DVM; serverless definition, FaaS vs BaaS, drawbacks, AWS Lambda / Google Cloud Functions / Azure Functions terms; sustainable cloud conceptual model (cloud architecture, cooling manager, power manager, remote CDCs), energy-vs-reliability trade-off, DVFS, taxonomy components and energy breakdown.

11.1 Dew computing (L51)

Motivation

  • Cloud (and fog/edge, cloudlet, MCC, MEC…) all depend on reliable, constant Internet connectivity; if it’s lost, work stops.
  • Dropbox shows the alternative: a local copy of your folder is usable offline and syncs with the cloud when the connection returns. Dropbox is the classic example of dew computing.

Definitions

  • Dew computing: a computing paradigm that combines the core concept of cloud computing with the capabilities of end devices (personal computers, mobile phones…), used to enhance the end-user experience compared with using only cloud computing.
  • It attempts to solve cloud’s major problem: reliance on (constant) network access — services keep working when connectivity is absent.
  • Alternative definition: a computing model enabling a ubiquitous, pervasive and convenient, ready-to-go, plug-in-facility-empowered personal network that includes a single-hybrid peer-to-peer communication link; primary goal: access a pool of raw data equipped with metadata that can be rapidly created, edited, stored and deleted with minimal Internet management effort (i.e., also offline).
  • Characteristics: user-centric, highly flexible, personalized; located very close to end devices — the first layer of the IoT–cloud continuum that the user interacts with; micro-service-based, in a vertically distributed hierarchy; made of smart devices (smartphones, smart watches, tablets, laptops) at the network edge that collect/process IoT data; services are relatively always available and permanent interaction (connectivity) is not mandatory; does not rely on centralized servers/cloud data centers or permanent network connectivity (but syncs with the cloud).
  • Bonus: you can save energy/cost by syncing only when a favourable (high-bandwidth) connection is available.

Two key features (very examinable)

Feature Meaning
Independence The local device must be able to provide service without a continuous connection to the Internet
Collaboration The application must be able to connect to the cloud service and synchronize data when appropriate (automatically; role/rule-based sharing possible)

Analogy: cloud is far above the ground (remote service), fog is closer to the ground (beside the user), dew is on the ground (at the user’s own system/premises).

Dew service categories (matching question)

Category Meaning Example
Infrastructure-as-Dew (IaD) Local device dynamically supported by cloud services — either an exact duplicate DVM instance in the cloud kept in the same state, or all local settings and data (system + each app) saved in the cloud iCloud
Software-in-Dew Configuration and ownership of software are saved in the cloud — apps a user installs are saved to the account and can be installed on any linked device Google Play, Apple App Store
Platform-in-Dew (PiD) A software-development suite installed on the local device, with settings and application data synchronized to the cloud — must sync development data, system deployment data and online backups GitHub
Storage-in-Dew Local device’s storage is partially or fully copied to the cloud; satisfies both independence and collaboration (offline access + automatic folder sync) Dropbox, Google Drive
Web-in-Dew (WiD) Local device possesses a duplicated fraction of the WWW (or a modified copy) → independence; that fraction syncs with the web → collaboration —
Database-in-Dew (DBiD) Local device and cloud both store copies of the same database; one is designated the main version by the DBA; increases reliability (one acts as the other’s backup) —

The lecture calls storage-in-dew “SID”; in the literature, SiD usually denotes software-in-dew and STiD storage-in-dew. Match by the description.

Dew architecture

  • Cloud ⇄ (single-hybrid P2P link, when connected) ⇄ Dew Virtual Machine (DVM) on the local host ⇄ IoT devices/sensors.
  • DVM = an isolated environment for executing the dew server on the local system (must be installed, like installing the Dropbox client). It contains a dew server (core), a dew client program, a dew DBMS/database, dew client services (and possibly AI modules that learn access patterns).
  • Dew server’s basic functions: serve the user with requested services (through client services) and perform synchronization and correlation between local and remote data. It aims at three goals: data replication, data distribution, synchronization (plus housekeeping of the local data organization).

Challenges

Power management · processor utility · data storage (local vs subscribed cloud space; hard on low-resource devices like smartwatches) · viability of the operating system (which OSs the DVM runs on) · programming principles · information/database security. Placement in the hierarchy: cloud servers → fog/edge servers → edge devices → smart devices → smart IoT modules; dew-enabled computing is realized at the lower levels (edge devices, smart devices, IoT modules), working from the last synchronized state and syncing upward when connected.

MCQ traps (11.1)

  • Dew’s two features: independence + collaboration (not “scalability + elasticity”).
  • Dropbox/Google Drive = storage-in-dew; App Store/Play = software-in-dew; GitHub = platform-in-dew; iCloud = infrastructure-as-dew.
  • DBiD increases reliability (backup); one copy is the main version.
  • Dew does not require permanent connectivity or a central server, but it does sync with the cloud.
  • DVM goals: replication, distribution, synchronization.

11.2 Serverless computing — concepts (L52)

Definitions

  • Serverless computing: a method of providing back-end services on an as-used basis; the provider lets users write and deploy code without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.
  • It simplifies code development and deployment and eliminates the need for system administration — developers focus on core business logic without overhead such as instantiating VMs or containers or monitoring infrastructure (needed even in IaaS/PaaS).
  • Developers express logic as functions submitted to the provider to run in a shared runtime environment; the provider manages scalability by running multiple functions in parallel.
  • After the container boom, providers offered better-fitting containers that need less time to boot and more automation in orchestration; serverless promises full automation in managing fine-grained containers.
  • Serverless computing is a form of cloud computing that allows users to run event-driven and granular applications without having to address the operational logic.
  • Developers work at high-level abstractions — functions, queries, events — and interconnect elements of business logic into workflows; the provider maps them to concrete resources and ensures applications are orchestrated (containerized), deployed, provisioned and available on demand, billing only for resources used.
  • The provider still has servers — it dynamically allocates and provisions them; code runs in almost stateless containers that are event-triggered and may be ephemeral (may last for one invocation).

Evolution leading to serverless

1960s mainframes (IBM) → 1970s virtualization → 1980s RPC → 1990s virtual private servers, CGI → 2000s AWS, Google App Engine, containers → 2010s Docker (2013), Kubernetes, event-driven architectures. Container orchestration + microservices → FaaS; FaaS + event-driven workflows → serverless computing.

FaaS vs BaaS

Function as a Service (FaaS) Backend as a Service (BaaS)
Definition A form of serverless computing in which the cloud provider manages the resource life cycle and event-driven execution of user-provided functions; users supply small, stateless functions Replaces server-side components with off-the-shelf services; developers outsource all behind-the-scenes aspects and keep app logic in the front end
Examples AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions; ExCamera (edits/transforms/encodes video with low latency and cost — many tasks run concurrently) Remote authentication, database management, cloud storage, hosting; Google Firebase (fully managed database used directly from apps)

How FaaS works

  • Serverless apps are event-driven, cloud-based, relying on third-party services, client-side logic and cloud-hosted RPCs.
  • Deployed code executes in an isolated environment when triggered; each function is a small part of the application.
  • Execution time is limited (e.g., AWS Lambda ≈ 15 minutes).
  • Functions are not constantly active — the platform listens for events that instantiate them: client requests, events from external systems, data streams.
  • The FaaS provider horizontally scales function execution with the number of incoming events.

Drawbacks/challenges (list question)

Issue Why it hurts
Asynchronous calls Async calls to/between functions increase complexity (request–response sync calls are easier)
Functions calling other functions Complex debugging, loss of feature isolation, extra cost (pay for two functions running at once)
Shared code between functions Changing shared code may break dependent functions
Image size limit / warm-up Risk of hitting the image-size limit (AWS Lambda ≈ 50 MB); bigger image ⇒ longer warm-up (start) time
Too many libraries More space, higher risk of hitting size limits
Too many technologies Many frameworks/languages ⇒ maintenance complexity and higher skill needs
Too many functions Since inactive functions cost nothing, people create new ones instead of updating/reusing ⇒ lower maintainability and understandability

Popular platforms: AWS Lambda (Amazon), Google Cloud Functions, Microsoft Azure Functions.

MCQ traps (11.2)

  • “Serverless” does not mean no servers — servers are hidden and managed by the provider.
  • FaaS = provider runs your event-triggered functions; BaaS = provider supplies ready back-end services (auth, DB, storage).
  • Functions are stateless, short-lived, event-triggered, billed only when executing.
  • Lambda limits quoted: ~15 min execution, ~50 MB image.

11.3 Serverless computing — platforms (L53)

Serverless vs cloud focus

  • Serverless hides servers by providing a programming abstraction for application builders → cloud software easier to write.
  • Cloud computing targeted system administrators; serverless targets programmers. The provider takes over many operational responsibilities needed to run applications (overlaps with PaaS but goes further).
  • Focus shifts from servers to applications (some literature calls traditional cloud “serverful”). Serverless will change how programmers work as dramatically as cloud changed how operators work.
  • Serverless applications need no server provisioning and no server management.

Provider comparison

AWS Google Microsoft Azure
Virtual servers AWS (EC2) instances VM instances Virtual machines
Functions (FaaS) AWS Lambda Google Cloud Functions Azure Functions
Database Amazon DynamoDB Google Cloud Datastore Azure Cosmos DB
Storage Amazon S3 Google Cloud Storage Azure storage

AWS Lambda

  • An event-driven, serverless computing platform provided by Amazon as part of AWS. You don’t worry about which AWS resources to launch or how to manage them — just put code on Lambda and it runs.
  • Code executes in response to events in AWS services, e.g., adding/deleting files in an S3 bucket, an HTTP request from Amazon API Gateway (also DynamoDB, SNS, Kinesis…).
  • Lambda is used to execute background tasks.
  • Frees you from managing OS access, patching, right-sizing, provisioning, scaling.
  • Flow: upload code (Java, Python, Go, C#, Node.js…) → AWS services trigger Lambda → Lambda executes → AWS charges only when Lambda executes code. | Lambda concept | Meaning | |—|—| | Function | A program/script that runs in Lambda; Lambda passes invocation events, the function processes them and returns a response | | Runtime | Lets functions in various languages run on the same base execution environment | | Event source | An AWS service (e.g., SNS) or custom service that triggers the function | | Lambda layers | Distribution mechanism for libraries, custom runtimes and other dependencies | | Log streams | Annotate code with custom logging statements to analyse execution flow and performance |

Google Cloud Functions

  • A serverless execution environment for building and connecting cloud services; write simple, single-purpose functions attached to events emitted from cloud infrastructure and services; a function is triggered when an event being watched is fired; runs in a fully managed environment.
  • Flow: GCP services (Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, Stackdriver, Datastore…) emit events (e.g., object uploaded/deleted/metadata updated in a bucket) → event data (metadata) → if a function is configured with that trigger, it is invoked with the event data → it may call other APIs (Google or external) and write back to cloud services → it signals completion. Multiple events ⇒ multiple invocations (handled by the infrastructure).
  • Keep functions single-purpose, with minimal execution time; functions are stateless — keep state outside (e.g., memcache). | Term | Meaning | |—|—| | Events | Things that happen in GCP services — file uploaded, message published to a queue, direct HTTP invocation | | Triggers | Choosing to respond to an event — event + function | | Event data | Data passed to the function when the trigger fires | | Event providers | HTTP, Cloud Storage, Cloud Pub/Sub, Firebase (DB, analytics, auth), Stackdriver Logging, Cloud Firestore, Compute Engine, BigQuery |

Azure Functions

  • A serverless solution that lets you write less code, maintain less infrastructure and save on costs; the provider supplies all up-to-date resources.
  • A function is the primary concept; it has two pieces: your code (many languages) and configuration (function.json). For compiled languages the config is generated automatically from annotations; for scripting languages you provide it yourself.
  • Languages: C#, Java, JavaScript, Python, PowerShell…; custom handlers for virtually any language. Automated deployment options; monitoring/testing for troubleshooting.
  • Pricing: Consumption plan — pay only while functions run; Premium and App Service plans for specialized needs.
  • Common serverless patterns: serverless APIs and mobile/web back ends · event and stream processing · IoT data processing · big-data and ML pipelines · integration and enterprise service bus · automation and digital transformation.
  • Scenarios: web-app back end — request in web app → queued in Service Bus → function processes → output to Cosmos DB; mobile-app back end (financial service) — HTTP API call from mobile app → processed by function → output to Cosmos DB → data transfer triggers a second function → notification via Notification Hubs.

MCQ traps (11.3)

  • Lambda / Cloud Functions / Azure Functions are the FaaS offerings; DynamoDB / Cloud Datastore / Cosmos DB the databases.
  • Lambda layers = libraries/runtimes/dependencies; event source = trigger origin; log streams = custom logging.
  • Google: trigger = event + function; functions are stateless, single-purpose.
  • Azure: function = code + function.json; config auto-generated for compiled languages only.
  • Billing is per execution (Consumption plan).

11.4 Sustainable cloud computing — I (L54)

Problem

  • CSPs (Amazon, Google, IBM, Microsoft…) run large, geographically spread cloud data centers (CDCs) for ever-increasing, peaky user demand.
  • They must honour SLAs (penalties otherwise) and keep energy, maintenance cost and carbon footprint down to earn a return on investment.
  • The financial and carbon-footprint costs of running such large infrastructure negatively impact the sustainability of cloud services.
  • Focus of sustainable cloud computing: minimize energy consumption and carbon footprint while ensuring the reliability of CDCs.
  • Putting lightly loaded servers to sleep saves energy, but wake-up delay can violate SLAs, especially with simultaneous peaks.
  • Network, storage and servers must be available round the clock; idle components still consume energy; creating, processing and storing every bit adds energy cost and heat, which needs more energy for cooling.
  • Projected CDC energy consumption ≈ 8000 TWh by 2030 (lecture graph).
  • Components other than servers (network, storage, memory, cooling) consume huge energy → need energy-aware resource management of all resources holistically; under-loading and over-loading make CDC energy use inefficient.
  • CSPs turn to renewable energy (often hybrid with grid); future CDCs must cut carbon emissions and heat release (greenhouse gases).
  • Data-center (re)location is driven by waste-heat recovery opportunities, access to green (renewable) resources, and proximity to cooling resources (short cooling ducts; near power stations to cut transmission losses).

Conceptual model of sustainable cloud computing (layered)

Component Role
Cloud architecture IaaS, PaaS, SaaS (with PaaS-level managers: remote-CDC manager, VM/resource manager, green resource manager, thermal profiling, cooling manager)
Cooling manager Issues thermal alerts when temperature exceeds a threshold; a heat controller acts to control temperature with minimal impact on CDC performance (temperature control, heat exchange)
Power manager Controls power from renewable sources (solar, wind) and grid/fossil fuel; grid energy used for deadline-oriented workloads to maintain reliability; ATS (Automatic Transfer Switch) manages energy from both sources; PDU (Power Distribution Unit) delivers electricity to servers and cooling devices
Remote CDCs VMs/workloads migrated to remote CDCs to balance load (e.g., where renewable energy is available)

Energy vs reliability (trade-off)

Energy goals Reliability goals
Reduce energy consumption · reduce under/over-loading (better load balancing) · minimize heat concentration and dissipation · reduce carbon footprint · improve bandwidth and computing capacity · improve storage management Avoid SLA violations · identify system failures and their reasons to manage risk · protect critical information from security attacks · secure VM migration · reduce turn-on (switching) time
  • Improving energy use reduces electricity bills and operational cost → sustainability. But reliability via service replication needs extra resources and energy → trade-off between energy consumption and reliability for cost-efficient services.
  • DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) reduces energy, but switching between high and low scaling modes increases response time and service delay → may violate SLAs.
  • Excessive turning off/on reduces reliability of components; power modulation decreases reliability of server components such as storage devices.
  • ⇒ Need energy-aware resource management that reduces power without affecting reliability.
  • Aspects to address: application model, virtualization, waste-heat utilization, thermal-aware scheduling, renewable energy, resource-targeted energy management, capacity planning (detailed in L55).

11.5 Sustainable cloud computing — II: taxonomy (L55)

Why it’s getting harder

  • IoT and streaming drive exponential demand → more data centers, denser servers → more heat, more power, more cooling. Chips shrink while compute grows, but heat dissipation limits density. In modern data centers, IT cost ≈ environment cost (cooling, power, controls) — “x and x”.
  • Must treat computing, cooling, heat, power together (integrated), including what to do with waste heat.

Taxonomy components (survey: Gill & Buyya, “Sustainable Cloud Computing: 360° view”)

Component Key points
Application model/design Data-parallel, function-parallel, message-passing; QoS, workload type (critical/interactive vs batch), architecture; an efficient application structure improves CDC energy efficiency; need green-ICT-based applications
Energy management Energy share of CDC components (lecture): processor ≈ 45 %, cooling ≈ 20 %, memory ≈ 15 %, storage ≈ 10 %, network ≈ 10 %; static (system/CPU level) and dynamic (resource management, consolidation, configuration) techniques; DVFS helps utilization but switching adds response time/delay; sleep/wake is risky
Virtualization VM migration, VM elasticity, load balancing, consolidation, fault tolerance, scheduling — move workloads where renewable energy is available
Thermal-aware scheduling Architecture (single-/multi-core), heat modelling, thermometers, scheduling, monitoring, simulation; tackles heating during workload execution; current approaches mostly aim to reduce PUE, but PUE reduction may not always reduce total cost of ownership
Cooling management Efficient cooling to keep CDC temperature in range as size and energy density grow
Renewable energy Solar, wind, hydro (near-zero CO₂); energy source, storage device, location (on-site/off-site); carbon usage effectiveness (CUE) can be reduced by adding renewable energy, but can renewables meet peak demand? → switching with grid; place CDCs near renewable sources (which need large areas)
Waste-heat utilization Reuse heat generated by the systems; vapour-absorption-based free cooling uses waste heat and can make PUE (near) ideal by neutralizing cooling expenses
Capacity planning Plan power infrastructure, IT resources, cooling, workloads; predictive models; investment is upfront while utilization grows slowly → plan for ROI; auto-scaling, utility functions; storage and processing capacity
Sustainability metrics Performance metrics for providers (throughput, application, security) and users (satisfaction, response time, correctness, reliability) plus metrics for waste heat, cooling, thermal-aware scheduling, energy management, virtualization, capacity planning, renewable energy

Research categories: application design · sustainability metrics · capacity planning · energy management · virtualization · thermal-aware scheduling · cooling management · renewable energy · waste-heat utilization. Conclusion: next-generation clouds must be energy-efficient and sustainable — powered by renewables, placed in cool locations near power generation, with lower carbon footprint — while keeping high performance and reliability.

MCQ traps (11.4–11.5)

  • Sustainable cloud = minimize energy + carbon footprint while ensuring reliability (not just cheaper hardware).
  • Grid power for deadline-oriented workloads; ATS switches sources; PDU distributes power.
  • DVFS saves energy but switching increases response time.
  • Two different breakdowns: L37 green cloud (whole data center: cooling 45 %, IT 40 %, power distribution 15 %) vs L55 (by component: processor 45 %, cooling 20 %, memory 15 %, storage 10 %, network 10 %). Read the question carefully.
  • CUE is reduced by adding renewables; vapour-absorption free cooling reuses waste heat.
  • PUE reduction ≠ guaranteed TCO reduction.

Week 11 — High-yield takeaways

  1. Dew = cloud concept + end-device capability; works offline; independence + collaboration; Dropbox example; categories IaD (iCloud), software-in-dew (Play/App Store), PiD (GitHub), storage-in-dew (Dropbox/Drive), WiD, DBiD; DVM with dew server (replication, distribution, synchronization).
  2. Serverless = back-end services as-used; event-driven, granular apps; developers write functions; provider handles provisioning/scaling; billing per use; still uses servers.
  3. FaaS (provider runs event-triggered stateless functions; Lambda ~15 min) vs BaaS (off-the-shelf back ends: auth, DB, storage — Firebase).
  4. Drawbacks: async calls, function chaining cost, shared code, image size (~50 MB) and warm-up, too many libraries/technologies/functions.
  5. Lambda (event source, runtime, layers, log streams; S3/API Gateway triggers; pay per execution); Google Cloud Functions (event, trigger = event + function, event data, providers HTTP/Storage/PubSub/Firebase…); Azure Functions (code + function.json; Consumption plan; Service Bus/Cosmos DB scenarios).
  6. Sustainable cloud: minimize energy & carbon, keep reliability; model = cloud architecture + cooling manager + power manager (renewable/grid, ATS, PDU) + remote CDCs; energy vs reliability trade-off; DVFS; ~8000 TWh by 2030.
  7. Taxonomy: application design, sustainability metrics, capacity planning, energy management (processor 45 %…), virtualization, thermal-aware scheduling, cooling, renewables (CUE), waste-heat utilization (vapour absorption).

Week 12 — Cloud in the 5G Era, CPS & Cloud, Case Studies: Spatial Cloud and Internet of Health Things (Lectures 56–60)

Week 12 — Cloud in the 5G Era, CPS & Cloud, Case Studies: Spatial Cloud and Internet of Health Things (Lectures 56–60)

Source: L56 Cloud Computing in 5G Era · L57 CPS and Cloud Computing · L58 Case Study I (Spatial Cloud Computing) · L59 Case Study II (Internet of Health Things) Part A · L60 Case Study II Part B

High-yield: 5G features and its three service classes (eMBB, URLLC, mMTC), two aspects of the 5G–cloud relationship; CPS definition, origin, characteristics, applications, cyber-physical cloud computing (CPCC) definition and benefits; spatial data, Tobler’s law, spatiotemporal cloud computing definition, OGC services, trajectory cloud; IoHT case-study topology, latencies, module placement, results, accelerometer pipeline (5-point smoothing, kNN), dew comparison.

12.1 Cloud computing in the 5G era (L56)

Why 5G matters for cloud

  • Cloud→fog→edge→IoT continuum tried to move computing towards the edge because of latency (round-trip delay) and data load from billions of IoT devices, mostly over mobile/wireless links.
  • Further cloud challenges: mobility (devices/edge, even fog, may move or switch), real-time applications (gaming, healthcare, traffic) needing quick responses, QoS for different traffic types, security.
  • Cloud’s success depends on ubiquitous connectivity; the mobile network is now the de-facto backbone → the mobile generation matters.

What 5G is

  • 5G = fifth-generation mobile network — a new global wireless standard after 1G–4G, designed to connect virtually everyone and everything together (machines, objects, devices).
  • Delivers multi-Gbps peak data speeds, ultra-low latency, more reliability, massive network capacity, increased availability, and a more uniform user experience to more users; improved efficiency, new industries.
  • Unified, more capable air interface with extended capacity for next-generation experiences, new deployment models and services; designed for forward compatibility.

Generations (lecture) | Gen | Era | Delivered | Speed (lecture figures) | |—|—|—|—| | 1G | 1980s | Analog voice | ~2 kbps | | 2G | Early 1990s | Digital voice (e.g., CDMA) | ~384 kbps | | 3G | Early 2000s | Mobile data | 56 Mbps | | 4G LTE | 2010s | Mobile broadband | 1 Gbps | | 5G | Now | Unified air interface; connect everything | **10 Gbps**, latency **1 ms** |

Three main classes of 5G connected services

Class Meaning Examples
Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) Better smartphones plus new immersive experiences — faster, more uniform data rates, lower latency, lower cost per bit VR, AR, enhanced indoor/outdoor broadband, enterprise collaboration
Mission-critical communications — URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication) Ultra-reliable, available, low-latency links that transform industries Remote control of critical infrastructure, vehicles and medical procedures; autonomous vehicles, smart grid, remote patient monitoring, telehealth, industrial automation
Massive IoT — mMTC (massive Machine-Type Communication) Seamlessly connect a massive number of embedded sensors, by scaling down data rates, power and mobility — extremely lean, low-cost connectivity Asset tracking, smart agriculture, smart cities, energy monitoring, smart home
  • Literature calls this “network as a platform”.

5G and cloud computing

  • 5G is a perfect companion to cloud — distribution and diversity of compute and storage. On-premise and edge data centers close the gap between resource-constrained, low-latency devices and distant cloud centers → heterogeneous, distributed computing.
  • Providers must offer full end-to-end orchestration; service orchestration lets applications interact with network resources — select location, QoS, influence traffic routing — to deliver apps on demand (e.g., classify streaming traffic by QoS).
  • Two key aspects of the 5G–cloud relationship:
    1. Further development of cloud computing has to meet 5G needs — reflected in the growing role of edge, mobile edge and fog computing in the cloud paradigm.
    2. 5G is undergoing “cloudification” through softwarization — NFV (network function virtualization), SDN (software-defined networking) (and serverless/FaaS-style functions).
  • Both influence each other; 5G brings convergence of computing, IoT and cloud → the era of hyper-connectivity.

Edge computing in 5G

  • (Mobile) edge computing enables the evolution of 5G by bringing cloud capabilities near end users (user equipment), overcoming cloud’s high latency.
  • Preferred for interactive, computation-intensive next-gen apps like AR/VR, which have stringent QoS (low latency, high throughput) and generate huge data processed at different hierarchy levels.
  • 5G is expected to: handle massive data from mobile devices and IoT · meet stringent QoS for highly interactive apps (ultra-low latency, high throughput) · support a heterogeneous environment (interoperability of diverse equipment, QoS needs, network types).
  • Edge-computing applications: healthcare · entertainment and multimedia · VR/AR/MR · tactile Internet · IoT · factories of the future · emergency response · Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS).

Mobile cloud computing in 5G

Key MCC features for 5G: sharing resources for mobile apps; improved reliability (data backed up in the cloud); fewer device resources consumed (processing offloaded); compute-intensive processing of mobile requests offloaded to the cloud; devices connect via base stations. 5G backbone gives higher data rates, low latency, reliability, QoS handling → a win-win for cloud.

MCQ traps (12.1)

  • eMBB = AR/VR & broadband; URLLC = autonomous vehicles, telesurgery, smart grid, industrial automation; mMTC = massive IoT sensors (smart agriculture, asset tracking).
  • 1G analog voice; 2G digital voice; 3G mobile data; 4G mobile broadband.
  • “Cloudification of 5G” = softwarization via NFV and SDN.
  • Edge computing brings cloud capability near the user equipment to cut latency.

12.2 Cyber-Physical Systems and cloud computing (L57)

CPS — definition and origin

  • CPS = an orchestration of computing and physical systems. Embedded computers monitor and control physical processes, usually with feedback loops where physical processes affect computations and vice versa.
  • Term coined around 2006 by Helen Gill at the US National Science Foundation (NSF).
  • CPS is about the intersection (interaction), not the union, of the physical and the cyber. It combines engineering models/methods from mechanical, environmental, civil, electrical, biomedical, chemical, aeronautical and industrial engineering with computer-science methods.
  • Examples: modern cars (brake lights on braking, airbags on collision, slow-vehicle alerts (SVA) in VANETs that react faster than humans), air-traffic systems (thousands of programs + humans in the loop), traffic control, medical devices/telehealth.
  • Applications: automotive systems, automated manufacturing, military systems, assisted living, medical systems, traffic control and safety, process control, energy, robotics…

Characteristics

  • CPS describes a broad range of complex, multidisciplinary, physically aware next-generation engineering systems that integrate embedded computing (cyber) into the physical world.
  • Physical and software components are deeply intertwined; they operate on different spatial and temporal scales, exhibit multiple distinct behavioural modalities, and interact in ways that change with context.
  • Transdisciplinary — merges cybernetics, mechatronics, design and process science. CPS = cyber + physical + computation + dynamics + communication + security + safety (+ human in the loop).
  • Modelling a CPS with multiple interacting computational units is a serious challenge.
  • Some literature treats the IoT-driven ecosystem (IoT + edge + fog + cloud) as a CPS.

Potential application areas (list question)

Area Examples
Intervention Collision avoidance
Precision Robotic surgery, nano-level manufacturing
Operation in dangerous/inaccessible environments Search and rescue, fire-fighting, deep-sea exploration
Coordination Air-traffic control, war-fighting
Efficiency Zero-net-energy buildings (lights/AC by occupancy and daylight)
Augmentation of human capabilities Healthcare monitoring and delivery

Cloud + CPS

  • Sensors–actuators–processors form a vast network; integrating computation with physical processes is “computing as a physical act”: the real world is monitored by sensors → data go to cyberspace where applications/services use them → affect the physical environment.
  • Cloud computing provides a flexible platform for realizing the goals of CPS (with the edge–fog–cloud layers; e.g., vehicle OBU = edge, RSU = fog, back-end cloud; location-driven services: safety, health, infotainment).
  • Cyber-Physical Cloud Computing (CPCC) architectural framework: a system environment that can rapidly build, modify and provision cyber-physical systems composed of a set of cloud-computing-based sensor, processing, control and data services.
  • Benefits: efficient use of resources · modular composition · rapid development and scalability · smart adaptation to the environment at every scale · reliable and resilient architecture (and stored data helps learn better CPS models).
  • Cyber-physical cloud services: sensor services, actuator services, processor services, data services (+ semantic engines), used by domains such as schools, hospitals, traffic control, ambulances, medical devices.
  • High-level CPCC: physical scenario (sensors, users, mobile objects such as an ambulance needing priority) ⇄ cyber-physical cloud platform (service catalog, cloud service API, runtime services) ⇄ CPS models (functional and non-functional requirements; system modeller/builder).
  • Example — intelligent machining monitoring: physical resources (CNC controllers, machine tools, local terminals/sensors) → local servers (pre-processing, diagnosis, decisions; actuate CNC controller) → cloud (advanced signal processing, feature extraction and selection, cognitive decision-making) → feedback.
  • Cloud–edge framework for cyber-physical-social systems (CPSS): many local CPSSs (cyber, social, physical worlds) solve local issues at the edge; the cloud plane takes global decisions; the application plane hosts smart city, home, factory, health, vehicles, grid.

MCQ traps (12.2)

  • CPS term: Helen Gill, NSF, ~2006.
  • CPS = intersection, not union, of cyber and physical.
  • CPS feedback loop is two-way (physical ↔︎ computation).
  • CPCC = rapidly build, modify, provision CPS from cloud sensor, processing, control, data services.
  • Zero-net-energy building = efficiency; collision avoidance = intervention; robotic surgery = precision; air-traffic control = coordination.

12.3 Case Study I — Spatial cloud computing (L58)

Spatial / geospatial data

  • Spatial data = a feature/attribute together with a location (coordinates), often with time (spatio-temporal: forest cover, river course, crops, weather over time).
  • Spatial objects (visible from above: building footprints, roads as polylines) vs non-spatial/attribute data (building name, departments, occupancy; road name, type, width).
  • Geospatial data = information describing objects, events or other features with a location on or near the Earth’s surface; it typically combines location information (coordinates, e.g., lat–long), attribute information and temporal information. (Spatial data can also be non-geographic, e.g., medical images — not in scope here.)
  • > 90 % of the world’s data has some spatial context.
  • Maps are turned into information — patterns, trends, decisions: crime-hotspot mapping (route limited police patrols by time/events), flood/drought analysis and prediction, optimal paths, congestion prediction, cyclone tracking and vehicle detours.
  • Spatial analysis solves location-oriented problems (“what happens around a place and how places relate”) — beyond mapping. Three steps: identify datasets (bring them onto the same base map/location reference) → analyse → draw inferences. Users: local/state/central government, businesses, utilities (telephone, water, electricity), e-commerce, researchers, NGOs.

Challenges that make cloud a good fit

  • Voluminous, spatio-temporal data; moving terabytes is a serious constraint.
  • Integration of heterogeneous, multimodal sources (e.g., crop-production estimation needs crop data, rainfall, drought, temperature, economic demand, fertilizer, water supply).
  • Better discovery, access and utilization of data and processing.
  • Real-time/near-real-time resources for emergency response (fire, cyclone).
  • Access spikes and the need for reliable, scalable service for massive numbers of concurrent users. ⇒ Spatial (spatio-temporal) analytics + cloud computing is a good match (elastic, on-demand platform; integrate observation systems; configure compute for intensive simulations, e.g., climate models).

Spatiotemporal cloud computing (definition)

A cloud computing paradigm that is driven by geospatial sciences and optimized by spatiotemporal principles for enabling geospatial science discoveries and cloud computing within a distributed computing environment.

  • Tobler’s First Law of Geography: everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things — e.g., Kharagpur’s temperature is closer to Midnapore’s (~10–15 km away) than to Darjeeling’s or Shimla’s. Domain science must be embedded in the analysis.
  • Spatial cloud supports shared resource pooling for organizations with common goals; choice of deployment/service/business models; managed services preventing data loss from outages; lower financial risk; easy to use, scalable, cost-effective, reliable.

Spatial cloud architecture

  • Cloud layers (SaaS, storage-aaS, PaaS, IaaS) host spatial web services: data provisioning (e.g., Web Feature Service, catalog service), processing services, map services, specific catalogues → used by organizations and individuals; organizations want to share spatial data; easier GIS decision-making (integrate latest databases, merge separate systems, exchange information).
  • OGC = Open Geospatial Consortium (makes standards for spatial data); any OGC client can find services in a registry and use feature, map and processing services over spatial databases (e.g., PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Oracle). These services can be instantiated as cloud services.

Mobility analytics and the trajectory cloud

  • Movement has intent (humans, animals, hurricanes, migratory birds). Urban travel time matters; knowing mobility patterns helps reduce congestion, predict travel time, plan buses, waiting places, signals; smart-home sensors track movement (e.g., of the elderly).
  • Data: daily GPS footprints, travel logs, check-ins, mobile-phone activity logs, vehicle/transport data, IoT home sensors.
  • A generic framework for trajectory-trace mining for smart-city applications (ex-PhD work at IIT KGP): model city dynamics, effective storage and computation, learning techniques to extract mobility patterns, recommendation systems. SDI (Spatial Data Infrastructure) built on web services.
  • Spatial trajectory = a trace generated by a moving object in geographic space (series of (x, y, t)); semantic trajectory adds intent/meaning (students stopping at food joints in the evening).
  • Trajectory cloud (“TrasCloud” in the transcript): an end-to-end cloud framework for analysing urban dynamics that enables trip planning, travel-time prediction, ride sharing, and minimizes service waiting and provisioning time for location-based services (food delivery, medical emergency); key to ITS.
    • Pipeline: urban sensing/data acquisition (GPS, road network, traffic info) → trajectory pre-processing → trajectory data modelling (map matching, geo-tagging) → trajectory trace processing (information retrieval, spatio-temporal range queries, trajectory-based query processing).
    • Services: trajectory trace indexing, map matching, query processing.
    • Implemented on Google Cloud Platform: indexing → BigQuery + Cloud SQL; map matching → Compute Engine; query services → Compute Engine + Cloud SQL (also tried on Meghamala).

MCQ traps (12.3)

  • Geospatial data = location + attributes + time.
  • Tobler’s first law: nearer things are more related.
  • Spatiotemporal cloud computing is driven by geospatial sciences and optimized by spatiotemporal principles.
  • OGC = Open Geospatial Consortium (standards); WFS/WMS-type services.
  • Trajectory cloud on GCP used BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Compute Engine.

12.4 Case Study II — Internet of Health Things (IoHT) (L59–L60)

Context

  • A cloud-to-things continuum — cloud, fog, edge, IoT must be viewed as one integrated system, not separate layers (orchestration across layers; aggregation at lower layers also protects privacy of raw data).
  • Cloud: subscription-based, (theoretically) infinitely scalable, ubiquitous — but needs good connectivity and everything travels to the cloud and back (e.g., room-temperature control could be decided by a local switch/router or an aggregate sent upward).
  • Layer roles: cloud — business analytics and intelligence; fog — local network data analysis, reduction, control response, virtualization/standardization; edge — large-volume real-time processing at source, on-premise visualization (industrial PCs, embedded systems, gateways, micro data storage); sensors/controllers — data origin.
  • Cloud limitations: high latency, large data volume, high bandwidth needs (for real-time responses). IoT limitations: processing, storage, power, and no global view (one sensor sees only its corner of a room; a switch/server aggregating 10–20 sensors can compute mean/variance and decide).
  • Benefits of fog/edge: reduced latency (real-time support), less network congestion, reduced cost of execution at the cloud (subscription), better handling of data near sensors (cleaning), location awareness, data/information security.
  • Downsides: edge devices must be smart enough; configuring an edge–fog–cloud infrastructure is much more complicated and the organization must manage it; proper orchestration needed.

Objectives of the case study (IIT KGP M.Tech project)

  1. Design a fog–edge-computing-based health model to reduce latency, network usage and cost incurred at the cloud.
  2. Test the model with the iFogSim simulator (initially developed by IIT Kharagpur and the University of Melbourne, now maintained by Melbourne’s CLOUDS lab; linked with CloudSim).
  3. Develop a customized wearable device to collect health parameters, and implement the model on hardware.
  4. Study dew-based computing and its efficacy. Workflow: conceptualization and modelling → design/implement the fog model → performance evaluation in iFogSim → results → hardware implementation (fabricate a customized body sensor; activity detection with an accelerometer; heart-attack alert — explicitly no medical/clinical implication; demonstration only) → propose a dew-based framework → inferences.

Topology and latency settings (iFogSim)

Level 0 = Cloud → Level 1 = Fog (ISP gateway / area gateway) → Level 2 = Edge (mobile) → Level 3 = IoHT (body sensors). The cloud is far more resourceful (MIPS, RAM, bandwidth); mobiles/edge are less. | Link | Latency (units used in the study) | |—|—| | Body sensor → mobile | 1 | | Mobile → area gateway | 2 | | Area gateway → ISP gateway | 2 | | ISP gateway → cloud | 100 | | Mobile → display | 1 | → the cloud hop dominates latency.

Application modules and placement

Flow: body sensors → client module → data filtering module → data processing module → event handler module → client module → display (alert: normal / visit a doctor), with a confirmatory module (confirms events against a knowledge base; logs data). | Module | Fog–edge-based placement | Cloud-based placement | |—|—|—| | Client module | Mobile (edge) | Mobile | | Data filtering | Area gateway (fog) | Cloud | | Data processing | Area gateway (fog) | Cloud | | Event handler | Area gateway (fog) | Cloud | | Confirmatory module | Cloud | Cloud |

Simulation results (configurations 1–5: increasing users and area gateways)

Metric Cloud-only Fog–edge
Average latency Increases drastically with configuration size ≈ constant, near zero (control-loop modules sit at the area gateway)
Network usage Much higher Much lower
Cost of execution (in cloud) Much higher — only cloud resources incur (subscription) cost; other resources are owned by the organization Much lower
Energy Data-center energy increases as modules shift to the cloud Fog devices take part of the load
Mobile energy Same in both (mobile load unchanged) Same

Caveat: with fog/edge, you manage those layers; with cloud-only, the provider manages everything.

Hardware implementation

  • Customized BP and pulse meter, NodeMCU board, accelerometer, data sent over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth to the mobile (edge) → Raspberry Pi as fog devices → AWS (also in-house Meghamala) as cloud.
  • Activity detection pipeline (accelerometer):
    1. Data extraction: three axes x,y,z → magnitude a=x2+y2+z2​.
    2. 5-point smoothing to reduce induced noise: each value = average of 5 signals — 2 preceding, the signal itself, 2 succeeding: a~i​=5ai−2​+ai−1​+ai​+ai+1​+ai+2​​.
    3. Feature extraction from the filtered signal: minimum amplitude, maximum amplitude, mean amplitude, standard deviation, energy in time domain, energy in frequency domain.
    4. Classifier: k-nearest neighbours (kNN).
    • Worked example: readings 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 → smoothed value at the centre = (2+4+6+8+10)/5 = 6. Magnitude of (3, 4, 0) = 5.
  • Heart-attack alarm: a simple if–then rule on BP/pulse thresholds (e.g., if P > 170 and S ≥ 180 then alarm = true, else false) — demonstration only, no clinical validity.

Dew-based extension

  • Dew computing = on-premise computing whose on-premise computers provide functionality independent of cloud services and also collaborative with them — fully realizing on-premise resources.
  • If the Internet connection breaks, the dew server keeps serving (sensors → dew server → display); the database is synced with the cloud (AWS) when the connection returns — useful when outages are short.

Comparison (lecture table) | Aspect | Cloud | Cloud–fog–edge | With dew | |—|—|—|—| | On-premise resource utilization | Low | Sub-optimal | Optimal | | Connectivity / uptime / bandwidth required | High | Low | Low | | Latency | High | Low | Low | | Processing power & storage | High (≈ infinitely scalable) | Limited | Moderate |

MCQ traps (12.4)

  • In the iFogSim topology, ISP gateway → cloud latency (100) dwarfs the other hops (1–2).
  • Fog placement: filtering, processing, event handling at the area gateway; confirmatory in cloud; client at mobile.
  • Mobile energy stays the same; cloud energy and cost rise in cloud-only; fog latency stays ~constant.
  • 5-point smoothing averages 2 before + itself + 2 after; classifier = kNN.
  • Raspberry Pi = fog; mobile = edge; AWS/Meghamala = cloud.
  • Dew gives optimal on-premise utilization and works during outages.

Week 12 — High-yield takeaways

  1. 5G: multi-Gbps, ~1 ms latency, massive capacity, forward compatible; eMBB (AR/VR) · URLLC (autonomous vehicles, telesurgery, smart grid) · mMTC (massive IoT); 5G–cloud: cloud must meet 5G needs (edge/MEC/fog) and 5G is cloudified via NFV/SDN; edge apps: AR/VR, tactile Internet, ITS, factories, emergency response.
  2. CPS: computing + physical with feedback; Helen Gill (NSF, 2006); intersection not union; intertwined, multi-scale, multi-modal, context-dependent; applications (intervention, precision, dangerous ops, coordination, efficiency, augmentation); CPCC = rapidly build/modify/provision CPS from cloud sensor/processing/control/data services.
  3. Spatial cloud: geospatial = location + attributes + time; >90 % data spatial; Tobler’s law; spatiotemporal cloud computing definition; OGC services; trajectory cloud (indexing, map matching, query) on GCP (BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Compute Engine).
  4. IoHT: levels cloud–fog–edge–IoHT; latencies 1/2/2/100/1; module placement; fog keeps latency ~constant and lowers network use and cloud cost; mobile energy unchanged; hardware (NodeMCU, BP/pulse, accelerometer, Raspberry Pi fog, AWS); magnitude → 5-point smoothing → features → kNN; dew for outages.

Formula Sheet — all numerical tools in the course

Formula Sheet — all numerical tools in the course

Format per formula: Purpose · Expression · Variables · Conditions · Meaning · ⚠️ Likely mistake. Week references point to the detailed notes.

A. SLA and availability (Weeks 3, 5)

A1. Availability (standard / Azure “monthly uptime %”) A(%)=TT−d​×100=(1−Td​)×100

  • T = expected (scheduled) service time in the period (days × service hours/day, or “maximum available minutes”); d = total downtime (sum of outages).
  • Meaning: fraction of scheduled time the service was up.
  • ⚠️ Use scheduled hours (e.g., 12 h × 30 d = 360 h), not 24 h × 30 d, when the SLA says 12 h/day. Convert minutes ↔︎ hours carefully.

A2. Lecture’s KPI form (L11, L21 Problem 1) A=1−uptimedowntime​

  • ⚠️ Slide form uses uptime in the denominator (L21 P1: 1 − 10.75/349.25 = 96.92 %). The standard form above gives 97.01 %. The verdict is usually the same; if options are close, check both.

A3. Allowed downtime for a target availability dmax​=(1−A)T

  • 99.9 % over 30 × 24 h → 0.72 h = 43.2 min; 99.95 % over 360 h → 10.8 min; 99 % over 30 × 24 h → 7.2 h.

A4. Service credit and payable amount Bill=rate×days,Credit=c%×Bill,Payable=Bill−Credit

  • c is chosen from the band containing the measured availability (e.g., < 99.95 % but ≥ 99 % → 10 %; < 99 % → 25 %).
  • L21 P2: $50 × 30 = $1500; A = 97.385 % → 25 % → credit $375 → payable $1125.
  • ⚠️ A lower availability falls in the bigger credit band.

B. Cloud economics (Weeks 3, 5)

B1. Coefficient of variation Cv​=∣μ∣σ​

  • σ = std. deviation of demand, μ = mean demand. Lower Cv​ = smoother demand = better utilization/risk–return.
  • ⚠️ Not variance, not correlation coefficient.

B2. Aggregating n independent identical demands μagg​=nμ,σagg​=n​σ⇒Cvagg​=n​Cv​​

  • 100 workloads → Cv​ falls to 1/10. Perfectly correlated: Cv​ unchanged (σ grows like n). Negatively correlated (X, 1−X): Cv​=0.
  • ⚠️ Factor is 1/n​, not 1/n.

B3. Utility pricing — owning vs cloud U=BC​,BT​=P⋅B⋅T,CT​=∫0T​UBD(t)dt=UBAT Cloud cheaper⟺U<AP​​

  • P = peak demand, A = average demand, B = owned unit cost, C = cloud unit cost, T = period, D(t) = demand.
  • Spiky demand (large P/A) favours cloud; cloud can be pricier per unit (U>1) and still win.
  • ⚠️ U=C/B (cloud ÷ owned), compared with peak ÷ average. Owned cost scales with peak.

B4. Penalty of mis-provisioning Penalty∝∫0T​∣D(t)−R(t)∣dt

  • Flat demand → 0; linear → periodic provisioning OK; exponential D=et with delay tp​ → D−R=(1−e−tp​)et → penalty grows exponentially.
  • L22 P1 (R=D+δD′, δ=π/12): lecture answer 30π/12≈ 7.86 (strict ∫∣D−R∣=70π/12≈18.33).

B5. Direct cost comparison (L22 P2) BT​=PBT,CT​=C∫0T​D(t)dt

  • D=50(1+e−t), P=100, B=120, C=200, T=100: BT​=1.2M, CT​≈1.01M → ratio 0.84 → cloud cheaper.

B6. Core-hour economics (L22 P3) cost/h=years×8760Capex​,per core-h=corescost/h​,per effective h=efficiencycost/h​ Total per effective h (in-house)=ecost/h​+power&cooling/h+mgmt/h

  • ₹6,00,000 over 3 y → ₹22.83/h → ₹1.90 per core-h (12 cores); cloud ₹42/h, 8 cores → ₹5.25 per core-h; effective: 57.08 vs 52.5; totals 85.075 vs 53.5 (ratio 1.59); in-house wins at ≈ 90 % efficiency (break-even ≈ 89.5 %).
  • ⚠️ 3 years = 26,280 h; divide by efficiency (40 % → × 2.5); add power/cooling and management.

C. Reliability and distributed storage (Week 3, 5)

C1. System failure with N components P(system failure)=1−(1−p)N

  • p = per-component failure probability. Approaches 1 as N grows → fault tolerance is necessary.
  • p=0.001,N=1000 → ≈ 0.63. ⚠️ Transcript wording suggests the opposite; trust the formula.

C2. HDFS/GFS blocks and storage blocks per file=⌈block sizefile size​⌉,stored blocks=∑blocks×r

  • Lecture: block 64 MB, r=3; files 64 KB, 65 MB, 127 MB → 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 → 15.
  • ⚠️ Lecture uses 64 MB (Hadoop 1 / GFS); Hadoop 2+ default 128 MB — use the question’s value. A small file still counts as one block.

C3. Dynamo quorum consistency R+W>N

  • N replicas, R read quorum, W write quorum; overlap guarantees the latest write is read. Small W (fast writes) needs large R, and vice versa.
  • ⚠️ Strictly greater: R+W=N is not enough.

D. Parallel computing and MapReduce (Weeks 3, 5)

D1. Parallel efficiency ε=pTp​T1​​(ideal Tp​=T1​/p⇒ε=1)

  • Scalable ⇔ ε stays constant as data and processors grow proportionally.

D2. Word counting (n docs, m words, f occurrences/word/doc, c = time per word read/sent; T1​=nmfc) Split words: ε=p1​Split documents: ε=1+nf2p​1​

  • Split-documents time: Tp​=pn​mfc+2mc. → ≈ 1 when p≪nf; scalable. Split-words is not scalable.

D3. MapReduce efficiency (uniprocessor time wD, map output σD, c = I/O per word) εMR​=1+w2cσ​1​

  • Independent of P (scalable); worse with larger map output σ or I/O cost c.

D4. Combining partial averages (L23) xˉ=∑i​ni​∑i​xˉi​ni​​

  • Mappers emit (avg, count) or (sum, count). {10,20},{30,40},{50} → (15·2 + 35·2 + 50·1)/5 = 30. ⚠️ Average of averages (33.3) is wrong.

E. VM migration (Weeks 9–10)

E1. Cold (non-live) migration Tmig​=RVm​​,Tdown​≈Tmig​

E2. Pre-copy live migration r=RP⋅D​,Tj​=rjRVm​​ Tmig​=RVm​​⋅1−r1−rn+1​+Tres​,Tdown​=rnRVm​​+Tres​ n=min(⌈logr​Vm​Vth​​⌉, Nmax​)

  • Vm​ = VM memory, R = transmission rate, P = page size, D = pages dirtied/s, Vth​ = stop threshold, Tres​ = resume time.
  • Needs r<1 to converge. Example: 1024 MB, 100 MB/s, r=0.2, n=3, Tres​=0.1 s → Tmig​≈12.88 s, Tdown​≈0.18 s (cold: 10.24 s each).
  • ⚠️ Downtime is only the last term; live migration increases total time but reduces downtime.

E3. Multiple VMs

  • Parallel: each VM gets ≈ R/m; downtime ≈ stop-and-copy time of one VM (at R/m) + resume.
  • Serial: first VM at full R; others suspended when it enters stop-and-copy; downtime = its stop-copy + migration of the other m−1 + resume.

F. Energy and green cloud (Weeks 5, 8, 11)

F1. Consolidation power (L24 example) Ptotal​=on nodes∑​P(load)

  • Idle 105 W, full (8 VMs) 170 W, 2 VMs ≈ 138 W: 8 VMs on 1 node + 3 idle = 485 W; spread 2/node = 552 W; 1 node with 3 off = 170 W.

F2. Linear server power model (standard clarification; real curve is non-linear/concave) P(u)=Pidle​+(Pmax​−Pidle​)u

  • Idle server ≈ 66 % of peak (L37) → consolidation pays.

F3. Switch power (L37) Pswitch​=Pchassis​+nlc​Plinecard​+r∑​nports,r​Pr​

  • Shares: chassis ≈ 36 %, line cards ≈ 43 %, port transceivers ≈ 11 %.

F4. PUE and DCiE (standard definitions) PUE=IT equipment powerTotal facility power​ (≥1),DCiE=PUE1​×100%

  • IT = 40 % of total → PUE = 2.5. ⚠️ Not IT ÷ total.

F5. Energy breakdowns (know which one is asked)

  • Whole data center (L37): cooling 45 %, IT 40 %, power distribution 15 %.
  • By component (L55): processor 45 %, cooling 20 %, memory 15 %, storage 10 %, network 10 %.

G. Mobile cloud computing — offloading (Week 7)

Esaved​=Pc​MC​−Pi​SC​−Ptr​BD​=MC​(Pc​−FPi​​)−Ptr​BD​,S=FM

  • Pc​,Pi​,Ptr​ = mobile power when computing/idle/transmitting; C = instructions; M,S = mobile/cloud speeds; F = speed-up; D = data; B = bandwidth.
  • Offload iff Esaved​>0 → large C, small D, large F, high B.
  • Example: C/M=2 s, Pc​=1, Pi​=0.2, F=20, Ptr​=1.5, D/B=1 s → 0.48 J saved.
  • ⚠️ The idle term uses cloud time C/S; the transmit term uses D/B.

H. Sensor/IoHT signal processing (Week 12)

a=x2+y2+z2​,a~i​=5ai−2​+ai−1​+ai​+ai+1​+ai+2​​

  • Accelerometer magnitude, then 5-point smoothing → features (min/max/mean amplitude, standard deviation, time- and frequency-domain energy) → kNN.

I. Quick unit conversions

  • 1 day = 1440 min; 30-day month = 720 h = 43,200 min; 1 year = 8760 h.
  • 1 GB = 1024 MB (HDFS/memory convention); 1 Gbps ≈ 125 MB/s (bits vs bytes!).
  • Percent ↔︎ fraction: 99.95 % = 0.9995 → unavailability 0.0005.

Classification & Comparison Sheet

Compact tables of every categorization the lectures emphasize. Rows reflect the lectures’ own classifications (⚠️ marks where today’s reality differs).

Item Members

Paradigm Key definition Types/notes

Grid Harness unused cycles; single system image; dependable, consistent, pervasive, inexpensive access Computational, data, collaborative, network, utility grids; analogy: power grid

5. Virtualization

Full (1st gen) Para (2nd gen) Hardware-assisted (3rd gen)
Technique Binary translation; all HW emulated Cooperative; modified guest (ring 1); special API CPU extensions Intel VT / AMD-V; guest at ring 0
Examples VMware, Microsoft; QEMU, Bochs VMware, Xen VMware, Xen on aware HW
Pro / Con Portable / slow Fast / kernel recompiled Unmodified OS / less portable, speed–flexibility issues
